News.title: Blood pressure drug urgently recalled due to 'health consequences' risk
News.content:
Blood pressure drug urgently recalled due to 'health consequences' risk

The FDA have urgently recalled a specific batch of blood pressure drugs as they may lead to 'temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences'

View 2 Images The blood pressure drug has been recalled (Image: Getty Images)

A drug used to treat high blood pressure is being urgently recalled as it could cause 'health consequences'.

‌



The valsartan drug was made by Novartis under the brand name Diovan and has been recalled as it does not meet dissolution specifications.

‌



The drug's effectiveness has therefore been impacted with the potential risk of harmful consequences to anybody who takes it.

‌



View 2 Images The drugs may cause 'health consequences' (Image: Getty)

Diovan is an angiotensin II receptor blocker used to treat hypertension and heart failure.

Patients may also be prescribed the drug after suffering a heart attack.

‌



The US Food and Drug Administration has determined the notice as a Class II recall, which means exposure to the drug may lead to “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.”

The impact is expected to stop once patients stop taking the drug, however they may cause harm and anybody who has their hands on the batch of drugs is urged to chuck them out.

The batch that is being recalled has AV5913C on the packaging and include packages of 90 160-mg tablets with an expiration date of June 2027.

‌



The drug was manufactured by Pantheon Manufacturing Services in Greenville, North Carolina, and distributed by Novartis Pharmaceutical Corp. in Hanover, New Jersey.

The FDA noted that the tablets have been distributed nationwide in the US.

Novartis made the recall on August 4.

‌



The recall comes as the UK is also facing difficulties regarding blood pressure drugs, as the nation faces a 'serious shortage'.

A review carried out by MediWatch on August 4 noted that there is a shortage issue of Ramipril 1.25mg capsules across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

A Serious Shortage Protocol was issued by the Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) on April 22 and then extended to beyond May 29.

Article continues below

This protocol limits community pharmacies to dispensing a maximum of one month's supply per prescription, even for those who usually have prescriptions for two to three months.

News.title: Teenager dead and 211 people evacuated from ferry fire in Bali as five still missing
News.content:
Teenager dead and 211 people evacuated from ferry fire in Bali as five still missing

Five people are still believed to be missing at sea after a ferry fire near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali saw 211 people evacuated and one teenager dead

View 3 Images The National Transportation Safety Committee investigators were determining the cause of the fire. (Image: BASARNAS via AP)

Crews rescued 211 people and recovered the body of a teenage passenger from a ferry that caught fire in rough seas on Wednesday.

‌



The tragic incident happened near the Indonesian tourist island of Bali, authorities said. Videos released by the National Search and Rescue Agency showed people wearing life jackets crowding an inflatable life raft in choppy waters during a rescue operation at sea, as thick black smoke billows from the ferry.

‌



The agency said that as of early Thursday, rescuers evacuated 211 people from the burned vessel, including seven foreign tourists, and recovered the body of a 19-year-old Indonesian woman.

‌



View 3 Images The ferry was transporting 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles. (Image: BASARNAS via AP)

Five homes completely destroyed as fire rips through residential street in Caerphilly borough READ MORE :

The Putri Yasmin ferry was traveling from Bali to the neighboring island of Lombok in West Nusa Tenggara province when the fire broke out at about 4:15 a.m. Wednesday. The ferry was also transporting 44 vehicles and 53 motorcycles.

The Search and Rescue Office in Mataram, the capital of West Nusa Tenggara province, received an emergency report almost half an hour later and immediately deployed personnel and rescue vessels.

‌



“Our top priority is the safety of all passengers and crew members,” said Muhammad Hariyadi, who heads the Mataram Search and Rescue Office.

The search was continuing Thursday. Relatives who gathered in a post command center in the port reported at least five of their family members still unaccounted for. Their names were posted at the center as missing.

View 3 Images The heat forced some passengers to jump into the sea (Image: BASARNAS via AP)

‌



It is common in Indonesia for the number of passengers to differ from the manifest, but authorities have not said why the number of people evacuated was so much greater. Transportation Minister Dudy Purwagandhi said officials will look into the discrepancy.

“The findings will be thoroughly reviewed as part of the ministry’s evaluation,” Purwagandhi said. “This is a serious issue that will be thoroughly investigated.”

He said the National Transportation Safety Committee investigators were determining the cause of the fire.

‌



Syamsurizal, head of the Lembar Port Authority in Lombok, said that survivors told authorities the blaze appeared to have started in a cargo truck before quickly spreading through the ferry. The heat forced some passengers to jump into the sea, he said.

“The response operation is ongoing, and authorities are continuing to account for all victims,” said Syamsurizal, who like many Indonesians uses a single name. He said at least two injured passengers were rushed to a nearby hospital.

Hariyadi said the rescue effort was supported by six vessels, a helicopter, two inflatable boats and two private yachts. He said rough seas with waves reported as high as 4 meters (13 feet) complicated rescue efforts.

Article continues below

The 62-meter (203-foot) ferry, built in Japan in 1992, can carry up to 220 passengers and 55 vehicles. It is primarily used to transport travelers and cargo between the Indonesian islands of Bali and Lombok, a journey that typically takes four to five hours.

Indonesia is an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands where ferries are a common method of travel. Disasters occur regularly, with weak safety enforcement often blamed.

News.title: Major UK train stations to close for weeks in £70million upgrade
News.content:
Major UK train stations to close for weeks in £70million upgrade

Major projects and will be carried out between September 19 and October 4 - including the completion of a new £70million train station - and there will be some disruption as a result

View 3 Images The Huddersfield and Slaithwaite train stations will close for two weeks (Image: Getty)

Two West Yorkshire train stations will close for weeks to allow for major upgrades.

‌



The Huddersfield and Slaithwaite train stations will close for two weeks from mid-September.

‌



Major projects will be carried out between September 19 and October 4 - including the completion of the new £70million Huddersfield train station.

‌



View 3 Images Huddersfield train station is getting a facelift (Image: Getty Images)

The subway at Huddersfield station will be extended to platforms 4 and 5. These platforms are also getting upgrades to be able to be accommodate longer trains.

The station roof is also getting repaired. A separate, 38-day closure is also planned for later in the year.

‌



The closure will be in place from Christmas Eve to complete Huddersfield station.

The entire project is part of the wider Transpennine Route Upgrade. The upgrade is focused on modernising the railway between Manchester, Huddersfield, Leeds and York.

"While we know there will be some disruption while this work takes place, these upgrades are essential to delivering the more reliable, accessible and higher-capacity railway that customers deserve," said Sophie Leishman, Transpennine Route Upgrade sponsor.

‌



"We're making real progress across the route, from the redevelopment of Huddersfield station to improvements that will support longer trains, better performance and future electrification."

View 3 Images The subway at Huddersfield station will be extended to platforms 4 and 5 (Image: Getty)

Liam O’Shaughnessy, Transpennine Route Upgrade Programme Delivery Lead at Northern, said: "There will be disruption to Northern and other operators’ services during these works, with services amended and some trains replaced with buses.

Article continues below

"We strongly advise all customers to check before they travel and use National Rail Enquiries to plan their journeys."

News.title: Nurses collapse and suffer seizures on hot wards 'not fit for humans', union warns
News.content:
Nurses collapse and suffer seizures on hot wards 'not fit for humans', union warns

The Royal College of Nursing became the latest union to warn of unsafe working conditions in extreme heat for many staff members in hospital wards and care homes

View 5 Images Some nurses have reported seizures and “dripping with sweat from head to toe” (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Nurses across England are collapsing at work and even suffering seizures as they are forced to care for patients in extreme heat, The Royal College of Nursing has said.

‌



Two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June led to more than 2,800 excess deaths across the country. An amber warning for heat across large parts of England will come into force again on Thursday morning, with temperatures forecast to reach 36C or potentially higher.

‌



Train passengers on some networks are being warned by rail operators to only travel if the journey is vital, saying services are likely to be disrupted because of the weather. The Royal College of Nursing became the latest union to warn of unsafe working conditions for many members in hospital wards and care homes.

‌



As temperatures continue to soar some nurses have reported seizures and “dripping with sweat from head to toe” as hospitals have been described as “unbearably hot” and “not fit for humans”.

View 5 Images The Royal College of Nursing has warned about staff working in extreem heat (Image: PA)

RCN chief executive and general secretary Professor Nicola Ranger said: “When nursing staff are collapsing, feeling dizzy, sick or even being admitted to the very hospitals they work in because their workplaces cannot handle the heat, it shows just how badly they are being failed.”

‌



The RCN compiled a series of testimonies to its advice line to paint a picture of conditions facing nurses during heatwaves, including: – A nurse in England reported collapsing from dehydration after working a long shift on a ward with no ventilation. They were admitted to the same organisation where they worked. – Pregnant nurses said the temperatures they were forced to work in impacted their health, while two nurses with pre-existing conditions reported seizures due to excessive heat. – One nurse told the RCN their workplace was “not fit for humans” while another described their working environment as “unbearably hot”. – Others reported broken air conditioning, fans or ventilation, with some reporting that they are unable to even open windows. – Multiple nurses reported working in rooms where the temperature was in excess of 30C, with one saying they were forced to work in a place which was 36C. – A nurse working in an NHS cancer service in England reported feeling “nauseous, dizzy and faint” after temperatures exceeded 33C. – A nurse working in a community health centre in England said: “It gets to the point you dread going to work, especially when wearing PPE (personal protective equipment) and providing patient care. We drip with sweat from head to toe.” – Others expressed concern for patients, with one saying the heat impacted surgical patients’ recovery while another said: “We have elderly patients in our clinic, who we are increasingly worried about. We have got to the end of our tether with no support from our immediate seniors.”

View 5 Images It is set to reach 36C in some parts of the UK today (Image: PA)

Prof Ranger said: “These testimonies should be a wake-up call. Swathes of the NHS and social care estate are in disrepair following decades of underinvestment and are utterly unprepared for extreme temperatures. “It’s becoming an impossible and inhumane place to work or receive care, with vulnerable patients, including the elderly and those recovering from surgery, receiving care in temperatures that risk making them sicker. It’s unacceptable. “Employers must also abide by their legal duties to make workplaces safe, by mitigating the risks to staff from the heat. This includes installing air conditioning, improving ventilation, ensuring water and heat-appropriate uniforms are available and guaranteeing risk assessments are a core part of business planning, especially for pregnant or vulnerable workers. “We also need specific actions to protect those working in the community, who often are travelling in hot cars, with poor access to parking and left to walk long distances carrying heavy bags to meet patients.”

‌



View 5 Images Hospitals can be hot and stuff but in 36C almost any building would be (Image: Jeff Moore/PA Wire)

Meanwhile Matthew Hopkins, director of the NHS Alliance ambulance and acute network, said NHS organisations were pushing for increased capital money from the Government to deal with maintenance of hospital buildings. Speaking on the NHS Alliance’s Health on the Line podcast, he said: “I think for a lot of our members that are running hospitals that are very old and where infrastructure’s really under pressure, many of those hospitals are carrying significant levels of backlog maintenance. “Some of our members tell us that that totals, in some cases, more than £100 million worth of cost. “And inevitably, the boards of those organisations will be regularly discussing and focusing on the risk management associated with the trade-offs that they’re going to have to be dealing with, you know, fixing a roof of a building to make it safe and watertight for winter versus installing air conditioning and potentially the impact on the electrical infrastructure.”

Ruth Wilkinson, head of policy and public affairs at the Institution of Occupational Safety and Health, has outlined proactive steps that employers can take to support their staff better.

‌



She said: “Indoor workers, like nurses, can find it just as challenging to work in extreme heat as outdoor workers. This can be due to poor ventilation, lack of cooling infrastructure, and outdated building designs that leave them to cope in stifling conditions.

“Heat stress can make it harder for people to work safely and effectively. When it’s too hot, the body has to work harder to stay cool, which can lead to health problems like dehydration, heat exhaustion, or even heat stroke. Employers can take proactive steps to manage these risks and support workers. These can include adjusting work hours, providing cooling stations, and encouraging hydration. It is also recommended that employers analyse the impact of heat stress on operational continuity and supply chain management.”

View 5 Images Yvette Cooper (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/PA Wire)

Article continues below

Health and Social Care Secretary Yvette Cooper said: “The extreme heat is hitting public health and our NHS. Across the NHS and social care, staff are doing a remarkable job to respond to rising A&E attendances and ambulance call-outs, heat problems amongst the elderly and difficult working conditions. I want to thank them for all their work. “But I have also been clear that the NHS now needs to plan for summer pressures in the way we currently plan for winter pressures. That includes making sure buildings are more resilient in these new extreme heat conditions as well as responding to additional patient needs.”

News.title: Zacatlan car crash: 'Several injured' during festival in Mexico's 'magic town' in Puebla
News.content:
Zacatlan car crash: 'Several injured' during festival in Mexico's 'magic town' in Puebla

Pedestrians were casually walking when a blue sedan sped into the crowd, injuring multiple people, with emergency services rushing to the scene.

View 3 Images

Horror footage shows the moment a car rammed into pedestrians at a festival in Mexico.

‌



Videos of the incident on Wednesday, August 12, show people walking casually through a tourist corridor in Zacatlán when a blue sedan speeds into them.

‌



Screams can be heard as people scatter. The vehicle is stopped when it slammed into what appears to be a concrete pillar.

‌



The Zacatlán City Council has said there are no fatalities.

View 3 Images The vehicle is stopped when it slammed into what appears to be a concrete pillar (Image: X)

A local news outlet has reported that the driver was arrested and several people attending the Gran Feria de la Manzana (Great Apple Fair) were injured,

‌



The car burst in from the Hotel Zacatlán area until crashing to one side of the Apple Pavilion, according to reports.

Red Cross paramedics are on the scene.

View 3 Images Emergency responders are on the scene (Image: X)

‌



Mayor of Zacatlán, Bety Sánchez, wrote in a post on X: "Between 5:00 and 5:30 p.m., a regrettable incident occurred, in which a blue Chevrolet-brand vehicle entered Juárez Pedestrian Mall and unfortunately struck several people.

"We immediately activated the emergency response protocols."

She said that the vehicle is in the custody and the driver has been detained.

Article continues below

"He appears to have some health issue that may have been the cause that triggered this incident, but acting responsibly and in accordance with regulations, we need the necessary expert examinations to be conducted to confirm or rule out this version," she said.

This is a breaking story and updates will follow...

News.title: 'Swamped' GP works 12-hour days without a break as doctors admit they struggle to care properly for patients
News.content:
'Swamped' GP works 12-hour days without a break as doctors admit they struggle to care properly for patients

General Medical Council reveals job satisfaction is falling among UK doctors while six in ten GPs admit they cannot provide 'sufficient care' at least once a week

View 4 Images Dr Tamara Keith tells how patients demand has surged

Doctors have admitted they struggle to care properly for patients, as one GP told the Mirror they are “swamped”.

‌



The General Medical Council says workload pressures explain why GPs, in particular, are struggling to provide "sufficient care" at least once a week. The regulator’s poll of more than 4,600 doctors found 41% said they found it hard to provide patients with sufficient care weekly, rising to 60% among GPs and 51% among recently qualified doctors.

‌



The annual survey found overall job satisfaction declined slightly in 2025, returning to levels last seen in 2023. The proportion of doctors considering leaving the profession permanently for reasons other than retirement rose to 22% from 19% in 2024.

‌



View 4 Images Stressed doctor in hospital (stock) (Image: Getty Images/Blend Images)

Heart attacks warning as pharmacists restricted from offering free blood pressure checks READ MORE :

NHS symptoms of deadly condition that could be mistaken for suntan READ MORE :

Charlie Massey, GMC chief executive, said: "Patients rightly expect good care from their doctors, and doctors are clear about what good care looks like. Yet many tell us that providing that level of care is difficult.

"It is not due to a lack of professionalism or commitment, but because of the pressures in their working environment. However committed doctors may be, the quality of care they can provide is shaped by the conditions in which they work."

‌



GP Tamara Keith runs a practice in Bottisham, Cambs, and is working with campaign group Rebuild General Practice. She said: “Workloads have hugely increased. I’m a partner so I have to stay until the work is done. It’s relentless. We need more GPs and bigger practice buildings to see more appointments because we are swamped.”

Tamara blames falling morale on government rule changes brought in across England this year to end the “8am scramble” for appointments via phone lines. Surgeries must now remain open to online requests for appointments throughout the working day from 8am to 6.30pm. Previously practices could suspend online bookings when all slots were filled and phone lines could remain engaged.

View 4 Images Dr Tamara Keith who is a GP partner near Cambridge (Image: Supplied)

‌



Tamara, 42, told the Mirror: “When I start on Monday I will have between 85 to 100 requests to triage and I only have 15 to 20 slots that day. I have to see the remaining three quarters myself either in person or over the phone.

"I will work solidly from 7am to 7pm and I won’t have a lunch break. It’s just not manageable. We understand this was designed for the benefit of patients but it’s got to be safe. We are not endlessly staffed so not being able to say ‘we are full today’ is not safe.

“The ‘morale injury’ comes because we are not able to provide the care we want to give or that we used to give. When I tell my friends who don’t work in medicine about my day they just can’t believe it.”

‌



A UK breakdown showed that in England and Northern Ireland four in ten doctors cannot provide the level of care they would like. However in Wales and Scotland the figure was almost 50%. Devolved governments are responsible for the NHS in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Dr Amit Kochhar, representative chair at the British Medical Association, said: "This report makes for concerning reading. The limited gains in job satisfaction for doctors over the last two years have been wiped out.”

Falling job satisfaction was linked to "clear emotional strains for doctors, including guilt, frustration, a reduced sense of purpose, and feelings of moral injury", the report said. Some 53% of doctors said delays to providing care, treatment or tests was the main barrier to patient care in the last year, rising to 73% among GPs.

‌



View 4 Images Stressed GP (stock) (Image: Alamy)

The Royal College of GPs (RCGP) said there were now on average 2,300 patients for every qualified full-time equivalent GP in England - a 13% increase since 2015. Over the last decade more senior GPs have taken early retirement due to unmanageable workloads.

Professor Victoria Tzortziou Brown, RCGP president and a family doctor in Tower Hamlets, East London, said: “This is not about a lack of commitment or professionalism, but whether GPs have the time and capacity they need to provide the standard of care our patients deserve.

‌



“It’s particularly concerning to hear that so many GPs are considering leaving the profession earlier than planned. Our workload is increasing in both volume and complexity, we don’t have enough GPs to deliver the care our patients need and general practice's share of NHS funding is at its lowest in a decade.

“These pressures are taking their toll, and it will be patients who bear the brunt. GPs and our teams deliver the vast majority of NHS patient contacts, and in doing so we alleviate pressure across the health service, keeping it cost-effective and sustainable.”

A new question added for the 2025 poll asked about poor co-ordination between GPs and hospitals. Only one in five doctors said co-ordination between primary and secondary care is currently effective.

Article continues below

The Department of Health and Social Care was approached for comment.

News.title: Two killed in helicopter crash as homes evacuated and incident sparks wildfire
News.content:
Two killed in helicopter crash as homes evacuated and incident sparks wildfire

The crash killed both people on board the Army Apache helicopter and sparked a wildfire that forced several homes to be evacuated - no structures were damaged in the crash

View 3 Images The crash caused a wildfire (Image: Cliff Coleman)

Both people on board a military helicopter have died after it crashed in a central Texas field.

‌



The Army Apache helicopter crash on Wednesday, August 13 then sparked a wildfire that forced several homes to be evacuated.

‌



The chopper crashed while on a routine training flight, according to reports.

‌



The AH-64 Apache attack helicopter set-up is such that crew sits behind each other. The pilot is in the rear and the co-pilot gunner in the front position.

No cause of the crash was immediately announced.

View 3 Images A AH-64 Apache attack helicopter has crashed in Texas (file image) (Image: Getty)

‌



Nearby Fort Hood's criminal investigation division is leading the crash investigation.

Spokesman for the Bell County Sheriff’s office, Cliff Coleman, said that the helicopter did not hit any homes or other structures when it crashed.

"You could tell it was a violent crash," he said.

‌



Photographs from the scene showed firefighters walking around a charred field as plumes of dark smoke rose from flames still burning in the wreckage.

View 3 Images A tanker aircraft dumps fire retardant on a field after the crash (Image: AP)

"Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts," said Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general.

‌



"Our thoughts are with the crew and their families as we await further information."

Fort Hood is a massive base used to train and deploy heavy forces. Its rolling, arid terrain around the base provides an ideal training ground, the Army says.

The crash on Wednesday is not the first instance in which military personnel have died in Fort Hood.

Article continues below

Four soldiers were killed when a Black Hawk helicopter crashed during a training exercise in November 2015.

In 2016, Nine Fort Hood soldiers died when a rain-swollen creek swept their vehicle into rushing waters.

News.title: Solar eclipse wows UK and Europe in once-in-a-generation display - dramatic images
News.content:
The first near-total solar eclipse visible from the UK since 1999 has given skygazers a night to remember with a total eclipse then wowing Spain and Portugal

A once-in-a-generation solar eclipse has stunned skygazers across the UK and Europe as pictures and video emerge of the spectacular event at its peak.

The celestial show saw the Moon slide in front of the Sun in the UK's first near-total solar eclipse in more than half a century. In Europe a spectacular total eclipse drew massive crowds in Spain and Portugal.

Van Sabellina, 31, from Truro, was among those watching the eclipse at Land's End in Cornwall - one of the places that saw the highest percentage of the Sun blocked out.

She said: "It was amazing - once in a lifetime. We were very lucky with the weather and being able to witness it in Land’s End was just spectacular. It was a bit eerie - you feel the change in temperature from hot to refreshing and cold."

Kim Rebecca, 26, watched the eclipse from Greenwich Park, south east London, and said it was "an amazing phenomenon". She said: "It is still hot but it is noticeably cooler than it was.

"You would normally think it would be quieter when it happened but, maybe because it is south east London, there was champagne corks popping."

The next eclipse in the UK is coming in August next year - you can read our complete list of eclipses that will be visible in the coming years here.

News.title: Once-in-a-generation solar eclipse wows millions in UK and Europe
News.content:
The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.

Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse, which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.

Large crowds at viewing sites across the UK and Europe reacted with gasps and cheers, with astronomy enthusiasts saying it served as a reminder of how "amazing" the universe is.

News.title: Temperatures to soar to 38C as amber extreme heat warning comes into force
News.content:
A rare amber weather warning for extreme heat will come into effect across a large swathe of the UK on Thursday, with temperatures set to soar as high as 38C (100F).

Thursday will mark the peak of the UK's fifth widespread heatwave this year, with temperatures to be in the mid-30s Celsius across most of the warning area.

Amber heat health alerts, external, which warn of significant impacts to health and social care services, are already in force for the entirety of England until 21:00 BST on Friday.

The searing heat could also lead to power cuts, rail and air travel delays, and cause serious health impacts such as dehydration and heat exhaustion.

News.title: Students wait for A-level, T-level and BTec results
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland will receive A-level, T-level and BTec results on Thursday morning.

Another record number of students are expected to find out they have secured a place at their first choice of university.

The cost of going to university has been in the spotlight this year, with mounting pressure on the government to reform student loan repayments, and there has been a renewed focus on technical education under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

But the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents more than 140 vice-chancellors, urged students to not "let politicians make your decision for you".

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer.

Around 250,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications are also expected to be released to students in England, including BTec National, Cambridge Technical, Cambridge Advanced National and T-level results.

AS-levels, which will count towards students' final A-level results next summer in Wales and Northern Ireland, will also be released.

This year, the pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board.

And last year, the proportion of students getting top A-level results reached a record high, with 28.3% of all grades across England, Wales and Northern Ireland marked at A* or A.

News.title: ICE plans to equip agents with gloves that can deliver electric shocks
News.content:
Unlike a taser, which uses sharp barbs in the skin to deliver a shock of up to 50,000 volts, the gloves do not complete an electrical circuit inside the body.

The gloves instead deliver a sharp shock to convince a subject to comply using "pain deterrence", says Lt Butch Gallion, an administrator at Hawkins County jail in Tennessee.

"We may or may not deploy them. It just depends on how they act. When you push the button to turn them on there's a light that displays. The inmates understand that light, and often just seeing the light brings compliance," he says.

The shocks can only be delivered when they contact skin, allowing an officer to touch a subject's clothing, and then move to the skin â typically the wrist or elbow - if they begin to fight.

If they become combative, he continues, "then you can apply the gloves to an area that the skin is exposed. And it's an instant complier for me".

According to the DHS note, GLOVE would be used by officers and agents in Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), which targets transnational criminal organisations, and Enforcement Removal Operations (ERO), which is responsible for arresting, detaining and deporting people who violate immigration laws in the US.

Some law enforcement agencies are already using the gloves but it's believed that the planned ICE purchase would be the largest from Compliant Technologies to date.

Civil rights groups, including the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), have expressed alarm about law enforcement using them.

"ICE spent the last year showing this country that they are willing to disregard the law and are too quick to use force, with devastating and at times fatal consequences for citizens and noncitizens alike," said Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU.

Federal immigration agents have been criticised in the wake of fatalities that have occurred during enforcement operations.

Recent incidents include the fatal shooting of Mexican national Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas, while Colombian national Johan SebastiÃ¡n DurÃ¡n Guerrero was killed during an immigration enforcement operation in Maine.

ICE has also been under pressure to deliver President Donald Trump's deportation agenda, which includes meeting a daily target of arrests.

"Now they [ICE] might be equipped with a device that allows them to deliver an electric shock with their hands by pushing a small button, in a move that might be imperceptible to those watching," Borchetta said.

"Giving immigration agents a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability."

With reporting by Max Matza

News.title: GB's Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold on home track
News.content:
On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.

A full-circle moment, completed by writing his name in history.

More than two decades after stepping foot inside Alexander Stadium for the first time aged nine, Hudson-Smith delivered Great Britain's latest gold in Birmingham to become the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships.

The 31-year-old celebrated the third European 400m title of his illustrious career by making his way into the crowd and placing a hand on the banner bearing his name.

Moments before, Hudson-Smith had stormed down the home straight, just as he had countless times before as a member of local club Birchfield Harriers.

This time, though, the Olympic and world silver medallist did so to rapturous cheers inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.

With his eighth podium at the championships, Hudson-Smith equalled French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally - with the relays still to come.

"Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," he told BBC Sport.

"Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home. I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!

"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplants
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: Burnham urges shops not to sell disposable BBQs over wildfire risks
News.content:
Andy Burnham has urged shops to stop selling disposable barbecues amid increased wildfire risk driven by this summer's droughts.

The prime minister said he was urging "all retailers big and small" to adhere to voluntary guidance to suspend sales during extreme heat.

He added that in the "longer term" the government would look at potentially banning the single-use grills during summer months.

It comes after a potential ban was discussed at an emergency Cobra meeting on the government's response to record temperatures.

A number of large retailers and supermarkets have voluntarily stopped selling the devices under a framework, external agreed in 2023 between fire chiefs and the British Retail Consortium (BRC).

This says that retailers should suspend sales once an extreme heat event has been declared as imminent, or in response to "reasonable, evidence based" requests from local councils.

Earlier, Burnham told reporters single-use grills had been behind a number of recent blazes and people should not be using them "at this moment in time".

"We do want people to take the greatest possible care when they are out in the countryside, both in terms of cigarettes, but also those temporary barbecues that we know are causing risk of fires."

After the Cobra meeting, Burnham said: "We would say to retailers do not put disposable barbecues on sale at this moment in time."

Nearly three-quarters of England and all of Wales have been officially declared in drought, creating conditions rife for fire to spread.

The Met Office has issued a rare amber extreme heat warning for Thursday, with temperatures peaking in the mid-to-high 30s across the Midlands and south-east of England, and a high of 38C possible.

News.title: First 100% British chocolate bar made since 1932
News.content:
A chocolate bar has been made using entirely British ingredients for the first time in nearly a century, with cocoa from not Brazil or Bali, but Berkshire.

Created at the University of Reading, it was named the Reading 100 Chocolate Bar to mark the university's 100th anniversary.

It is the first of its kind since 1932, when Rowntree's gifted a six-year-old Princess Elizabeth the only other bar of UK-grown chocolate ever made.

Food security master's student Maha Khan created the chocolate bar by harvesting, fermenting and processing the Reading-grown cocoa.

While the UK's chocolate market is worth Â£10.4bn, it is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.

Maha told the Today programme she made the bar to highlight the challenges facing the cocoa growing industry.

She said: "It is incredible that we can make 100% British chocolate â but in the context of climate change, pests and diseases, there are estimates that 30 to 40% is lost.

"And we've seen with these heatwaves, climate change, these problems and challenges are only going to get exacerbated."

News.title: I've been fighting wildfires while I wait for my A-level results
News.content:
An 18-year-old firefighter who combined his A-levels with responding to emergency calls is among thousands of students getting results on Thursday morning.

Bobi Jones from Newcastle Emlyn in Carmarthenshire said he felt "quite relaxed" about his grades after having "plenty on my plate" responding to recent wildfires.

As well as A-levels, results for AS, BTec and other vocational qualifications will also be published, with many students hoping to progress to university.

A-level grades can be shared with students from 08:00 BST but arrangements vary depending on the school or college.

Bobi is waiting for results for A-level business and sport, as well as the Welsh Baccalaureate qualification.

He said his school, Ysgol Bro Teifi, had been "very flexible", with teachers allowing him to leave class when his work alarm went off as long as he caught up with schoolwork afterwards.

"The past few months have been very busy with exams and also the fire brigade. We've been really busy with fires and wildfires," he said.

Fortunately the problem has not been as serious as in some areas, but Bobi has been regularly responding to "a few patches of grass going up on fire and just spreading very fast".

He is now planning to take on an apprenticeship with a local electrician which he will combine with on-call shifts for Mid and West Wales Fire and Rescue Service.

Last year, the proportion of A* grades rose slightly to 10.5%, while 29.5% of results were A or A* which was lower than in 2024.

Data shows 32.8% of Welsh 18-year-olds had applied for university places by the end of June - slightly up on last year but lower than figures for other UK nations.

News.title: Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions
News.content:
Scottish Labour leadership contenders have warned about the dangers of internal feuds and briefings at their first party hustings in Glasgow.

Monica Lennon, Joe Fagan and Michael Marra made their cases to succeed Anas Sarwar as they pitched to rebuild Scottish Labour after May's crushing electoral defeat.

Those attending the hour-long event were met by a handful of pro-Palestine protesters, whose shouts were heard during the first part of the event.

All three candidates promised to change, rebuild and unite the party following its worst Holyrood election defeat since devolution.

News.title: New Forest wildfire continues as temperatures rise
News.content:
Firefighters on the fourth day of battling a wildfire in the New Forest are facing "challenging" weather conditions with temperatures set to rise again

The blaze began on Sunday 9 August when a van caught fire on the A31, with 23 drivers abandoning their vehicles as the fire took hold.

Hampshire & Isle of Wight Fire and Rescue Service (HIWFRS) said crews had implemented fire breaks and had a 'good hold' of the perimeter of the fire, while changing wind conditions were proving challenging.

National Highways said repairs to the A31 were not expected to be begin until Friday 14 August at the earliest.

News.title: Green councillor charged with assaults
News.content:
A Birmingham Green Party city councillor has been charged with attacking a member of the public, three police officers and a member of police staff.

Siobhan Harper-Nunes, 66, was arrested on suspicion of assault after police were called to the junction of Monument Road and Hagley Road in the city, at about 17:00 BST on Thursday.

Harper-Nunes, of Monument Road, was charged on Friday.

West Midlands Police said that she was arrested again at Monument Road on Wednesday morning on suspicion of harassment.

She remained in custody while inquiries continued, police said.

Harper-Nunes will appear at Birmingham Magistrates' Court on 10 September on the assault charges, the force said.

The councillor was elected in May to represent the Ladywood ward for the city council.

She previously stood as the Green Party's candidate for West Midlands mayor in the 2024 election.

The Birmingham Green Party has been approached for comment.

News.title: Victim of fatal Clapham shooting named
News.content:
A man who was shot dead in south-west London has been named by police as Auguste-Marie Bile-aka Amoa.

Officers and paramedics were called to Willington Road, Clapham, just before 22:00 BST on Monday following reports of gunshots near The Landor pub.

The 25-year-old, who worked as a bus driver, was pronounced dead at the scene, the Metropolitan Police said.

A 22-year-old man was later arrested on suspicion of murder after attending hospital with a gunshot wound on Tuesday. He remains in hospital under police guard.

Det Ch Insp Claire Guiver said her thoughts were with the victim's family as they "come to terms with this tragic incident".

News.title: Double killer and rapist given whole life sentence
News.content:
A serial sex attacker who had a "morbid fascination" with sex has been jailed for the rest of his life after he was found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later. Earlier that year, he raped a third woman in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, Judge Mark Lucraft KC sentenced Levy to a whole life order, meaning he will never be released.

The sentence comes after police and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) apologised over a series of disastrous decisions that left him free to roam the streets.

When Levy carried out the attacks, he was on bail and being monitored by the Met.

The police watchdog is currently examining how he was managed over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

Following Wednesday's sentencing, Met Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said the handling of Levy's case was a "whole system failing".

News.title: Ministers push ahead with housing asylum seekers on ex-military sites
News.content:
Home Office minister Anna Turley has said the government is sticking with plans to accommodate asylum-seekers on former military bases despite protests from local residents.

She told the BBC the government's priority was to ensure asylum-seekers were looked after in a "secure" and "appropriate" place.

That included disused Ministry of Defence properties because they had on-site facilities and were "more contained," she added.

But campaigners in areas earmarked for asylum centres have said small communities with limited infrastructure would not be able to cope with large numbers of people.

There have been protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, over plans to house more than 1,000 asylum seekers at a site near the village.

Mike Nixon, the vice-chairman of Piddington Parish Council, said there was a "huge amount of concern and worry" among residents and that an asylum centre would have a "dramatic effect" on the way they lived their lives.

The proposal has prompted Piddington to hold a symbolic independence referendum, asking its 400 or so residents if they want to remain part of the UK.

Nixon said: "We're still very frustrated. Andy Burnham did say that he's willing to listen, but we've had no formal contact. No consultation, nothing from the Home Office.

"We felt that the only way of making our views felt was to say 'well if we're not going to be listened to, what's the point of being a part of the country?'"

The government has promised to end the use of hotels for asylum seekers, announcing on Wednesday that a further 13 across England had been closed.

It plans to use former military sites instead with two already up and running - RAF Wethersfield in Essex, and Crowborough Training Camp in East Sussex.

In June, it announced proposals to open three more, including the site near Piddington.

The two other planned sites are a former RAF base in Barnham in Suffolk where there were protests last week and RAF Linton-on-Ouse in North Yorkshire where the area's Labour mayor said it was "simply the wrong place".

Defending the proposals on BBC Breakfast, Turley said the public wanted the government to end the use of hotels, pointing to how an "iconic" hotel in Blackpool, the Metropole, was no longer being used to accommodate asylum-seekers.

She said it sent "an important message" that the government wanted the hotel to be part of Blackpool's future.

"The priority is to ensure we look after asylum seekers in a secure place that is more appropriate and we limit the impact on communities."

Asked what she meant by secure, she said: "Examples we are looking at is former military bases and we have two up and running and possibly another three.

"They have have facilities on site and are more contained and it limits the impact on on communities.

"We are looking at other sites such as former industrial sites, student accommodation - accommodation that is more more appropriate than hotels."

News.title: GB's Evans wins European gold in 100m breaststroke
News.content:
Great Britain's Angharad Evans won her first European Championship gold in the 100m breaststroke final in Paris.

The 23-year-old comfortably finished first in a championship record time of one minute and 4.87 seconds, which was also a lifetime best and British record.

Having also broken the championship record in the semi-final, Evans claimed gold ahead of Ireland's Mona McSharry in second, while Italy's Benedetta Pilato took bronze.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki, who made history for Jersey by claiming gold in the 200m breaststroke at the Commonwealth Games last month in Glasgow, was the fastest qualifier in the semi-final of the same event at the European Aquatics Championships.

The 18-year-old's time of 2:08.60 held off GB team-mate Greg Butler in the first semi-final, with the 25-year-old also progressing to the final.

GB's Amalie Smith picked up a silver medal in the 400m individual medley final, finishing 0.7secs behind Ireland's Ellen Walshe, with Poland's Justina Kozan claiming bronze.

The 16-year-old Smith, who won gold on Monday in the 4x200m freestyle relay, was also part of the part of the 4x100m freestyle relay team that finished fifth.

Another teenager, Italian Sara Curtis, also shone as she broke the women's 50m backstroke world record with a time of 26.63 seconds.

The 19-year-old bettered the world record set by Australia's Kaylee McKeown three years ago by 0.23secs in her semi-final.

An Alaskan community is split on a plan to create a gold mine in the middle of a national park amid environmental concerns.

The federal government granted Alaska Native-owned Cook Inlet Region Inc. the rights to Johnson Tract, a nearly 21,000-acre property surrounded by Lake Clark National Park, in the 1970s as part of a land exchange agreement. Mining company Contango Silver & Gold now has a lease agreement with Cook Inlet Region and plans to create a mine on the mineral-rich Johnson Tract.

While opponents of the project have voiced concerns over the potential effects on beluga whales and brown bears in the region, supporters say the environmental impacts will be minimal, and it would be an economic boost for local tribes.

Contango plans to ship ore mined at Johnson Tract to an existing mill facility, instead of processing the materials there. This would lessen the company’s environmental footprint in the area, but according to The Wall Street Journal, local business owners worry transporting ore through the park will scare off the brown bears that visitors come to see.

open image in gallery An Alaskan community is split on a plan to create a gold mine in the middle of a national park amid environmental concerns ( Getty Images )

“Over many, many years, they started bringing their cubs into the yard, and then they started nursing in front of us,” Joanne Edney-Coray, who runs the Silver Salmon Creek Lodge with her husband, told the publication. “It can be ruined in an instant with teams of people on mining trucks.”

Environmental groups and the Chickaloon tribal council filed a lawsuit last year against the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, arguing that it violated the Clean Water Act by granting a permit for the Johnson Tract project.

The Army Corps did not ensure endangered Cook Inlet belugas are protected from water and noise pollution or thoroughly evaluate the project’s potential to cause acid mine drainage and leach contaminants into the nearby Johnson River, the Center for Biological Diversity, one of the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, alleged in a May 2025 press release.

When The Independent reached out to the Army Corps of Engineers, it said it “does not comment on matters in litigation,” and referred to the Justice Department.

open image in gallery Supporters of the project say the environmental impacts will be minimal, and it would be an economic boost for local tribes ( AFP via Getty Images )

Contango CEO Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse argued that his company is “not ruining a park.”

“We’re going to do everything in a way that is really minimizing any of the impacts,” he told the Journal.

The Journal noted that Contango is performing a baseline wildlife survey, which includes monitoring the belugas to assess where they swim.

Greg Encelewski, the president of the local Ninilchik Traditional Council, also pointed out the potential economic benefits of the mining project.

“Our tribes are trying to become self-sufficient, and without some type of economic engine we’re not going to,” he told the Journal.

The Independent has reached out to Contango, Cook Inlet Region and the Justice Department for comment.

News.title: Bomb squad shuts down DC street for hours over suspicious device - that turns out to be a sex toy
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

That one probably wasn’t in the training manual.

First responders in Washington, D.C., got an unusual surprise on Wednesday when a suspicious package outside an area fire station turned out to be a sex toy.

The device was reported to officials around 7 a.m., after a bystander saw someone leave it in the trash near the Tenleytown fire station.

The individual with the object allegedly approached a member of the firehouse, then left the device, which could be seen with exposed wires, behind.

The encounter triggered a large emergency response, which shut down Wisconsin Avenue NW from 40th Street to Warren Street for nearly two hours.

A suspicious package left outside a Washington, D.C., fire station turned out to be a sex toy, police said ( Google Street View / WUSA screengrab )

The Washington Metropolitan Police Department’s bomb squad and K-9 unit cleared the item, which was first thought to be a thermos.

Police later described the object as an "electronic sex portable pump device.”

News photos showed a technician carrying a blue and black cylindrical object about the size of a large water bottle.

The Independent has contacted the police department for comment.

The area has been cleared and reopened to traffic.

Though today’s firehouse incident was a false alarm, the threats in the nation’s capital are very real.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran recently warned that threat levels facing the agency are “off the charts” in the current political climate.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran has revealed that the current threat level his agency faces is “off the charts,” blaming a political climate more volatile than anything he said he has seen over his 24-year career.

Around 10,000 threats have been made against government officials and Supreme Court justices so far in 2026, a 40 percent increase on the same period in 2025, he said last month.

Last November, a bomb threat temporarily halted flights at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Virginia.

A shooting at a Georgia high school on Wednesday left one student injured, while a teenage suspect who fled the scene was later taken into custody, police said.

The shooting at Warner Robins High School involved two ninth-grade students and occurred just one week into the new school year, prompting a response from dozens of law enforcement officers. Warner Robins is about 102 miles (164 kilometers) southeast of Atlanta.

“Today a call that we train for every year happened to Houston County,” Sheriff Matt Moulton said at an evening news conference.

The injured student was taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Moulton did not provide further details about the nature of the injuries.

The sheriff said a group of students was inside a school bathroom when a verbal altercation between two students escalated into a physical fight ( Joe Kovac/Atlanta Journal-Constitution via AP )

According to the Houston County School District, the high school was placed under a code red lockdown, with students and staff secured inside their classrooms. It wasn’t immediately known whether the school had metal detectors in place.

Moulton declined to take questions at the news conference, citing the active investigation.

The sheriff said a group of students was inside a school bathroom when a verbal altercation between two students escalated into a physical fight. One student was shot at 2:15 p.m., and the suspect fled. A school resource officer arrived quickly, applied tourniquets to the student’s injuries and remained until emergency services personnel arrived.

Authorities said the suspect fled the school in an unknown direction. After reviewing surveillance footage, officers located and arrested the suspect an hour later in the Huntington Hills neighborhood, across the street from the school.

“The school threat protocol and our training was followed perfectly today," Moulton said. "Fortunately what could have been a much-worse incident was minimized to us only having one student injured.”

The school principal, Brett Wallace, said the school would be closed to students on Thursday and Friday and to staff on Thursday. Crisis counselors would be available at the school for staff on Friday and for students on Monday when they return.

He added that there would be no virtual learning for the students.

“We want our students to have the opportunity to be at home, surrounded by family, and to take the time they need to process, heal, and care for one another,” Wallace said in a statement.

Two U.S. Army soldiers were killed on Wednesday when an Apache military helicopter attached to Fort Hood base crashed into a field in Texas, igniting a large grass fire, according to officials.

Representatives from nearby Fort Hood confirmed the crash of the AH-64 Apache helicopter. Cliff Coleman, a spokesman for the Bell County Sheriff's Office, verified the deaths of both occupants.

A military official told the Associated Press the helicopter was undergoing a routine training flight before it went down. The official spoke anonymously because the situation is still developing.

Representatives from nearby Fort Hood confirmed the crash of the AH-64 Apache helicopter

No cause of the crash was immediately announced. Fort Hood’s criminal investigation division was leading the crash investigation, Coleman said. The identities of the two soldiers are still being withheld pending notifications to their families.

"Today, an Apache helicopter crashed in Bell County during Fort Hood operations, killing two members of our military," Texas Governor Greg Abbott said on X.

Fort Hood is a massive base with 214,968 acres (336 square miles) that is used to train and deploy heavy forces. The Army says the rolling, arid terrain around the base provides an ideal training ground.

In November 2015, four soldiers were killed when a Black Hawk helicopter crashed during a training exercise. And nine Fort Hood soldiers died in 2016 when a rain-swollen creek swept their vehicle into rushing waters.

The helicopter did not hit any homes or other structures when it crashed, Coleman said.

“You could tell it was a violent crash,” Coleman said. Photographs from the scene showed firefighters walking around a charred field as plumes of dark smoke rose from flames still burning in the wreckage.

“Our immediate priority is securing the site and supporting the initial response efforts,” said Brig. Gen. Ethan Diven, acting commanding general. "Our thoughts are with the crew and their families as we await further information.”

The AH-64 Apache attack helicopter has been a key part of the military’s fleet since the first versions were deployed in 1984. The Apache crew sits behind each other with the pilot in the rear and the co-pilot gunner in the front position.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is now the frontrunner to become the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee, according to Polymarket odds, marking the first time she has led the pack.

As of Wednesday evening, 21 percent of traders backed the New York progressive, who was trailed by California Governor Gavin Newsom at 17 percent. On rival prediction site Kalshi, the results were the same, with Ocasio-Cortez narrowly topping Newsom.

Meanwhile, conventional political polls still put former Vice President Kamala Harris at the top spot, with Newsom in second and AOC in a distant fourth.

Ocasio-Cortez has not announced a formal presidential bid, nor has she sworn one off. Right now she’s focused on helping Democrats win the midterms, she recently told The Independent.

“I think my main focus is really genuinely just the midterms right now, and we have to make sure that we win this majority,” she said.

open image in gallery Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is the top prospect to become the 2028 Democratic presidential nominee, according to Polymarket traders ( AFP/Getty )

Ocasio-Cortez recently made headlines for detailing the process of freezing her eggs on social media and reflecting on the precarious state of women’s healthcare in America.

“In the political context that we're in, in an administration that is dedicated to politicizing women’s bodies and taking our choices away from us and punishing us around decisions to be pregnant or not be pregnant — and, frankly, this administration has made pregnancy more dangerous than probably at any point in the last 30 plus years — we’re gonna take our power back,” she told her followers.

She also generated considerable discussion in political circles for branding 2020-era “woke” ideas “crazy,” reflecting that while many of the social justice-focused discussions of that era were “fruitful,” the "rhetoric in that time is not rhetoric that we would use today.”

open image in gallery Former Vice President Kamala Harris continues to lead the pack in conventional 2028 polling ( Getty )

An AOC 2028 bid would be the latest test of whether Democrats will move further to the left, in line with rising Democratic socialists and progressives such as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, or whether the party will tack back to the center.

In many ways, the party is still reeling from the 2024 election, where Harris replaced President Joe Biden in the late stages of the race and lost to Donald Trump, despite the Republican campaigning under a cloud of lawsuits and government investigations.

Considerable divides remain in the party over issues including healthcare, U.S. support for Israel and immigration.

The Democrats are projected to retake at least the House in the midterms, according to polling, on the back of high gas prices and an unpopular war in Iran.

Denver is smoking mad over the “enormous quantities” of cigarette butts littering its public places — so it's suing Big Tobacco to help pay for the cleanup.

In a 72-page lawsuit, the Mile High City accuses 10 cigarette companies of creating a “public nuisance” by selling smokes with environmentally “persistent” synthetic plastic filters instead of biodegradable ones.

“We want to make sure that they pay their fair share of the cost that cities are bearing to clean up their mess and that we want to see them change the practice," Mayor Mike Johnston told the Denverite website.

The World Health Organization estimates that 4.5 trillion cigarette butts are tossed away in public annually, and Johnston said research suggests they account for up to one-quarter of Denver’s litter problem.

The defendants named in the city’s lawsuit include tobacco giants Philip Morris USA, manufacturer of the top-selling Marlboro brand, and R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., which makes Camel, Newport and Pall Mall cigarettes.

open image in gallery Denver Mayor Mike Johnston says cigarette butts account for up to one-quarter of the city’s litter ( AFP/Getty )

In a statement to The Independent, a spokesperson for defendant ITG Brands — which makes Winston, Kool and Salem cigarettes — said the company was aware of the lawsuit.

“As a responsible manufacturer, we take this matter seriously and disagree with the claims made against us. We will respond through the appropriate legal process,” spokesperson Lucas Seiler said.

None of the other companies immediately returned inquiries from The Independent.

Denver's lawsuit begins by citing the Philip Morris International website, which says in part, “By 2030 there could be more cigarette butts than fish in the oceans.”

Philip Morris International isn’t among the defendants named in the lawsuit. Its website says the company is focused on “replacing cigarettes with smoke-free products.”

open image in gallery The lawsuit faults the tobacco industry for selling smokes with environmentally ‘persistent’ synthetic plastic filters instead of biodegradable ones ( PA Wire )

The complaint alleges that discarded butts have piled up around the city on “streets, sidewalks, parks, public rights-of-way, parking areas, public facilities, stormwater infrastructure, drainage systems, waterways, and other publicly owned or maintained property.”

“Denver does not allege that a single discarded cigarette filter, standing alone, caused the injuries at issue,” court papers say. “Rather, the physical condition affecting Denver-owned or maintained property and infrastructure results from the continuing accumulation of enormous quantities of discarded cigarette filters introduced into Denver through Defendants’ respective commercial activities.”

The lawsuit demands unspecified damages on grounds that include negligence, product liability and alleged violations of the Colorado Consumer Protection Act.

It also seeks a court order requiring that the defendants take "reasonable measures to prevent, reduce, manage, remove, or remediate continuing cigarette-filter impacts."

The complaint doesn't cite the city's cost of cleaning up the butts, and a mayoral spokesperson didn't immediately return an inquiry from The Independent.

Denver's legal action follows similar moves by Baltimore and Sacramento County, California, according to Denverite.

Johnston said city officials spent about a year deciding whether to file the lawsuit, which it outsourced to law firms in Denver; Overland Park, Kansas; and West Islip, New York.

“All of our city attorneys are working every day on day-to-day enforcement around the city,” Johnston told Denverite. “We didn't have a lot of bandwidth to spend to bring a national suit like this, but we think it's the right one to bring and are delighted to have partners to help us do it.”
