That unfortunate development typifies the Nigerian culture of grand public spectacles that rarely translate into measurable improvements in governance, even when the issue concerns life and death. The figures remain disturbing. About 46 million Nigerians still practise open defecation because they lack access to safe toilets, while only a fraction of the country’s 774 local government areas has attained Open Defecation-Free status. Human waste continues to contaminate streams, rivers and shallow wells, exposing millions to cholera, typhoid, diarrhoea, dysentery and other preventable diseases. Children bear the greatest burden through malnutrition, stunted growth and avoidable deaths. Beyond the health catastrophe, the practice diminishes Nigeria’s international image, discourages tourism and investment, and imposes enormous economic costs. India demonstrated that determined leadership can reverse even an entrenched sanitation crisis. Through the Swachh Bharat (Clean India) Mission, the government combined massive investment in household toilets with relentless public education, community mobilisation, strict monitoring, local government accountability and sustained political commitment from the highest level. Millions of toilets were constructed, open defecation became socially unacceptable in many communities, and measurable progress followed.

While some challenges remain, India proved that political will backed by resources and accountability can change long-established behaviour. Nigeria can do likewise if it abandons tokenism. First, governments at every level must substantially increase funding for sanitation infrastructure and ensure affordable household toilets, especially in rural communities and urban slums. Second, reliable water supply must accompany toilet construction because sanitation cannot flourish without water. Third, sanitation laws should be firmly enforced, with local authorities empowered to monitor compliance while rewarding communities that achieve Open Defecation-Free status. Fourth, sustained behavioural change campaigns involving schools, religious bodies, traditional rulers, market associations and the media must replace intermittent publicity drives. Citizens also have responsibilities. Households should prioritise hygienic toilets, reject indiscriminate defecation, participate in community sanitation efforts and demand accountability from elected officials. Open defecation is demeaning and acceptable. Nigeria must do away with it.

World.title: Osun 2026: Ballot paper or gun battle
World.content:
By OKE MICHAEL

Democracy should never become a battle of violence, intimidation, and fear.

It is universally acknowledged that democracy means “government of the people, by the people, and for the people.” The ballot is at the core of democracy, as it is the peaceful method used by people to express themselves on who should rule them.

However, with the Osun State gubernatorial election just a few days away, there are increasing apprehensions regarding the increasingly negative climate in politics. This is an unavoidable question being raised regarding OSUN 2026: Will it be fought on ballot papers or in gun battles?

This is not a political question. It is the question of the future of democracy in Osun State. An election should never be turned into a war. The political contest must remain a contest of ideas, policies, competence, accountability, and people’s trust, not of intimidation, violence, harassment, arbitrary arrests, or the employment of federal power against one’s political adversaries.

The latest news and charges of shootings, beatings, arrests, intimidation, and other instances of political confrontation in some parts of Osun State are very disturbing. Each charge merits immediate, transparent, and impartial investigation by the relevant authorities. In case of any criminality, those involved must face justice regardless of their political and social affiliations.

While the biggest threat to democracy is not only the presence of political differences, it is the normalization of violence as the tool of resolving political differences. Once citizens start to believe that victory in politics may be secured by using force and not ballots, democracy is put on trial. Another area that needs immediate attention in the country is public trust in the fairness of the institutions that provide law and order. aThe police, EFCC, and other law enforcement and regulatory agencies are supposed to perform their duties with professionalism and objectivity and be free from any partisan considerations according to constitutional requirements. The trust in these institutions among people is based largely on their ability to uphold the law without fear or favor. If people start thinking, or there is some credible proof, of the selective use of such institutions against political opponents, not only will the victims be affected but even these institutions themselves will be damaged.

None of the political parties must ever exercise control over the mechanisms of law enforcement. It is unfair to persecute any opposition party for opposing the powers. Similarly, no person or organisation can be allowed to evade investigation due to their political affiliation. In cases of complaints regarding wrongful arrests and detention or any kind of abuse of power and intimidation, they must be looked into and dealt with through the process of law. Democracy is not possible where the citizen is afraid to speak out, campaign, or vote.

An election must never be a do-or-die affair. The final say in a democratic election lies in the hands of the electorate. Political figures are contesting, not owning the electorate. Political parties are platforms, not alternatives to the will of the electorate. Security agencies are agencies of the state, not means of political warfare.

The people of Osun State are able to make up their own minds. They don’t need political threats to be told whom to vote for. They don’t need violence from political hooligans to decide their political choices. They don’t need intimidation, coercion, or manipulation.

What they need is an atmosphere to listen to the different contestants, judge their records and programmes, and vote accordingly. The question must not then be “Who has the most potent political machinery?” The question must be: “Who has earned the trust of the people?” That is the spirit of democracy. Osun should not be a political battleground. Osun State is the property of its people. It is not the exclusive property of any political party, political dynasty, godfather, or any incumbent or opposition. Osun should not be made a battleground just because people are fighting for power. Politicians seeking elective positions need to realise that political power is transient, but the damage done to democratic institutions will stay on for a long time to come. It is, thus, very important that all the political parties, candidates, their supporters, and allies pledge to conduct themselves peacefully.

The security agencies also need to show professionalism and impartiality in the run-up to the elections, during, and after the voting process. It is not their duty to protect one political party but rather the Nigerian citizenry.

Finally, the electoral commission should make sure that every citizen who is qualified to vote is allowed to do so freely and that the votes are counted accurately.

“VOTE IS MORE POWERFUL THAN BULLET.” It is not democratic to force a citizen to vote under the threat of a gun. It is not democratic to deny one’s political opponent the right to campaign. And there is nothing democratic in using state machinery to resolve political disputes. A bullet may silence an individual, but it will not provide legitimacy to the leader. A threat may intimidate a voter, but it will not make the leader popular. An arrest may get a political rival off the streets for the moment, but it cannot extinguish the dreams of millions of people.

The people alone can give legitimacy in democracy. That is the reason why all parties to the 2026 Osun elections must safeguard the integrity of the ballot.

Political leaders need to cool down the atmosphere. The candidates should control their followers. Security agencies should behave professionally. Election officials should maintain neutrality. Civil society groups and the media should hold the powers to account. And, above all, the people must be allowed to exercise their democratic rights freely. Let the vote decide. Osun State boasts of an illustrious past, a politically enlightened populace, and citizens who deserve much better than political violence.

The elections in 2026 should thus serve as a showcase of democratic maturity and not a game of threats. Let the campaign revolve around roads, education, health care, jobs, security, farming, infrastructure, economic growth, and people’s well-being — and not “Baba Sope.” Let the aspirants sell themselves to the electorate by means of their credentials and manifestoes.

Let the political parties fight each other, but in peace. Let the people choose.

And once the choice has been made by the people, everybody should respect it except for the prescribed legal process. The decision facing Osun State is clear — ballot or blood; democracy or intimidation; peaceful contestation or political violence.

As fellow Nigerians who are dedicated to the cause of democratic governance, it is incumbent on us to ensure that the ballot prevails above all else and not the bullet.

Osun 2026 should not go down in history as an election conducted through fear but one where the people chose their leaders democratically. The power resides in the people. The mandate lies with the people. And only the people, not godfathers, thugs, or coercive apparatuses, can decide who will rule them.

World.title: Fake independence: So, Tinubu can tell EFCC what to do! By Olu Fasan
World.content:
Olu Fasan

Some Nigerians commit the delusional sin of believing that once a state institution has the word “independent” prefixed to its name, it is, indeed, independent. They believe that critical state agencies created by statute or the Constitution to ensure security and law and order, to guarantee justice and rule of law, to safeguard electoral integrity and democratic norms and to fight corruption and malfeasance in public office do, in fact, discharge their responsibilities dutifully without fear and without favour, deliberately removed from presidential control. Now, however, everyone knows what has long been clear, thanks to President Bola Tinubu who recently shredded the deceptive façade into pieces. That’s how to interpret the president’s recent “directive” to the anti-graft agency, the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, EFCC, to lift a freezing order it placed on the Osun State Government’s statutory allocation account over alleged diversion of public funds.

Perversely, some commentators praised the president for his “shrewd” intervention. Few considered the bigger picture; few saw the wider implication of a president inviting the country to accept he could and, indeed, would interfere in any state agency because “as the president, the buck stops with me”; few understood that wielding power in that manner comes straight from an autocrat’s playbook. Tell me, what could be more corrosive of institutional independence than subjecting every agency to the whims of the president? The answer was less obvious from those who gave Tinubu a thumbs up for his action. I disagree! Why? Well, let’s start with the facts. Last week, on August 5, the EFCC asked First Bank to freeze the Osun State Government’s statutory allocation account, explaining later that “we observed in the past one week that activities on that account looked suspicious, so we took the step of placing a restriction on the account to preserve it.” Given that the EFCC’s action came just over a week to the state’s governorship election, on August 15, it inevitably created perception of the agency acting on a partisan direction to favour the federal ruling party’s candidate, who was the governor’s main opponent. Governor Ademola Adeleke immediately sued the EFCC, accusing the agency of acting “unlawfully”. Ostensibly, one could argue, the EFCC acted as it felt it should, and the governor behaved as he should, swiftly taking the matter to court: the law must then take its course.

But, alas, not so. President Tinubu intervened politically; in doing so, he went for the nuclear option. He ordered the EFCC to lift the order freezing the Osun State government’s account and to “discontinue whatever action it had instituted against the government”. In a statement, dated August 6, which he personally signed, the president said: “I must state that I feel deeply embarrassed not by the EFCC’s exercise of its mandate, backed by a court order, but by the timing of the agency’s action.” That should have been a sufficient response, leaving the matter to the courts, but he went on: “Based on the foregoing premise, I am duty-bound to issue a directive on this issue in consonance with the overriding public interest in preserving public confidence and the integrity and fairness of our democratic process.” Consider the above statement closely. First, President Tinubu acknowledged the EFCC acted “in the exercise of its mandate”; second, he acknowledged the agency’s action was “backed by a court order”. But because he was “deeply embarrassed” by “the timing” of the action, he overrode the agency’s mandate and quashed its court order. What about Governor Adeleke’s suit challenging the EFCC’s action? Why did the president think his political intervention was more appropriate than the judicial process? President Tinubu invoked “the overriding public interest”. But where did the overriding public interest really lie in this case? Was it in a meaningless political grandstanding purporting to restore public confidence in the integrity and fairness of the Osun State governorship election when, in fact, everyone knew “federal might” was ruthlessly deployed in other guises? Or was it in preserving the veneer of independence that the EFCC had hitherto clothed itself with? Sadly, that pretence to independence, to immunity from partisan influence, is now completely gone!

Truth is, President Tinubu acted as he did because he believes the EFCC is subject to his direction, and federal agencies must not make him “feel deeply embarrassed”. Some already got the memo. For instance, in the “fake agency” case, once President Tinubu publicly declared “100 per cent confidence” in his top aides, the Independent Corrupt Practices and Other Related Offences Commission, ICPC, knew the president would “feel deeply embarrassed” if it named the high-profile collaborators in the presidency. Hence, last week, the ICPC submitted a whitewash report that exonerated key suspects in the scandal, as if the fake agency created and enabled itself. But strong state institutions do, in fact, without intentionality, “embarrass” leaders. Take the US, whose system of government Nigeria claims to practise. While President Trump has no doubt been undermining US democratic guardrails, US institutions have fought back, often successfully. For instance, President Trump has lost several court actions, on tariffs, birthright citizenship, etc, which caused him huge domestic and international embarrassments. In 2020, Trump asked Georgia’s Secretary of State, Brad Raffensperger to help him “find” votes to beat Joe Biden. “I just want to find 11,780 votes,” Trump told Raffensperger. But he refused. How many election officials would reject such pressure in Nigeria? Also, amid concerns that Trump might use the military to stop Biden’s inauguration in January 2021, the US Joint Chiefs of Staff issued a rare statement, saying: “The US military will obey lawful orders from civilian leadership.” Can security forces in Nigeria vow to obey only lawful orders from an incumbent president during elections? Utterly doubtful.

To be sure, in a presidential system, the executive power is vested in the president, as stated in section 5(1) of the 1999 Constitution, and, as such, an executive agency cannot be so independent as to be free of presidential control. However, the US Supreme Court made a powerful distinction between “executive” and “non-executive” agencies. The court held that executive or political agencies are those exercising executive powers or functions directly on behalf of the president; most agencies in Nigeria, such as the National Sports Commission, fall into this category. However, non-executive agencies are those whose duties are “neither political nor executive but predominantly quasi-judicial and quasi-legislative.” The EFCC and the CBN fall into the non-executive category, and the convention worldwide is that such agencies should be insulated from presidential control and operate at a distance from partisan politics. Which was why, recently, the US Supreme Court rejected President Trump’s decision to fire Lisa Cook, a member of Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The court argued that allowing Trump to sack Cook at will would violate “our Nation’s long tradition of independent central banking protected from political interference.”

Unfortunately, in giving orders to EFCC, President Tinubu implies he doesn’t believe the anti-graft agency should be insulated from presidential control. Of course, past presidents used EFCC as a political tool, but they acted subtly. Tinubu’s blatantly “directive” to the EFCC replaces behind-the-scenes interference with open erosion of institutional independence and integrity. Put simply, President Tinubu is saying: “EFCC is under my control, I can tell it what to do.” But that strips the agency of the moral clout and legitimacy to act as a truly independent anti-graft body because EFCC’s credibility lies not only in the fact of independence but also in the appearance of independence.

Last year, in a piece titled “EFCC’s failure: Olukoyede’s blame-shifting is mere shadow boxing” (Vanguard, February 13, 2025), I questioned the agency’s independence. In a rejoinder titled “Olukoyede’s record-breaking strides in EFCC and Olu Fasan’s errors of analysis”, published in virtually all national newspapers, Dele Oyewale, EFCC’s head of media and publicity, accused me of “mud splashing”. Well, if I ever needed vindication, President Tinubu’s action has now provided it: EFCC is not truly independent!

World.title: Malawi to face Cameroon in WAFCON final
World.content:
Malawi and Cameroon have reached the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) final after contrasting semi-final victories on Wednesday.

Malawi defeated Algeria 3-1, with Tabitha Chawinga scoring twice and her sister Temwa adding another goal. Cameroon, meanwhile, edged hosts Morocco 3-1 on penalties after a goalless draw.

Cameroon goalkeeper Michaely Bihina was the hero in the shootout, saving four Morocco penalties before Myriam Maéva Nyadjou converted the decisive kick.

All four semi-finalists — Malawi, Cameroon, Morocco and Algeria — have also qualified for next summer’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil.

For Malawi and Algeria, it will be their first appearance at the tournament.

Morocco will make its second World Cup appearance after reaching the last 16 in 2023, while Cameroon have previously featured in the 2015 and 2019 editions.

The WAFCON final between Malawi and Cameroon will take place on Sunday.

World.title: Bihina saves four penalties as Cameroon beat Morocco to reach WAFCON Final
World.content:
Cameroon goalkeeper Michaely Bihina produced a remarkable performance as the Indomitable Lionesses defeated hosts Morocco on penalties to reach the 2026 Women’s Africa Cup of Nations (WAFCON) final.

The 22-year-old was the heroine in a dramatic semi-final in Rabat, making a crucial save in extra time before stopping three more penalties in the shootout.

With the match still goalless in the 118th minute, Morocco were awarded a penalty, but Bihina kept out Fatima Tagnaout’s effort from 12 yards to keep Cameroon alive.

Neither side could find a breakthrough before the final whistle, sending the contest into a penalty shootout after 120 minutes of action.

Bihina then delivered again, brilliantly saving attempts from Kenza Chappelle, Maryame Atiq and Sakina Ouzraoui as the hosts struggled from the spot.

With Morocco’s players and supporters stunned at the Moulay Hassan Stadium, teenage Cameroon defender Maryam Nyadjou held her nerve to convert the decisive penalty and seal a 3-1 shootout victory for the Central Africans.

The result sends Cameroon into Sunday’s final, where they will face Malawi at 19:00 GMT.

Malawi booked their place in the title decider earlier on Wednesday after beating Algeria 3-1.

Cameroon will now look to complete their impressive run by lifting the WAFCON trophy, while Malawi will

be aiming to claim the continental title in what promises to be a historic final.

World.title: How Chief Abiola was killed in government custody
World.content:
Falana

By FEMI FALANA

On June 12, 1994, Chief M. K.O. Abiola declared himself President on the basis of the June 12, 1993 presidential election, which he won fair and square. General Sani Abacha’s military junta arrested him and charged him with treasonable felony at the Federal High Court. While he was held incommunicado in a military custody for 4 years, Chief Abiola was subjected to horrendous psychological and mental torture. Even though Chief Abiola had severe health challenges, he was denied medical attention by the maximum dictator. His parlous medical state was confirmed on April 27, 1998 by Archbishop Desmond Tutu who had visited Nigeria at the instance of President Nelson Mandela and met with the imprisoned Chief Abiola. The revered priest reported that Abiola’s health and living conditions were severely deteriorating and called for his urgent release to enable him to take care of his failing health. The call was ignored by the military regime.

Following the controversial death of Abacha on June 8, 1998, he was succeeded by his Chief of Defence Staff, General Abdusalami Abubakar as Head of State and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Nigeria. The new military junta ordered the immediate release of all political prisoners including General Obasanjo (rtd) and other convicted coup plotters from prison custody. However, the detained Abiola was not released by Abubakar on the ground that he refused to renounce his claim to the presidency. Nigerians were shocked when the American delegation announced that Abiola had passed away during a brief meeting with him on July 7, 1998. The Chukwudifu Oputa Panel instituted by the President Olusegun Obasanjo administration to investigate the egregious human rights abuse which defined military rule in Nigeria probed the death of Chief Abiola. Abubakar turned down the request of the Oputa Panel to explain his role in the entire saga as he did not want to be subjected to cross examination by lawyers. About 28 years later, the former military ruler has, in his autobiography entitled “Call of Duty,” dismissed claims that Abiola was poisoned, insisting that an autopsy conducted by foreign pathologists had attributed his death to natural causes.

In dismissing the allegation that Chief Abiola was poisoned, Abubakar did not react to the evidence led before the Oputa Panel that there are poisons that cannot be detected by autopsy. In washing off his hands like Pontius Pilate, Abubakar stated that, “As far back as 1994 when he was arrested by the Abacha Administration for declaring himself President, it was public knowledge that Abiola was managing certain medical conditions which could seriously affect the quality of life of any human being.” Abubakar also relied on the text of the press conference of Thomas Pickering and the account of Susan Rice contained in her memoir titled, “Tough Love: My Story of the Things Worth Fighting For.” While denying that Abiola was poisoned, she confirmed that he had suffered medical neglect. According to her, she noticed that “Abiola’s ankles were swollen and that about five minutes into their conversation, Abiola started to cough, at first mildly and intermittently, and then wrackingly with consistency.’’

Abubakar further referred to a radiological report by Colonel (Dr) O. Awofeso, then Chief Consultant Radiologist at the Nigerian Army Defence Hospital, Sokoto, dated September 28, 1994, which had found that Abiola’s heart was enlarged with “right ventricular preponderance” consistent with hypertensive cardiac disease. Abubakar therefore argued that, “it was public knowledge that Abiola was managing certain medical conditions which could seriously affect the quality of life of any human being.” Even though, General Abubakar knew that Chief Abiola’s health was endangered during his 4-year dehumanizing incarceration by the maximum ruler, Abacha, he deliberately refused to accede to the request to allow him to attend to his health. The request of Abiola’s personal physician, Dr. Ore Falomo to visit him was equally turned down. As if that was not enough, Abubakar subjected Abiola to undeserved mental torture to make him jettison his claim to the presidency.

After the fruitless meetings held between Abiola and the service Chiefs on the mandate, Abubakar decided to involve the so-called international community in resolving the political logjam. The then Secretary General of the United Nations, Mr. Kofi Annan, and the Secretary General of the Commonwealth of Nations, Chief Emeka Anyaoku, were flown in to mount pressure on Abiola to renounce his mandate. In their separate meetings with Chief Abiola, they asked him to trade off the June 12 mandate for his release from custody. Even though rejected the offer of conditional release, both diplomats gave the impression, in their press statements, that he had agreed to forgo the mandate. In a letter addressed to Chief Gani Fawehinmi SAN on July 6 1998, Abiola denied the claim of both diplomats. He said: “True, both Annan and Anyaoku (apparently working together, although I saw them separately), wanted me to sign a statement that I will not, once again, demand my mandate, once released… Both diplomats spoke of arranging my UNCONDITIONAL release. With the demand for that sort of statement that would render me ‘a deserter’ Any release obtained on that basis would be the worst form of ‘capitulation.’ “

Chief Abiola further disclosed that he reviewed “the history of June 12, I told them that quite at the beginning, Obasanjo in July 1994 came to me with 26 traditional rulers to seek a similar statement. He was told off in no uncertain terms in the presence of the retinue of traditional fathers, after I had explained that the issue is one of God vs. a few ‘powerful elements’. The voice of the people is the voice of God, ‘Vox Populi Vox Dei’ a popular maxim long before Jesus Christ arrived.” It ought to be pointed out that the Americans were invited by Abubakar after the failed efforts of Annan and Anyaoku to persuade Chief Abiola to renounce his mandate. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the suspicious death of Abiola, Abubakar could not justify while he allowed the American delegation to breach the prison regulations of both Nigeria and the United States during the visit.

Specifically, under the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) and state equivalents in the United States, visitors are totally prohibited from bringing food or beverages including tea into prisons. The purport of the rule is to prevent the smuggling of contraband, narcotics and poisons to prisons. Accordingly, all meals and beverages inside correctional facilities are supplied exclusively by the institution or purchased through the secure prison commissary. In Nigeria, visitors are permitted to bring outside food or water to inmates or detainees in police stations, correctional centres and other detention facilities. But the visitors are absolutely required to taste the food or water in front of the officers on duty before serving it to the prisoners or detainees. The food or water must be tasted by the visitors to ensure that it is not poisoned or adulterated to harm the prison inmates or detainees in the custody of the government.

Whereas visitors are strictly prohibited from bringing, serving, or passing any outside food or beverages—including tea—to prisoners in the United States, the American visitors led by that visited Abiola on July 7, 1998 were allowed by the Abubakar military junta to bring a tea flask to the detention facility. And in utter breach of the rules of correctional centres in Nigeria, a member of the delegation, Susan Rice, who served the tea did not taste it before passing it to the detainee. ACP Zadok who had who guarded Chief Abiola from 1996-1998, testified before the Chukwudifu Oputa Panel. In his testimony, the police officer said that, in strict compliance with prison regulations, he tasted the food, water or tea prepared for Abiola before passing same to the detainee. However, on the fateful day, Zadok said that he was removed from his duty post by Major A. S. Aliyu, the Chief Security Officer to the head of the military junta.

Aliyu had abandoned his own primary duty of protecting the head of state in order to attend to the American delegation. In his oral testimony at the Oputa Panel, Major Aliyu confirmed that Susan Rice did not taste the tea before serving it to Abiola. He agreed with Zadok that this was the first and the only time that a foreign visitor was allowed to serve tea to a detainee in the custody of the government. Although Major Aliyu turned round to say that the tea in question was prepared by a villa staff, he could not name the staff during his highly misleading testimony. At the end of his the proceedings, it was crystal clear that Aliyu had set out to cover up the actual cause of Abiola’s death. Hence, he could not explain why Zadok was removed from the Akinola Aguda house and why he took charge of Chief Abiola’s security when the American delegation visited him.

In his memoir titled, “Interventions (A Life in War and Peace)”, the late Kofi Annan revealed that he had warned Abubakar that “Abiola needed to be released if he was to obtain international goodwill—and mine. On this Abubakar wavered slightly. He pledged his willingness to release Abiola immediately, but under the condition that he made no attempt to reclaim the presidency.” Mr. Kofi Annan equally stated that even though the foreign pathologists had established that “it was the result of heart condition, and there was no foul play—other than the fact, I thought that Abiola had been denied adequate medical care throughout his incarceration. Either way, he was yet another casualty of the systematic violations of a whole range of human rights that are inevitable under personalised and oppressive regimes.”

Before then, the Oputa Panel had, after a critical review of the evidence presented before it, stated thus, “In the case of Chief Moshood Abiola, we are of the view that the government of the day knows much more than it has admitted. We believe that the denial of Chief Moshood Abiola’s mandate was a violation of the rights of Nigerians to freely choose their leaders. We regard this as a serious infringement.” Thus, the Oputa Panel came to the conclusion that, “Chief Moshood Abiola’s death was the result of his incarceration and the denial of access to adequate medical attention. The testimony of the Chief Security Officer to the then Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, was full of contradictions. From the evidence before us, Chief Abiola died in suspicious circumstances. The Commission therefore recommends a thorough investigation to throw light to and inform the Nigerian people on what killed Chief Moshood Abiola.”

In view of the denial of Abubakar and the members of the American delegation of any involvement in the suspicious death of Abiola, the Federal Government should, without any further delay, reopen investigation into the case. The fresh investigation will, as opined by the Oputa Panel, “throw light to and inform the Nigerian people on what killed Chief Moshood Abiola” in the custody of the Abubakar military junta.

World.title: The words you choose shape how people hear you, by Ruth Oji
World.content:
Dr. Ruth Oji

Why vague language undermines your authority—and what to do about it

Imagine a senior manager presenting quarterly results to the executive team. Her data are solid, and her analysis is sound. But every few sentences, she says something like: “We had some problems with vendor compliance, and people were not happy about the delays.”

Later, over coffee, a colleague would say what everyone else felt: “She sounded uncertain. Like she wasn’t in control of the situation.” The manager wasn’t uncertain.

She knew her material cold. But her word choices—”had some problems,” “people were not happy”—made her sound passive, vague, and tentative. She’d undermined her own authority without realising it.

This happens constantly in professional communication. We reach for weak, generic words because they feel safe. We say “said” when we mean “insisted.” We write “big decision” when we mean “critical decision.” We describe ourselves as “happy with the results” when we’re actually “gratified by the outcomes.” These small choices accumulate. Over time, they shape how colleagues, clients, and supervisors perceive our competence. The good news? Precision is a skill you can develop. And it starts with recognising the words that weaken your message.

The usual suspects

Certain words show up everywhere in workplace writing and speaking, and they’re almost always too vague to do the job you need them to do.

Take “said.” It’s a neutral reporting verb—it conveys no tone, no emphasis, no commitment. Compare these two sentences:

“The director said the policy would be reviewed.”

“The director insisted the policy would be reviewed.”

The second version tells you something about the director’s determination. It removes ambiguity. When you’re delivering that sentence aloud, your voice naturally firms up on “insisted.” The word demands a stronger delivery.

Or consider “big.” It’s casual and imprecise. A “big decision” could mean anything. But a “monumental decision” conveys scale and significance. A “critical decision” emphasises urgency. A “substantial decision” suggests careful weighing of options. Each alternative gives your audience more information—and signals that you’ve thought carefully about what you’re communicating.

The same principle applies to “happy.” In a professional context, “happy” can sound informal or even childish. “We’re happy with the quarterly results” lacks the weight of “We’re gratified by the quarterly results” or “We’re encouraged by the quarterly results.” The upgraded versions convey earned satisfaction and professional judgment.

And then there’s “problem.” It’s not wrong, exactly, but it can sound like complaining. “We have a problem with the budget” feels passive. “We face a challenge with the budget” frames the issue as something you’re actively addressing. “We’re confronting a crisis in the budget” escalates the urgency and demands action. Choose based on the severity and the response you want from your audience.

A word of caution

Precision doesn’t mean reaching for the fanciest word in the thesaurus. I’ve seen writers replace “use” with “utilise” or “help” with “facilitate” in a misguided attempt to sound more professional. That’s not precision—that’s pretension, and your readers will sense it. The goal is to match your word choice to the meaning you actually intend. If your team solved a minor scheduling conflict, don’t call it “a triumph over adversity.” If a client expressed mild concern, don’t write that they were “outraged.” Exaggeration damages credibility just as much as vagueness does.

Pronunciation matters, too

Here’s something most people don’t think about: even if you choose the perfect word, mispronouncing it can undercut your authority.

I’ve heard professionals stumble over words like “comparable” (it’s COM-pra-ble, not com-PAIR-a-ble), and “formidable” (in British English, for-MID-a-ble; in American English, FOR-mi-da-ble).

These aren’t obscure terms—they’re common in workplace communication. But if you stress the wrong syllable, your audience notices. They may not consciously register the error, but it creates a moment of friction. Your credibility takes a small hit. The fix is simple: when you’re preparing a presentation or an important email, read it aloud. If you stumble over a word, look up the pronunciation. Practise it until your mouth knows where the stress falls. This is especially important for words you’ve chosen specifically for impact. Nothing undercuts “formidable challenge” faster than mispronouncing “formidable.”

Try this

Open the last email or report you sent. Scan for these weak words: said, big, happy, problem, good, bad, nice, thing, got, very.

For each one, ask yourself: What do I actually mean? Then replace the weak word with a precise alternative. Don’t overthink it—just choose the word that most accurately conveys your intended meaning.

Now read the revised version aloud. Notice how your delivery changes. The stronger words will naturally command more authority in your voice.

That’s the power of precision. Your ideas haven’t changed, and neither has your expertise. But the way your message lands—with your reader, with your listener—has shifted. You sound more confident, more credible, more in command of your material. And that’s exactly the impression you want to make.

Next week: Even the most powerful words fall flat if your writing is riddled with mechanical errors. I’ll show you the six mistakes that show up constantly in professional communication—and how to catch them before your reader does.

World.title: Saraki’s Shadow and Abdulrazaq Political Mirror: Who is really fighting for Relevance in Kwara
World.content:
By Abdulyekeen, Mohd Bashir





There is something rather amusing about the argument that Bukola Saraki is suddenly fighting for political relevance in Kwara. For about 7 years now, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq has spent a remarkable portion of his political life chasing Saraki’s shadow. Yet after the years in office, he has still not come close to matching the former Senate President in intellect, political organisation, leadership and, most importantly, the understanding of democratic politics. Saraki has been out of government in Kwara for years and still remains a reference point in the state’s political conversation. So, who exactly is struggling for relevance?

The growing closeness between the G-15/TOP and the PDP is something that has been giving the Governor Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq’s camp headache and they should really be worried. These are not people who woke up one morning and suddenly decided to realign themselves with the former governor. They were part of the same APC structure that produced AbdulRazaq. They saw the government from inside. They participated in the politics that brought it to power. If some of them are now finding their way back towards Saraki and the PDP, perhaps the more honest question is not what Saraki is doing to regain relevance, but what AbdulRazaq has done to make former allies look elsewhere.

There is nothing superior to a man’s ego. For the G-15/ TOP to look at the man they once opposed and decide that working with Saraki again is preferable to continuing with AbdulRazaq tells its own story. It is difficult to convince Kwarans that all these people suddenly became bad politicians while the man at the centre of the government remains perfect.

Loyalty is no longer the currency of APC politics in Kwara. Interest is. Many of the people standing with the Governor today are not necessarily there because they are loyal to Abdulrahman AbdulRazaq. They are there because they have something to gain from remaining close to power. That is politics, of course. But let us not dress interest up as loyalty.

Who, then, is more desperate to retain power? Is it the G-15/TOP that is questioning the direction of a government they once supported, or the Governor who wants to replace the party’s internal competition with his own anointed candidate? A Governor who cannot allow a genuinely competitive process within his own party but wants to determine who succeeds him should perhaps be the last person accusing others of political desperation.

The truth is that AbdulRazaq’s greatest political gamble may not be the opposition. It may be his belief that his own political preference can be transferred to another man simply because he occupies the Government House today. President Bola Ahmed Tinubu does not see AbdulRazaq as some indispensable Queen on the Kwara chessboard. With or without him, the President knows how to navigate Kwara politics. To describe AbdulRazaq’s political position as some guaranteed federal insurance is therefore a little delusional. Whatever calculations are being made in Abuja, the will of Kwarans will still matter at the ballot.

APC should also look carefully at the people it is taking into the 2027 contest. Take the three senatorial candidates.

In Kwara South, Lekan Adewoye is a candidate whose public personality and record have raised questions. A quick search of his name on Google brings up reports and allegations concerning fraud running into millions of naira. Punch Newspapers reported that the EFCC arraigned him and his companies over alleged stealing and obtaining property by false pretence involving $680,622.65. The case concerns construction materials supplied by a German company between 2013 and 2014. He pleaded not guilty, so this is not a conviction. But it is certainly a pattern that must not be overlooked. And what exactly has he done in Kwara South to make the people believe that he deserves to represent them? If his strongest qualification is that he received the ticket from the man who handed it to him, then the relationship may be more with AbdulRazaq than with the people of Kwara South. A senator should not owe his political existence to a Governor more than he owes it to his constituents.

In Kwara Central, we have Abdulrahman Abdulrazaq, a former Governor seeking another political role after eight years in which, by every reasonable measure, the state has struggled economically and developmentally. He presents himself as a political godfather, yet one of the criticisms surrounding his politics is the deliberate prevention of strong and independent political figures from emerging around him; no ranking senator, no independent power centre. Kwara Central will not suddenly lower the bar because somebody wants another political appointment.

Then there is the Kwara North candidate, a former director of a government agency who, until the emergence of this ticket, remained relatively unknown to many Kwarans, both online and offline. Where is the grassroots support? Where is the political connection with the people? Where is the record that makes the candidate more than simply another beneficiary of a ticket handed down from above?

The irony is that the same people now accusing the G-15 of disloyalty are the ones who have made loyalty increasingly transactional. When political interests are protected, everyone is loyal.

The PDP has become a safe haven for members of the G-15 because they have apparently come to the conclusion that whatever problems they had with Saraki are preferable to what they have experienced under AbdulRazaq. They have made their choice. And whether one agrees with them or not, they have every moral right to make it, if they believe their interests are better protected elsewhere, why should anyone expect them to remain in a house where they no longer feel welcome?

Saraki, for all the criticisms that can be made against him, has demonstrated something AbdulRazaq has struggled to demonstrate: the ability to maintain political relationships beyond the people currently useful to him. He built alliances. He created political structures. He governed. He went to Abuja. He returned. He lost elections. Yet he did not burn every bridge behind him.

AbdulRazaq spent many years of political battles which have left him with fewer friends and more former allies than when he started. That is the part the propaganda cannot explain.

President Tinubu can work with whoever emerges from Kwara. The President’s political future does not begin and end with AbdulRazaq. If APC loses Kwara, it will not mean Tinubu has lost Nigeria. The people of Kwara will simply have made their choice. Kwara APC should be more worried about its candidates than about Saraki’s alleged desperation.

•Abdulyekeen, Mohd Bashir, a Kwara-born political analyst, writes from Ilorin

World.title: Strategic Underwriting of the Life of Olusegun Ayo Omosehin @59
World.content:
By Tola Ogunnubi





Today, with a heart full of gratitude, I join the entire insurance community, colleagues, friends, and the beautiful family of Mr. Olusegun Ayo Omosehin, our distinguished Commissioner for Insurance and Chief Executive Officer of the National Insurance Commission (NAICOM), in celebrating the gift of his life.

Allow me to take you back to a rainy September evening in 2004. I was standing in the car park under the Apongbon Bridge on Lagos Island, an insurance agent living solely on commission, when I spotted a sharply dressed man. With the boldness that only hunger and hope can give, I approached him, hoping to underwrite a policy. He listened with quiet amusement, smiled, and then asked a question that would change the course of my life: “Would you like to work in an insurance company where you earn a steady monthly salary instead of living on commission alone, as a graduate of Actuarial Science from the University of Lagos?”

I seized the offer without hesitation. He gave me an address in Ikoyi. Two days later, on a wet Thursday morning, I arrived before 7:30 a.m. The office was not yet open, so I waited outside and watched the staff arrive, all well dressed, purposeful, and professionally looking. In that moment I silently prayed that I would one day belong to that fold. When the doors finally opened, I met Mr. Moruf Apampa, then Assistant General Manager (and today the MD/CEO of one of our leading insurers). He welcomed me with warmth, praised my boldness, and later took me upstairs to meet the Managing Director.

There, seated with quiet authority, was Mr. Olusegun Ayo Omosehin, MD/CEO of Admiral Insurance Company Limited. He looked at me briefly, as if assessing both the risk and the potential in equal measure, and asked just one question: “Are you ready to work?” I answered “Yes.” He simply said he liked my person. No further formal interview. No lengthy assessment. Just a handshake and a start date of 4th October 2004. In the language of our industry, that was pure strategic underwriting of talent (smiles), a decision taken on character and promise rather than on paperwork alone. That day, my path crossed with a man who would become far more than an employer.

Originally inclined toward the foreign service, he chose instead the path of insurance in June 1993 at Crusader Insurance Plc. Hailing from Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State, he was educated at United Anglican Primary School, Abe-alala, and C&S Academy, Ugbo-nla, before earning a Second Class Upper degree in Political Science from the then Ondo State University (now Ekiti State University) in 1990. After National Youth Service in Ikot-Ekpene, he obtained a Master of International Law and Diplomacy from the University of Lagos in 1992 and later an M.Sc. in Economics from the same institution. His professional armory was further strengthened at Lagos Business School and the Saïd Business School, University of Oxford. He became an Associate of the Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria in 1996 and is today a Fellow (FIIN), as well as a Fellow of the Institute of Directors and the Nigerian Institute of Management.

At Custodian and Allied Insurance, he rose to Divisional Head of Operations. In 2003 he took the helm at Admiral Insurance, a long-standing loss-making company, and restored it to profitability within his first year, proving once again that disciplined underwriting and sound risk selection can rewrite even the most difficult accounts. After the 2007 industry consolidation he led AIICO General Insurance through a comprehensive transformation. In 2010 he assumed leadership of Mutual Benefits Assurance Plc, repositioning it especially in the oil and gas segment over a decade of steady growth. In 2020 he became Managing Director of Old Mutual Nigeria Life Assurance Company Limited, continuing his pattern of strengthening balance sheets and institutional culture.

As the 25th Chairman of the Nigerian Insurers Association, he championed market discipline, self-regulation, insurance awareness, human capital development, and the faithful enforcement of compulsory insurances, always with the quiet conviction that a credible industry is the best protection for both policyholders and practitioners.

In April 2024, President Bola Tinubu appointed him the seventh Commissioner for Insurance and Chief Executive Officer of NAICOM. Since assuming office, he has steered the Commission with a clear five-point agenda: protecting policyholders and restoring public confidence through a better claims-settlement culture; strengthening NAICOM’s own regulatory capacity; safeguarding the solvency and financial soundness of operators; fostering innovation; and expanding accessibility and penetration across the nation. Under his watch the Nigerian Insurance Industry Reform Act (NIIRA) 2025 has been advanced, a major recapitalization exercise successfully concluded, and the Insurance Policyholders’ Protection Fund established which are all steps toward a more resilient, trustworthy, and inclusive market.

The successful completion of the insurance sector recapitalization exercise is a strong indication heralding a new era of insurance in Nigeria. Driven by the NIIRA 2025, signed into law by President Bola Tinubu on 31 July 2025, this reform forms part of broader financial-sector initiatives aimed at supporting a US$1 trillion economy by 2030. These reforms have seen insurance stocks lead market gains (contributing, for instance, to a N481 billion rise in market capitalization in a single session), with several names posting strong double-digit percentage gains as confidence in the sector grew and its contribution to the nation’s GDP strengthened.

Beyond the titles and the turnarounds, he remains a pioneer of many firsts, a devoted husband, a wonderful father, a reliable and responsible boss, supportive to a fault, and a defender to the end. His frequent reference is admirable; he would often say, “Oga Tola, look I started early and I am grateful to God for His grace. I have been lucky by working hard.” His corrective glance still speaks a million words of guidance and care.

In the vast ledger of life, where destinies are underwritten by the invisible hand of Providence, he appears, from time to time, as a rare soul whose presence becomes both premium and protection to all who walk under his shadow. He is a man whose life is itself a master policy of excellence, written in the indelible ink of integrity, wisdom, and quiet strength.

He is not merely a boss; he is a sanctuary. He is not merely a mentor; he is a living lighthouse, standing firm on the rocky shores of ambition, casting a steady beam that guides young sailors safely through the fog of uncertainty into the harbour of purpose. Over two decades later, Mr. Omoschin remains my coach, mentor, preceptor, torchbearer, and living exemplar. He is an insurance industry enigma, a man whose career has been one long masterclass in risk management, institutional turnaround, and the patient building of trust.

On this special day, as you mark your 59th birthday, I thank God for the gift of your life and for the privilege of walking part of this journey under your mentorship. May the years ahead bring you continued success, long life, sound health, peace of mind, a bountiful harvest from every seed you have sown in career and family, and the joyful fulfilment of every good dream still held in your heart.

To all admirers, friends and family, please join me in wishing my boss, mentor, and role model a truly happy birthday. Thank you, and may Heaven continue to underwrite every good intention of your life.

•Tola Ogunnubi NAICOM, Abuja

World.title: Dr. Adefunke Soyibo: 19 Years On, Betting Big on Affordable Furniture at HNK Interiors
World.content:
Dr. Adefunke Soyibo, Founder and CEO of HNK Interiors and HNK Designs Centre, recently commissioned the new HNK Interiors Manufactory and unveiled the HNK Design Centre in Lekki, Lagos. The event was flagged off by Senior Pastor of Trinity House, Pastor Ituah Ighodalo, who cut the tape and prayed for both the space and its founder. It was more than a launch. It was proof that Nigerian design can build, manufacture, and dream big – all under one roof. After 19 years in business and five years in manufacturing, HNK is betting big on local production, faster delivery, and furniture Nigerians can actually afford. Writes Mary Nnah

The launch comes 19 years after HNK began and 5 years after it ventured into manufacturing. According to Soyibo, the goal is simple: scale local production, cut delivery times, and make quality furniture available to more Nigerians.

The message was clear. Nigerian creativity can design, build, and manufacture world-class pieces — all under one roof.

This wasn’t just another opening. It was a statement.

After nearly two decades in interiors and five years in production, HNK is doubling down on Made-in-Nigeria, faster turnarounds, and furniture the average Nigerian can afford.

Outgrowing Small

For Dr. Soyibo, the move was inevitable. HNK started in 2007, and five years ago opened its first furniture manufacturing company in Nigeria. But the space quickly became too tight.

“Five years after that, we realised that the space was no longer conducive. It was becoming rather too small. And we were not able to achieve as much as we wanted to,” she said.

The solution wasn’t just a bigger factory. It was a purpose-built space to express creativity, keep up with fast-changing interior trends, and showcase everything HNK can manufacture locally.

“We decided it was time to move into a more purpose-built space where we will be able to express ourselves more. Our turnaround time can be faster. And above all, to be able to express ourselves better.”

90% Made in Nigeria

Walk through the new Design Centre, and you will see kitchen cabinets, walk-in closets, wall panels, velvet baths, rattan lampshades, and “HNK Casa” – a staged restaurant setting for baby showers, bridal showers, and intimate dinners.

“A good 90% of what you see here, we made at the HNK Interiors factory,” Dr. Soyibo said. “We’re trying to promote the Made in Nigeria business.”

The push is driven by economics as much as pride. With rising exchange rates, full importation is pricing out the average Nigerian.

“If we are going to keep up with importation alone, we won’t be able to meet up. A lot of people won’t be able to afford our stuff.”

So HNK imports what can’t be sourced here – like foldable plywood and certain fabrics – then assembles and finishes in Lagos. Rattan lampshades are sourced locally, then styled and sprayed in-house.

“We want the quality to be high, but at the same time we want it to be affordable. So we are merging the two. That local control also means speed. A client who wants a dining chair in beige instead of wine? “Give us three days. We will turn it around.”

A Showroom That Pays for Itself

The Design Centre isn’t just for display. It’s designed to generate income and stay fresh. The plan is to change the entire setup every quarter. Old pieces won’t go to waste – HNK will hold “yard sales” with 30-50% discounts.

In the meantime, the space rents by the hour, minimum two hours. There’s “The Globe” for album promos, “The Velvet Bath” for talk shows, a “dialogue zone” with podcast mics, and “The HNK Concert” – a 25-30 seater for training, corporate meetings, and surprise parties.

“If you are a fashion designer, you sell wigs, you sell hair products – come do a video shoot. Change your outfit. Be very happy. Bookings are live at www.hnk.org/design-centre ”, she said.

The Hard Parts: Power, People, and Purpose

Manufacturing in Nigeria comes with power issues, logistics, and staffing challenges. Dr. Soyibo was blunt about finding skilled artisans.

“I started with Nigerian guys. Yoruba boys and Igbo boys. It was a nightmare,” she said. “Until we discovered the Benin Republic artisans. They pay attention to detail. They are not lazy.”

Her survival mantra: “When there is a will, there is a way.

The power issue has been there before we were born. You’re not going to say because you have all those issues, you are not going to do what you have to do.”

The Sector is Evolving

Dr. Soyibo believes Nigerian design is in a golden era, helped by hard work, the internet, and AI. “If you are very creative, the sky is not even the limit because you can FRIDAYachieve so much more.”

She started HNK in 2007 with a small idea. Today, the company serves other designers as a one-stop shop and is already dreaming of more HNK centres.

In his remarks, Pastor Ighodalo called it “discovery of purpose.” “Start small, grow big. Start small, grow big. But start small. That’s the most important thing.”

In his remarks, Senior Pastor of Trinity House, Pastor Ituah Ighodalo, called the launch a “discovery of purpose” and a lesson in faith-driven growth.

“Start small, grow big. Start small, grow big. But start small. That’s the most important thing,” he told guests.

“What we are seeing here today is the result of vision, hard work, and staying power.”

He commended Dr. Soyibo for building steadily over 19 years and for choosing to invest in Nigeria at a time when many businesses are looking outward.

“This is not just about furniture or interiors. This is about nation building. When you manufacture here, you employ here. When you train here, you build capacity here. That is how nations grow,” he said.

Pastor Ighodalo then cut the ceremonial tape and offered prayers for the new HNK Interiors Manufactory and HNK Design Centre, dedicating the space, the staff, and the founder to God.

“We pray that this place will be a centre of creativity, of excellence, and of prosperity. That every hand that works here will be blessed, and every client that walks through here will find beauty and value”, the cleric prayed.

He added that businesses like HNK are proof that Nigeria’s creative sector can compete globally if given the right support and mindset.

As the prayers ended, guests toured the facility – “Every single piece of furniture you see here tonight, we manufactured at HNK Manufacturing. To the glory of God,” Dr. Soyibo said.

World.title: Benin Artifacts: How Museum Attack, Handover to Oba is Threatening US-Nigeria Treaty
World.content:
Crusoe Osagie writes that the attack on the museum in Benin City and the propriety of an individual taking sole possession of globally significant artifacts puts the future of cultural restitution in jeopardy

The battle over the ownership and custody of Nigeria’s returned Benin artefacts has moved beyond an internal Nigerian dispute. It is now threatening to undermine one of the country’s most important international cultural-property arrangements — the bilateral agreement with the United States designed to protect Nigerian heritage from illicit trafficking.

That is the uncomfortable reality confronting Nigeria as Washington considers the future of its cultural-property restrictions on Nigerian archaeological and ethnological material.

The question is no longer simply whether the Benin Bronzes should return home. They should. The deeper question is what happens to them after they arrive — who owns them, who has custody, where are they kept, who can access them, who can study them, who can exhibit them and, most importantly, who is ultimately accountable for their safety?

The events surrounding the Museum of West African Art (MOWAA) in Benin City have transformed those questions from theoretical concerns into an international credibility crisis.

In November 2025, protesters disrupted a preview event at MOWAA, forcing the evacuation of visitors and international guests. The confrontation was rooted in a dispute over the museum’s relationship with the Oba of Benin and the custody and display of returned Benin artefacts. The museum’s opening was subsequently postponed, while the controversy escalated into a wider political and institutional battle.

For a country seeking the continued cooperation of the United States in protecting its cultural heritage, the optics could hardly be worse.

A treaty built on mutual confidence

The United States and Nigeria signed their bilateral cultural-property agreement on January 20, 2022. Implemented under the U.S. Cultural Property Implementation Act, the agreement allows the United States to impose import restrictions on specified categories of Nigerian archaeological and ethnological material.

The restrictions cover archaeological material dating approximately from 1500 BCE to 1770 CE, as well as certain categories of ethnological material extending into the modern period. The underlying purpose is straightforward: to prevent the illicit trafficking of Nigerian cultural property into the United States and to support the preservation of Nigeria’s heritage.

This is an important international instrument.

It means that American customs and law-enforcement authorities can act to prevent certain Nigerian cultural objects from entering the United States without the documentation required under the agreement.

But such arrangements are based on a fundamental assumption: that the country asking the international community to protect its heritage has credible systems for protecting, documenting and accounting for that heritage at home.

That assumption is now under pressure.

The United States is not being asked merely to recognise the historical wrong committed against the Kingdom of Benin in 1897. It is being asked to help Nigeria protect cultural property as a matter of continuing national policy.

And that requires more than moral arguments about colonial plunder.

It requires institutions, inventories, chain-of-custody records, professional museums, security and a clear answer to the question: who is responsible?

The Benin Bronzes could disappear again

The Benin Bronzes occupy a unique position in the history of restitution.

British forces invaded Benin City in 1897, looted the royal palace and dispersed thousands of objects across Europe and North America. The objects subsequently became some of the most important and celebrated African works in the world’s great museums.

The restitution movement has therefore been driven by a powerful moral proposition: objects taken through colonial violence should be returned to their communities of origin.

That argument has gained extraordinary momentum.

Germany, for example, reached an agreement with Nigeria concerning the return of Benin Bronzes, with UNESCO describing the 2022 arrangement as involving the return of 1,130 objects and broader cultural cooperation, including archaeological research, museum training and support for a new museum in Benin City.

The Netherlands and other European countries have likewise returned objects.

The international restitution movement is therefore producing precisely the outcome Nigeria has long demanded.

But restitution creates a new obligation.

Once an object is returned, the receiving country assumes responsibility for proving that it can protect what the world has entrusted to it.

That is where Nigeria’s current predicament becomes particularly serious.

Placing the artefacts entirely under the Oba

In 2023, the Federal Government formally recognised the Oba of Benin as the custodian of returned Benin Bronzes. The decision has fundamentally altered the institutional landscape surrounding restitution.

The problem is not the cultural authority of the Oba.

There is no question that the Benin monarchy is central to the history and meaning of the artefacts. The objects were looted from the royal palace in 1897. The Oba therefore has an entirely legitimate and profound cultural interest in their restitution and interpretation.

The problem is the absence of a sufficiently robust institutional framework separating cultural custodianship from exclusive administrative control.

That distinction matters enormously.

A traditional institution can be the symbolic guardian of a people’s heritage without becoming the sole institutional gatekeeper of nationally and internationally significant cultural property.

Indeed, the distinction is at the heart of the international museum system.

The objects are not merely valuable possessions. They are historical records, works of art, archaeological evidence and sources of scholarship. Their significance extends beyond the walls of a palace.Researchers need access. Students need access. Museums need access. Future generations need access. The Nigerian public needs access.

And international partners whose institutions surrendered the objects need confidence that they have not simply exchanged one uncertain custody arrangement for another.

The museum confrontation

The events at MOWAA in November 2025 should therefore not be dismissed as an isolated disturbance.

They exposed the consequences of failing to resolve the institutional question before the artefacts began returning in significant numbers.

MOWAA was conceived as a major cultural institution in Benin City, with international backing and substantial investment. The museum was designed to provide modern conservation, research and exhibition infrastructure and was initially associated with plans to accommodate returned Benin artefacts.

But by the time of its planned opening, the Bronzes were not going to be displayed there.

The dispute erupted publicly when protesters entered the museum during a preview event. International and Nigerian guests were evacuated. MOWAA subsequently clarified that it did not own or claim title to the Benin Bronzes and said its focus was broader West African art, research, education and conservation.

That clarification is important.

But it does not make the underlying problem disappear.

A multimillion-dollar museum built with international support had become embroiled in a dispute over whether an institution devoted to art, conservation, research and public education had the legitimacy to participate in the stewardship of the very cultural heritage that had helped inspire its creation.

That should alarm everyone involved in the restitution movement.

Because the message being transmitted internationally is potentially devastating:

Return the artefacts to Nigeria — and then watch Nigeria fight over where they should go.

The land controversy made matters worse

The crisis subsequently expanded beyond the artefacts themselves.

In November 2025, Edo State Governor Monday Okpebholo revoked the Right of Occupancy previously granted to MOWAA. The action came amid the escalating controversy involving the museum, the Oba’s palace and the previous administration of Governor Godwin Obaseki.

Whatever one’s position on the competing claims, the international implication is troubling.

A museum supported by international partners suddenly found itself caught in a domestic struggle involving the traditional institution, the state government, federal authorities, donors and the museum’s trustees.

This is precisely the sort of institutional instability that can make foreign museums and governments hesitate before surrendering priceless cultural objects.

The restitution movement depends on trust.

And trust is fragile.

The United States asking difficult questions

This is why the renewal of the U.S.–Nigeria cultural-property agreement matters.

The agreement is not an unconditional declaration of faith in Nigeria.

It is a reciprocal cultural-protection mechanism.

The United States has effectively accepted an obligation to restrict the importation of specified Nigerian cultural materials because those materials are regarded as part of Nigeria’s cultural patrimony and are vulnerable to illicit trafficking.

But Washington can reasonably ask:

If Nigeria cannot clearly demonstrate who has custody of returned objects, how can American authorities confidently distinguish legitimate cultural circulation from illicit trafficking?

If national institutions, state governments and the palace can assert competing claims, who is legally accountable when an object disappears?

If a museum can become the subject of physical confrontation because of disagreements over cultural authority, what does that say about the security environment for returned objects?

And if returned artefacts are placed outside conventional public museum structures, how does Nigeria demonstrate that they remain accessible for scholarship, conservation and public education?

These are not anti-Nigeria questions.

They are precisely the questions that a serious heritage-protection regime should ask.

Nigeria, demanding foreign security, perpetuating uncertainty at home

The strongest argument against Nigeria’s position would not come from a foreign museum defending its possession of a Benin Bronze.

It would come from Nigeria’s own failure to establish an unimpeachable system of stewardship after restitution.

This is the central danger.

The international community has been persuaded that returning the Benin Bronzes to Nigeria is morally and historically justified.

But the next stage of the argument requires Nigeria to demonstrate that restitution will result in better stewardship, not simply a change in the location of custody.

There should therefore be a single authoritative national inventory of returned Benin artefacts.

Every object should have a unique identification number.

Its provenance should be documented.

Its ownership status should be clear.

Its custodian should be identified.

Its physical location should be known.

Its conservation status should be recorded.

Its movements should be traceable.

And the public should be able to consult an authoritative digital record.

This is not excessive bureaucracy.

It is the minimum standard required to protect objects whose international value can run into millions of dollars and whose historical significance is, in many cases, literally priceless.

The wider danger is to restitution itself

There is an even bigger issue here.

If Western museums are persuaded to return African cultural objects and those objects subsequently become trapped in political disputes, placed in uncertain custody or removed from public access, the next generation of restitution negotiations will become considerably harder.

Museum directors in London, Berlin, Paris, Amsterdam and New York will inevitably ask whether returning objects represents the end of a historical injustice or the beginning of a new governance problem.

That would be a tragedy.

The restitution campaign has taken decades to build.

Nigeria must not inadvertently weaken it.

The answer is not to abandon restitution.

It is to make restitution more institutionally sophisticated.

Returned heritage should be protected through structures that bring together the authority of the traditional institution, the legal authority of the Nigerian state, the technical expertise of professional museums and the resources and standards of international cultural institutions.

The Godwin Obaseki foresight

Former Edo State Governor Godwin Obaseki was never opposed to the role of the Benin Palace in the restitution process.

On the contrary, his proposed solution explicitly sought to place the Palace at the centre of a broader institutional structure.

In March 2021, while discussing the return of looted Benin artefacts with German officials, Obaseki advocated the establishment of an independent trust involving the Royal Family, Edo State Government, Federal Government and international stakeholders. The stated objective was to create a transparent and properly resourced structure capable of overseeing the museum project and activities relating to the returned works.

That proposal now looks less like bureaucratic caution and more like a remarkably prescient attempt to prevent precisely the crisis Nigeria is experiencing today.

The idea was not to exclude the Oba.

It was to include the Oba.

It was not to diminish the Federal Government.

It was to include the Federal Government.

It was not to subordinate Edo State.

It was to give Edo State a defined institutional role.

And it was not to shut international partners out.

It was to bring them into a transparent governance structure.

In other words, the proposed trust recognised a simple truth: no single institution should be expected to carry the enormous responsibility of managing one of Africa’s most consequential collections of cultural heritage.

A properly constituted trust, with trustees representing the Palace of the Oba of Benin, the Federal Government, Edo State Government and credible international partners, could have provided precisely the institutional bridge that is now missing.

Such a structure could have created clear rules for custody, conservation, exhibition, research, loans, insurance, provenance documentation, security and public access.

Most importantly, it could have insulated the artefacts from changes in political administration.

That is the real tragedy of the present controversy.

The argument over who should control the Benin artefacts has become so politicised that the world is beginning to see not a united Nigerian campaign for restitution, but a contest among competing Nigerian authorities.

Institutional maturity over institutional rivalry

The solution is still available.

Nigeria should not respond to the international concerns by attacking those who raise them.

Nor should it respond by portraying every question about accountability as an attempt to keep African heritage in Western museums.

That would miss the point.

The world has already moved significantly toward accepting Nigeria’s moral and historical case.

Now Nigeria must win the next argument: that it has the institutional maturity to be entrusted with what it has fought so hard to recover.

The answer should be a comprehensive Benin Heritage Trust.

The Palace should be represented. The Federal Government should be represented. The Edo State Government should be represented. Professional museum and heritage experts should be represented. And credible international partners should have a defined role.

The Trust should maintain a publicly accessible inventory, establish internationally credible conservation and security standards, publish audited accounts, document every returned object and its location, facilitate research and exhibition, and guarantee that the artefacts remain protected as heritage held for the benefit of present and future generations.

The choice before Nigeria

The Benin Bronzes were taken from Nigeria through one of the most infamous episodes of colonial violence in African history. Their return is therefore a matter of justice.

But justice does not end at the airport runway.

It continues in the museum. It continues in the archive. It continues in the conservation laboratory. It continues in the classroom. It continues in the public exhibition.

And it continues in the governance structures that guarantee that these objects will remain available to Nigerians and to humanity.

The United States should continue supporting the protection of Nigerian cultural heritage. Germany, the Netherlands, Britain and other countries should continue engaging with Nigeria on restitution. International institutions should continue helping Nigeria build world-class museums and conservation capacity.

But Nigeria must meet that international goodwill with an equally serious commitment to accountability.

The attack on MOWAA, the continuing dispute over custody and the decision to place returned artefacts under the control of the Oba have combined to create a question that Nigeria can no longer avoid: who ultimately protects the protectors of Nigeria’s heritage?

The answer cannot be one politician. It cannot be one government. It cannot be one museum. And it cannot, however revered, be one individual. It must be an institution.

That was precisely what Obaseki was trying to prevent when he insisted on a trust structure bringing together trustees from the Palace of the Oba of Benin, the Federal Government, the Edo State Government and international partners to oversee the returned Benin artefacts.

The wisdom of that proposal is now painfully apparent.

If Nigeria wants the United States to continue standing guard against the illicit export of its cultural patrimony, Nigeria must first demonstrate that the patrimony which has already come home is safe, accounted for, professionally managed and held in trust for the public.

The Benin Bronzes were stolen from Nigeria once. The country must ensure that institutional confusion does not become the reason the world begins to fear losing them a second time.

And if Nigeria fails to resolve that problem, the greatest casualty may not be the U.S.–Nigeria cultural-property agreement alone. It may be the international confidence on which the entire African restitution movement depends.

World.title: Dr. Adegbajo Odedina: Building Haven Pediatrics to Fight Nigeria’s Child Mortality Crisis
World.content:
Dr. Adegbajo Odedina once planned to join the wave of Nigerian doctors leaving the country. But he walked away from that plan and from a comfortable life abroad to come home with a mission.

Faced with Nigeria’s staggering child and neonatal mortality rates, the pediatrician and neonatologist set out to build something different: a hospital that treats only children. What started as a modest 9-to-5 clinic in GRA, Ikeja, has grown into Haven Pediatrics, a 24-hour mono-specialist facility. Here, there are no adult wards. Just pediatric consultants, a NICU, and every sub-specialty a child might need, all under one roof. For premature babies and children with complex conditions, it is a place built for one purpose: to give them specialists, equipment, and round-the-clock care and a real fighting chance. Writes MARY NNAH

At 1am on a quiet night, the phone at Haven Pediatrics rang. A baby, just 4 days old, was being rushed in from a general hospital in the Iyana Ipaja axis. The child was already on a makeshift “bottle CPAP” – tubes in a bottle of water being used to push oxygen.

“We see this too often,” said Dr. Adegbajo Odedina, Chief Medical Director of Haven Pediatrics. “By the time some babies get to us, they have lost precious hours.”

Four hours later, that baby was on a proper CPAP machine, in a temperature-controlled incubator, under the watch of a pediatrician. It is the save Dr. Odedina left the UK for.

There Is Something I Can Fix

Dr. Odedina trained and worked in both public and private hospitals in Nigeria and abroad. Like many doctors, he once planned to leave for good.
