Madbouly explained that implementing this massive project faced numerous challenges, particularly the lack of comprehensive information at the outset regarding the services already available in villages, the complexity of implementing the projects, and challenges related to allocating land needed for their construction.

He pointed out that overcoming these challenges required tremendous efforts involving millions of Egyptians, including consulting firms, universities and construction companies, stressing that the scale of the work carried out reflects the magnitude of the project and the extensive efforts it has required over the past years.

Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said the government is contributing to improving the quality of life for more than 60 million citizens through the three phases of the major “Decent Life” (Haya Karima) initiative.

He said the government had gained considerable experience following the completion of the first phase of the initiative, adding that the new phase is currently focused as a top priority on sanitation projects and improving water quality, as well as healthcare projects, including hospitals and health and medical units, in addition to schools.

Madbouly said the initiative had also created significant employment opportunities, noting that the unemployment rate had fallen below 6 percent. “We are moving in the right direction despite all the unprecedented challenges we are facing,” he said.

The prime minister also highlighted the “Ras El Hekma” medical project in Matrouh, which has been fully developed, as well as expansion plans across the governorate. He pointed to the construction of an entirely new building for Alamein Hospital and the “Alam El Roum” Hospital, the governorate’s main hospital, which has hundreds of beds.

He added that major medical services are being implemented alongside housing and development projects, as well as the Alam El Roum project being developed through an Egyptian-Qatari partnership.

Madbouly stressed that tourism is a genuine source of income for Egypt, saying it is encouraging to see the large presence of foreign tourists on the North Coast. This, he noted, means an inflow of foreign currency into the country, as well as job opportunities for young people living in these areas throughout the year.

He noted that the North Coast has strong tourism potential, pointing to the acceleration in the development of tourism projects. Such projects, he said, will create job opportunities and generate billions of dollars in revenues for the state.

The prime minister also touched on the high-speed railway serving the development process, saying it would help citizens travel from Cairo to Matrouh, as well as along the “Ain Sokhna-Matrouh-Salloum” route, alongside electricity, energy and development projects.

He stressed that the government is safeguarding the state’s rights and that an integrated vision for the development of the North Coast will benefit the people of Matrouh by generating jobs and development opportunities.

Madbouly affirmed that development is at the heart of every part of Egypt, urging people to consider the scale of development achieved over the past 12 years, compared with the situation in Egypt before that period and the country’s current position, despite the unprecedented external challenges.

He added that the government is focusing on improving citizens’ quality of life and has comprehensive plans to address existing challenges. The government is nearing completion of a program aimed at launching an economic transformation over the next three years.

“Our goal is to anticipate all possible scenarios that could unfold globally and their impact on us, including the continuation of the conflicts currently taking place,” he said.

On the energy sector, Madbouly said the government reviews the file on a weekly basis with the officials responsible for it.

He added that, under the visions and strategies set by the political leadership for the sector since 2014, the state has undertaken a large number of projects whose benefits are now being realized and whose returns are being reaped during the current phase.

He affirmed that Egypt is capable of meeting the energy sector’s needs over the coming period.

World.title: Finance Minister: LE 6 bln targeted for cash payment of third tranche of exporters’ dues
World.content:
Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk said the government is targeting the allocation of six billion LE to pay in cash the third tranche of overdue dues owed to exporters for shipments made before July 1, 2024.

Kouchouk said applications from exporting companies seeking to benefit from the third tranche of the cash payment initiative will be accepted from Aug. 16 through Oct. 1, with payments scheduled to be disbursed on Oct. 22.

In a statement issued on Tuesday, August 11, 2026, the minister said more than LE 80 billion has been paid to exporters over the past six years, adding that the government aims to clear all outstanding dues within two years.

He noted that LE 48 billion has been allocated in the current budget to accelerate the provision of export support, while export subsidies reached LE 28 billion in fiscal year 2025/2026, marking annual growth of 55%.

Kouchouk said there is ongoing coordination and integration with the Ministry of Investment and Foreign Trade to develop the export system and boost the export sector.

He stressed that the government is working to provide exporters with liquidity to support the growth and competitiveness of Egypt’s goods and services exports, adding that it aims to significantly increase annual allocations for export support and promotion in order to open new markets for Egyptian products.

Meanwhile, Nevine Mansour, the minister’s adviser for economic institutions’ relations, said LE 12.6 billion in cash had been paid to around 2,500 exporting companies during the last fiscal year.

She noted that the amount represented the total value of the first and second tranches of overdue dues paid in cash during fiscal year 2025/2026, instead of being paid over two fiscal years.

World.title: Petroleum Minister: Proactive plans remain in place to secure natural gas market needs
World.content:
Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources Karim Badawi has affirmed that the petroleum sector continues to implement comprehensive, proactive plans to secure the local market’s natural gas needs.

He stressed the importance of managing shifts in consumption with high efficiency and flexibility, while maintaining maximum readiness to handle any emergencies or developments.

This came as the minister reviewed the operational status of the national natural gas grid directly from the Egyptian Natural Gas Company (GASCO) control center.

He inspected the steady flow of gas to various domestic sectors and evaluated strategic plans to meet energy demands through the remainder of the summer season.

During his visit, the minister verified uninterrupted gas supplies to power generation plants to ensure grid stability amid soaring temperatures.

He also monitored deliveries to the industrial sector to guarantee that factories operate at full capacity, alongside fulfilling domestic market requirements and export commitments.

Badawi noted that decisive state measures, backed by the political leadership and the government, have successfully met local demand throughout the first half of the summer.

Key actions included procuring regasification vessels and natural gas shipments, boosting domestic production, and implementing forward-looking supply strategies, he said.

Concluding his remarks, the minister underscored the necessity of continuous coordination between the petroleum and electricity sectors, alongside other relevant authorities.

This integrated approach aims to guarantee sustainable energy supplies for all state sectors moving forward, supported by real-time monitoring of the grid, consumption rates, and supply flows.

World.title: Miss Rachelle Gayee is the Newly Crowned Miss Liberia USA 2026
World.content:
Miss Rachelle Gayee was crowned Miss Liberia USA 2026 at Square Globe Studios in Atlanta, Georgia, on July 26, 2026. She proudly represents the Liberian community with grace, purpose, and a heart for service. Rachelle, who previously held the title of Miss Liberia Pennsylvania, earned the crown at the Miss Liberia in the U.S. Pageant 2026.

A first-generation Liberian American from Pennsylvania, Rachelle is currently pursuing a degree in Psychology and aspires to become a pediatric psychologist. Her passion for mental health, particularly among children and underserved communities, inspired her platform, Wellness Without Walls, which focuses on increasing access to mental health education, reducing stigma, and encouraging open conversations about emotional well-being.

Winning the title of Miss Liberia USA 2026 marks a significant milestone in Rachelle’s journey. More than a personal achievement, she views the crown as an opportunity to advocate for meaningful change, celebrate Liberian culture, and inspire young people to pursue their dreams with confidence and purpose.

As Miss Liberia USA 2026, Rachelle will represent Liberia at the Miss Global pageant in Thailand this fall, where she will compete alongside contestants from around the world. She hopes to use this international platform to shine a positive light on Liberia, promote cultural pride, and continue raising awareness for mental health initiatives.

World.title: Liberia: LIPO Awards Prize Money to Maretha, Other Schools
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Liberia Intellectual Property Office (LIPO) has awarded Maretha International Preparatory High School US$1,000 for winning the national final of the WIPO-ARIPO Intellectual Property Club Competition and an additional US$700 for winning the regional final in Harare, Zimbabwe.

As the national champion, Maretha represented Liberia against schools from other African countries, including Tanzania, Rwanda, and Ghana, and won the regional championship in the process.

The competition is organized by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) and the African Regional Intellectual Property Organization (ARIPO) to promote intellectual property awareness among secondary school students across Africa. Participating students demonstrate their knowledge through quizzes, presentations, role-playing and practical exercises focused on copyright, trademarks, patents, creativity and innovation.

William V.S. Tubman High School and St. Theresa Convent Catholic High School also received monetary awards after finishing as first and second runners-up, respectively, in the national phase. Tubman High received US$700, while St. Theresa Convent received US$500. The total prize money disbursed included US$2,200 from the Government of Liberia and US$700 from WIPO, bringing the overall prize money to US$2,900.

According to the competition assessment data, the second edition of the IP Club program reached 360 students across 18 schools in Nimba, Montserrado and Grand Bassa counties, with female students accounting for 57.7 percent of participants (208 students) and male students accounting for 42.3 percent (152 students).

The data further showed that students aged 13 to 15 constituted the largest participant group, accounting for 48.8 percent (176 students), followed by those aged 16 to 18 at 33.7 percent (121 students) and those aged 0 to 12 at 17.5 percent (63 students). According to the release, the average proportion of students demonstrating an overall understanding of intellectual property rights increased from 22.9 percent (82 students) at baseline to 93.3 percent (336 students) at endline.

“These results show that the second edition of the IP Club Competition, implemented across 18 schools, achieved its overall objective of expanding access to intellectual property education among secondary school students,” LIPO Director General Hon. Garmai Koboi said. “The increase in student understanding confirms that consistent intellectual property education can produce measurable results. It also gives us a strong foundation for expanding the program to more schools and counties.”

Meanwhile, LIPO has announced that the call for applications for the third edition of the IP Club Competition will be issued soon, with the program set to expand to 36 schools across six counties and reach 720 students and 72 teachers, compared with 18 schools, 360 students and 36 teachers during the second edition.

World.title: Liberia: Five LDEA Leadership Changes in Two Years—Senator Konneh Warns Liberia Cannot “Change the Figurehead” and Cure the Cancer
World.content:
MONROVIA— President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s decision to replace the leadership of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency marks the latest turn in a revolving door that has seen the agency change hands five times in just over two years.

By Obediah Johnson, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The appointment of retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, Jr. as Director General-designate comes as the LDEA and Liberia’s wider security establishment face perhaps their most serious credibility crisis in years.

But for Senator Amara Konneh, the latest change raises a question that goes beyond the credentials of the incoming director: Can Liberia fix a deeply troubled security institution simply by repeatedly changing the person at the top?

Konneh’s answer is no.

“Changing the leadership at LDEA does not automatically fix the cancer eating away at our security system,” the Senate Public Accounts and Audit Committee chairman warned Tuesday.

His argument goes to the heart of Liberia’s ongoing cocaine crisis. The country has recorded cocaine seizures valued at more than US$336 million, including an approximately US$317 million shipment intercepted in the VOA Community in Paynesville and a roughly US$19 million consignment seized at Roberts International Airport.

The investigations have generated allegations involving individuals connected to the security and law-enforcement establishment, triggered internal investigations and produced leadership changes.

Now, President Boakai has turned to Ziankahn, a retired military general and former Defense Minister, to restore stability and credibility to an agency that has experienced extraordinary leadership turbulence.

But the question remains whether another change at the top can address what critics describe as deeper institutional weaknesses.

Five Changes, One Troubled Agency

The significance of Ziankahn’s appointment is best understood against the backdrop of the leadership changes that preceded him.

Since taking office in January 2024, President Boakai has overseen five changes involving the top leadership of the LDEA—three director-general-level appointments and two periods in which officials served as Officer in Charge.

The revolving door is striking, particularly because the fight against illicit drugs was one of Boakai’s prominent campaign commitments.

After his inauguration, Boakai moved quickly to appoint Abraham Kromah, a veteran security officer who had previously served as Deputy Commissioner of Police for Operations under former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

Kromah arrived with a reputation as a tough law-enforcement officer, and his appointment was initially welcomed by many Liberians who expected him to bring a more aggressive approach to the fight against drugs, particularly the synthetic drug commonly known as Kush.

Instead, his tenure became embroiled in an internal management crisis.

A public confrontation involving Kromah and his deputies, Hassan Fadiga and Gbawou Kowou, escalated into a physical altercation and resulted in their suspension. The administration subsequently ordered an investigation, and following the submission of the report, Kromah and his deputies were removed.

But the report was never made public. That unresolved issue continues to hang over the agency. For the public, the unanswered question is simple: What did the investigation find? The absence of a public explanation has contributed to a recurring problem within the LDEA—major decisions are announced, but the underlying findings are often kept from public view.

Peters Leaves With a Warning

Following Kromah’s removal, Christopher K. Peters Sr. was appointed Officer in Charge of the LDEA on June 4, 2024. Peters’ tenure was brief.

Although he pointed to drug seizures worth more than US$4 million and lengthy prison sentences secured against traffickers, he resigned only months after taking office.

His resignation letter, addressed to then-Minister of State Sylvester M. Grigsby (now deceased), offered perhaps one of the clearest diagnoses of the agency’s institutional weaknesses.

Peters argued that winning the war on drugs required strategic reforms, enhanced training, additional personnel, adequate funding and sustained support from key partners. He also stressed the need for leadership capable of promoting calm, maturity and teamwork within the agency.

His resignation became effective October 31, 2024. Whether his recommendations were fully acted upon remains an open question.

Souh Returns—Then Leaves

Peters was succeeded by Anthony Souh, another experienced law-enforcement officer and former LDEA Director General during the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf administration, when Boakai served as Vice President.

Souh returned to the agency with institutional experience and familiarity with Liberia’s drug-enforcement challenges.

But his return did not produce lasting stability. About a year later, the Boakai administration removed Souh and other senior LDEA officials, paving the way for another restructuring.

Again, the cycle continued.

Then Came Biago

The next major leadership arrangement brought Fitzgerald T. M. Biago, a Deputy Commissioner of Police, into the agency’s leadership.

On August 28, 2025, President Boakai appointed Biago, a Deputy Commissioner of the Liberian National Police, as Officer-In-Charge. He led an interim management structure alongside Ernest T. Tarpeh of the National Security Agency and Patrick B. Kormazu of the LNP following the removal of Souh and other senior officials.

Nearly a year later, his leadership was thrown into controversy after activist Martin K. N. Kollie alleged that Biago had received a vehicle as a gift from Leroy Harris, a suspect in the US$317 million cocaine investigation.

Biago denied involvement in the drug allegations and stepped aside to make himself available for investigation.

A Ministry of Justice review did not establish his involvement in narcotics trafficking. But the government said the review identified ethical concerns, prompting President Boakai to indefinitely suspend Biago from the Liberia National Police and order a more detailed investigation.

Again, the distinction is important: the government did not establish that Biago was involved in the narcotics trade, but it found ethical concerns serious enough to warrant further action. And again, the LDEA was left with a leadership problem.

Now comes Ziankahn.

The retired major general brings perhaps the strongest national-security credentials of any of the recent LDEA appointees.

He became the first post-war Liberian Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia, appointed in 2014 after the restructuring of the military following the civil war. He had enlisted in the newly restructured Armed Forces of Liberia in 2006 and rose through the ranks before becoming Chief of Staff, a position he held from 2014 to 2018.

He subsequently served as Liberia’s Minister of National Defense under former President George Weah and later became Military Advisor to President Boakai.

Analysts say his appointment represents a significant shift in the profile of LDEA leadership. The administration appears to be betting that Ziankahn’s military and national-security experience can bring discipline, stability and strategic direction to an agency that has repeatedly struggled with internal turmoil. But that is precisely where Konneh’s warning becomes relevant.

A Revolving Door at the LDEA

Ziankahn’s appointment marks what amounts to the fifth leadership change at the LDEA in roughly two years under President Boakai—three director-general-level appointments and two individuals who have served as Officer in Charge.

The frequency of those changes raises a fundamental institutional question: If leadership keeps changing but the underlying vulnerabilities remain, is the problem really the person at the top?

The “Self-Policing” Problem

Senator Konneh argued that institutions implicated in allegations surrounding a major criminal investigation should not be left to investigate themselves.

“Institutions with heavy corruption and cartel allegations cannot investigate themselves,” he said, calling for an open, credible and independent inquiry into high-ranking individuals allegedly connected to the narcotics network.

That demand strikes at the heart of the cocaine investigations.

The magnitude of the seizures has transformed the issue from an ordinary drug-enforcement matter into a national security question.

A shipment valued at hundreds of millions of dollars does not move through international supply chains, ports, airports and local communities without sophisticated organization, financing, logistics and access.

That inevitably raises questions about whether criminal networks operated entirely outside the state—or whether individuals with access to official systems may have facilitated, enabled or shielded elements of the trade.

Those questions cannot be answered merely by replacing one agency director with another. They require investigators capable of following the evidence wherever it leads. And that means senior officials cannot be treated differently from ordinary suspects simply because of their positions.

Ziankahn’s Appointment: A Strong Man for a Weak System?

There is little doubt that Ziankahn brings considerable experience to the position. The retired major general previously served as Liberia’s Minister of National Defense and, more recently, as Military Advisor to President Boakai.

His background gives him significant exposure to national security operations and strategic decision-making. That experience could prove valuable to an agency that has been battered by leadership instability and public distrust.

But experience alone does not answer the central problem.

The question is whether Ziankahn will inherit an agency capable of functioning independently—or an institution whose credibility has been damaged by allegations that reach beyond its current leadership.

Konneh acknowledged Ziankahn’s credentials while making clear that his appointment does not erase the unresolved questions.

“We wish Gen. Ziankahn success in his Senate confirmation and in his tenure, but we will observe closely,” he said.

That may ultimately become the defining test of the new LDEA leadership.

Ziankahn will not merely be judged by the number of drug seizures under his watch. He will be judged by whether his tenure produces an agency in which investigations are insulated from political influence, evidence is protected, officers are held accountable, and no official is considered untouchable.

World.title: Liberia’s Drug Crisis: Accountability Must Begin Within the Security Sector
World.content:
Senator Amara Konneh’s latest intervention raises an important question that Liberia can no longer afford to avoid: Can the government effectively fight transnational drug trafficking while simultaneously confronting allegations of corruption within the very institutions responsible for fighting it?

By E. W. Cooper, contributing writer

I believe the answer must be yes—but only if the government is prepared to apply the same standard of accountability to everyone.

This is not about protecting the opposition, defending the government, or creating political scapegoats. It is about protecting Liberia’s national security.

The reported US$317 million cocaine seizure is not an ordinary criminal matter. It involves alleged transnational criminal networks, international partners, substantial financial resources, and allegations involving individuals within Liberia’s security architecture. That requires an investigation that is professional, evidence-driven, and insulated from conflicts of interest.

I therefore agree with Senator Konneh on one fundamental principle: there must be no sacred cows.

But accountability must be based on evidence.

If an officer is accused of accepting money, investigate the financial trail.

If an officer claims he was instructed to escort a shipment, examine the communications records.

If someone is alleged to have facilitated communication between detained suspects and an international network, examine the phones, financial transactions, surveillance footage, and other available evidence.

If an official is accused of interfering with an investigation, determine exactly what action was taken, when it occurred, and whether it violated the law.

And if allegations are made against the Inspector General or any other senior official, those allegations should receive the same objective scrutiny.

Recusal Is About Integrity

This is where my position remains consistent.

When serious allegations begin pointing toward an official who has a significant role in overseeing an investigation, recusal can be an act of institutional integrity rather than an admission of guilt.

The objective is not to remove someone because they have been accused. The objective is to ensure that the person being questioned is not simultaneously in a position to influence the investigation into those questions.

If the official is innocent, an independent process can establish that.

If the allegations are unsupported, the official’s credibility can be restored.

And if evidence establishes wrongdoing, the law should apply.

That is precisely why an impartial process matters.

International Assistance Should Strengthen, Not Replace Liberia

There is another important point.

International involvement in a case of this magnitude should not be interpreted as evidence that Liberians are incapable of investigating their own country. Liberia has capable law-enforcement and security professionals.

International partners can provide specialized expertise, intelligence, forensic capabilities, financial investigations, and transnational investigative connections that are particularly valuable in organized-crime cases.

But Liberian institutions must remain part of the process.

The objective should be partnership—not institutional surrender.

The President’s Test

President Boakai now faces an important test of leadership.

The public does not simply need arrests. It needs to see a process that is credible.

The President must demonstrate that accountability is not determined by rank, political affiliation, personal relationships, or institutional loyalty.

If someone is innocent, clear them.

If someone violated administrative rules, discipline them.

If someone committed a crime, prosecute them.

And if the evidence leads to someone at the highest level of government or security institutions, follow the evidence there as well.

That is what the rule of law means.

The government should not fear the truth. The truth, properly established through evidence and due process, ultimately protects legitimate institutions.

The greatest danger would be for Liberia to investigate this matter selectively—protecting some, sacrificing others, and allowing public pressure rather than evidence to determine the outcome.

This investigation should not be about Cocaingate as a political slogan.

It should be about establishing exactly who knew what, who did what, who benefited, who facilitated the operation, who attempted to obstruct the investigation, and whether anyone within Liberia’s security apparatus compromised the Republic for personal gain.

Follow the evidence.

No sacred cows. No scapegoats. No selective justice.

Just truth, accountability, due process, and the rule of law.E. W. Cooper is a Law enforcement supervisor, Homeland Security & Emergency Management professional, and a Criminal Justice scholar.

World.title: U.S. Signal to Liberia’s Drug War Carries Extra Weight After Record Busts — and a Cloud Over Its Chief Enforcers
World.content:
The U.S. Embassy meeting between Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny and Liberia’s top police officials — Inspector General Gregory Coleman and EPS Director Sam Gaye — comes at a fraught moment: a $19 million cocaine bust in July was followed by a record $317 million seizure implicating senior police officers themselves, some now facing charges. Coleman has also faced unproven allegations of ties to the trafficking network, making the embassy’s emphasis on “accountability” read as pointed encouragement rather than blanket endorsement.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia- By any measure, U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny’s meeting with Liberia National Police Inspector General Gregory O.W. Coleman and Executive Protection Service Director Sam Gaye should have been a routine diplomatic courtesy. Instead, it lands at one of the most consequential moments in Liberia’s modern anti-narcotics effort — and its timing, coming just as President Boakai reshuffles the LDEA’s leadership for the third time in two years, makes it read as something closer to a signal than a formality.

Why the timing matters

The meeting follows two extraordinary seizures in the space of a few weeks. In July, security personnel intercepted six cargo boxes at Roberts International Airport disguised as textiles and seasoning cubes; inside were nearly 200 compressed blocks of cocaine, ultimately valued around $19 million — a case that drew public criticism after delays in identifying suspects raised fears that individuals connected to the shipment had already fled the country. Weeks later came a seizure of a different order of magnitude entirely: nearly four tonnes of cocaine, worth an estimated $317.7 million, recovered from what investigators described as an organized, sophisticated, and well-funded trafficking network that may have operated in Liberia for more than six years. Authorities later incinerated 4.2 metric tons of the drug, sending what Coleman called a message that Liberia was no longer “a place of comfort” for traffickers.

What has made the second bust politically explosive, however, is who it implicated. Coleman confirmed that Liberia’s chief of highway patrol and the head of the major crimes unit face charges, with a deputy police commander at the main airport also under suspicion — meaning the very institution now meant to lead enforcement, the Liberia National Police, has senior officers accused of facilitating the trafficking it is supposed to stop.

The credibility problem the U.S. visit runs into

That is precisely why Zadrozny’s meeting cannot be read purely as encouragement. Coleman himself has become a subject of serious, if unproven, allegations. In a July 15 letter to Zadrozny, CDC Secretary General Jefferson Koijee requested U.S. backing for an international investigation, alleging that Coleman took vehicles from a drug cartel and distributed them to President Boakai, Vice President Koung, and the presiding officers of the Legislature, and separately that the 2024 removal of former LDEA head Abraham Kromah was orchestrated by Coleman to protect a cartel he was allegedly connected to, and that Coleman later maneuvered Fitzgerald Biago — his own deputy at the police — into the LDEA’s top job. Koijee’s broader argument was structural: that repeatedly installing senior police officers atop the drug agency has blurred the LDEA’s independence and concentrated excessive influence within Liberia’s security apparatus.

Notably, Boakai’s own government has now partly validated that structural critique without validating the corruption allegation. Monday’s Executive Mansion release states that the Justice Ministry’s probe into Biago “did not establish any involvement… in illegal narcotics trafficking” but did identify unspecified “ethical concerns” — landing in a gray zone that neither clears the LDEA leadership pipeline of suspicion nor confirms the most serious claims against it. Biago’s own departure now repeats the very pattern Koijee flagged: a police-to-LDEA pipeline replaced, once again, by another appointee — this time a retired general rather than a police officer, which may itself be read as an attempt to break that cycle.

What the U.S. statement does — and doesn’t — say

Read against this backdrop, Zadrozny’s language is carefully calibrated. It reaffirms partnership and frames Liberian institution-building as serving “regional stability” and the “enduring friendship” between the two countries — standard diplomatic register. But it also pointedly addresses itself to “law and order” and “a just and accountable legal system,” phrasing that functions as quiet pressure on Coleman and Gaye specifically to see the investigations — including into their own ranks — through to a credible conclusion, rather than as an unqualified vote of confidence in current leadership.

The U.S. has skin in this game beyond diplomacy: earlier reporting has linked American law enforcement, including the Department of Justice, to the broader trafficking investigation tied to the record cocaine seizure, and West Africa’s role as a transit corridor — now carrying an estimated 30 percent of Europe-bound cocaine, according to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime — makes Liberia’s enforcement capacity a matter of direct interest to Washington and European partners alike, not just Monrovia.

The stakes for the investigation ahead

For Ziankahn’s incoming LDEA leadership, the practical effect of the U.S. engagement is likely to be twofold: continued technical and possibly intelligence-sharing support for dismantling the trafficking network behind the record bust, paired with implicit international scrutiny of whether Liberia’s own police leadership — the officials the U.S. just met with — can be trusted to police itself.

Whether Coleman and Gaye emerge from the ongoing probes as central figures in prosecuting this case, or as subjects of it, may do more than any embassy statement to determine whether Liberia’s “war on drugs” produces lasting institutional reform or simply another rotation of the same personnel through different chairs.

World.title: Guinea Border: Time for Government to Level with the Liberian People
World.content:
Since February, Liberia’s border with Guinea has seen repeated incursions, a flag removal, troop deployments, and the displacement of thousands of residents in Lofa County. President Boakai has pursued the right diplomatic path — tripartite summits, joint technical commissions, a special envoy — but the public has received only sporadic updates since. This editorial argues that quiet diplomacy without public transparency risks eroding trust at home and, given West Africa’s history, could let a manageable dispute harden into something far more dangerous. It calls on the government to communicate more regularly and plainly with affected communities, not just with counterparts in Conakry.

FOR NEARLY a year now, communities along Liberia’s border with Guinea have lived with a question their government has not fully answered: what exactly is happening on our land, and what is being done about it?

PICTURE A FAMILY in Sorlumba, in Foya District, going about an ordinary morning — tending a farm plot, walking to a river crossing they’ve used their whole lives — when armed soldiers from across the border appear and declare the ground beneath their feet belongs to someone else. That is not a hypothetical. It is close to what residents there say happened earlier this year, when Guinean soldiers reportedly crossed into Liberian territory, seized construction equipment from a Liberian road contractor, and — most provocatively — ordered the removal of the Liberian flag that had flown at the riverbank for decades, even through the years of civil war. ￼ For people who lived through that war, watching their flag come down was not an abstract diplomatic incident. It was personal.

THE BARE FACTS, as they have trickled out through news reports rather than official candor, are troubling enough on their own. Alleged incursions in February sent panic through border communities. Guinea responded to the rising tension not with reassurance but with troop deployments to the frontier, and Liberia’s own rights commission later found that the affair had displaced thousands of residents and exposed serious gaps in both border protection and regional diplomacy. Thousands of displaced people is not a statistic to file away — it is thousands of individual decisions to grab what could be carried and walk away from home, uncertain when, or whether, it would be safe to return.

TO ITS CREDIT, the Boakai administration did not let the crisis spiral into confrontation. President Boakai joined his Guinean and Sierra Leonean counterparts in Conakry in March for a tripartite summit that produced commitments to dialogue, joint technical commissions on border delimitation, and a pledge to convene a full Mano River Union summit within a month to “revitalize” the organization. In June, Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah reaffirmed that Liberia remained committed to resolving the dispute through diplomacy, and that a special presidential envoy had been dispatched to follow up on the Conakry commitments.

THESE ARE THE RIGHT instincts. Nobody serious wants Liberia and Guinea shooting at each other over a riverbank in Foya.

BUT GOOD INSTINCTS are not the same as good governance, and here is where the government’s approach has fallen short: the Liberian public still does not know, in any real detail, where things stand. The promised MRU summit, floated for July, has come and gone without a clear public accounting of whether it happened, what it produced, or why it may have slipped. The joint technical commissions on border delimitation — the actual mechanism that would settle, once and for all, whose land is whose — have operated largely out of public view. The people of Lofa County did not get to choose whether their homes sat on contested ground. The least they are owed is honesty about what their government is doing to protect them.

THIS MATTERS for reasons beyond transparency as a good-governance principle. West Africa has spent the better part of four decades relearning, at enormous human cost, how quickly a border dispute can metastasize into something far worse. Liberia’s own seven-year civil war and Sierra Leone’s decade of conflict were not born in a vacuum — porous, poorly governed borders and cross-border grievances were accelerants for both. Analysts tracking the current tensions have noted that all four Mano River Union countries have emerged from civil conflict, yet peace remains fragile due to weak border governance, contested territorial claims, and shifting political transitions ￼ — a diagnosis that should concentrate minds in Monrovia as much as in Conakry.

THERE IS ALSO a very human political risk in silence. When government communication goes quiet, the space fills with rumor, opposition point-scoring, and — as nearly happened in Foya, where young residents reportedly moved to confront Guinean soldiers directly rather than wait for diplomacy to work — with ordinary citizens deciding to defend their own communities because no one has told them help is coming. A government that explains its strategy clearly gives frightened people a reason to trust the process instead of taking matters into their own hands.

WE ARE NOT calling for saber-rattling, nor for the kind of “inflammatory rhetoric” the government has rightly said it wants to avoid. We are calling for the opposite: more information, delivered more often, in language ordinary Liberians in Foya and Vahun can understand and act on — not just diplomatic communiqués aimed at regional bodies and foreign audiences.

PRESIDENT BOAKAI has said, correctly, that this is “not a matter for confrontation, but for calm, facts and sustained engagement.” We agree entirely — provided that “facts” reach the farmers, traders, and families living along that border, and not only the diplomats in closed-door rooms in Conakry. Liberia has been here before. The region does not need reminding of what happens when land disputes are left to fester unexplained. Let this government show, through consistent and honest public communication, that it has learned that lesson.

World.title: Liberians Trapped in Cambodian Detention Plead for a Way Home
World.content:
A group of Liberian nationals, writing through spokesperson Emmanuel Johnson, say they’ve been held at a Cambodian immigration detention center in Phnom Penh since May 25, 2026 — not for any crime, but because they can’t afford flight tickets home. They say they were trafficked to Cambodia under false job promises, had their passports and phones confiscated, and were eventually rescued by Cambodian police. Their overstay violations were later resolved through Liberia’s Embassy in China. Still, with no funds for airfare, they remain detained — now facing the threat of transfer to Cambodia’s main prison if tickets aren’t secured soon.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia- Emmanuel Johnson, writing on behalf of the group, says they have been held at the Cambodian Immigration Detention Center since May 25, 2026. Their offense, in the eyes of Cambodian authorities, is not one of intent — it is one of poverty. Officials have told them the only thing standing between them and freedom is a plane ticket home. They cannot afford one.

A Promise That Became a Trap

The group’s story follows a pattern that has become disturbingly familiar across Southeast Asia in recent years. Johnson says the Liberians did not travel to Cambodia seeking trouble — they went believing they had secured legitimate jobs. The recruiters who arranged their visas and flights delivered them instead into a scheme with no real employment waiting on the other end. Their passports and phones were confiscated on arrival, and they were held until Cambodian police intervened and rescued them.

It is a story that echoes what international human rights investigators have been documenting for more than a year. Amnesty International, which interviewed 73 survivors of Cambodia’s scamming compounds — including nationals of Liberia, Ghana, Kenya, Ethiopia, and more than a dozen other countries — between July 2025 and April 2026, has found that victims recruited under false employment promises are routinely trafficked into compounds where they are confined and coerced. What makes the aftermath particularly cruel, according to that research, is what happens after rescue: not one of the 73 survivors Amnesty interviewed was recognized by Cambodian authorities as a victim of human trafficking, despite meeting the internationally agreed legal definition — instead, many were detained in overcrowded immigration centers, charged for visa overstays, and in some cases threatened with return to the very compounds they had escaped.

That is precisely the limbo in which Johnson and his compatriots now find themselves — rescued from exploitation, only to be imprisoned for the crime of having nowhere to go and no means to get there.

Government Channels, Dead Ends

According to Johnson’s account, the group has not sat passively. They say they approached Liberia’s Embassy in China, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission (LRRRC), and were told that officials would work with the International Organization for Migration (IOM) in Cambodia to arrange their return. That effort, they say, stalled: IOM reportedly informed them it lacked the resources to provide flight tickets.

The Liberian Embassy in China did intervene on one front — securing a resolution of the group’s immigration overstay violations with Cambodian authorities. But that diplomatic success solved only part of the problem. Without tickets home, the men and women remain detained, their overstay technically resolved but their freedom still contingent on money none of them have.

A Race Against Time

The appeal carries new urgency because of what Johnson describes as an explicit threat: if flight tickets are not secured soon, the group will be moved from the immigration detention center into Cambodia’s main prison system — a transfer that would mark a sharp escalation for people who, as Johnson puts it, “have committed no crime.”

Their situation is not unique in scale, even if it is deeply personal in its telling. Regional reporting has described escapees from Cambodia’s trafficking and scam-compound networks as frequently left without documents, shelter, or access to social services after their rescue, with some detained for immigration violations even as enforcement against the criminal networks themselves gradually increases. Investigators covering the broader crisis have also noted that Cambodian authorities have in some cases threatened trafficking survivors with return to the compounds they fled, while journalists attempting to report on the crisis have themselves faced arrest and intimidation.

“We Are Not Asking for Special Treatment”

What Johnson’s letter makes clear is that the group is not seeking exceptional intervention — only the ordinary mercy of a way home. “We are simply pleading for an opportunity to return home to our families and rebuild our lives,” he writes, adding that every additional day in detention worsens their physical and emotional condition.

For now, their fate rests on whether Liberian authorities, humanitarian organizations, or public pressure generated by their appeal can produce what months of formal channels have not: the price of a plane ticket, and a door out of detention before it becomes a cell.

World.title: Growth Without Development: Again, Liberia’s Self-Inflicted Development Crisis
World.content:
In the early 1960s, a Northwestern-led team of economists arrived to study what was then one of the fastest-growing economies on earth. Liberia was booming. Iron ore was moving through new ports, rubber was flowing, and foreign capital was arriving faster than almost anywhere in the world. They spent years examining this miracle, and in 1966 they published their conclusion under a title that should have haunted us forever: Growth Without Development: An Economic Survey of Liberia.

By Sei Philip Pleiwon, contributing writer

Their verdict was simple and devastating. Liberia had enormous economic activity and almost no economic transformation. The concessions operated beside the country, not inside it. Money moved through Liberia without becoming Liberia.

Sixty years have passed. We have lived through the boom, the coup, the war, the recovery, and five national development strategies. Billions of dollars in aid, investment, and public spending have entered this country. And the central diagnosis of that book remains uncomfortably current.

We have just marked 179 years of independence. Here is the plainest way I can put our condition:

Liberia is trying to develop without building an economy.

Before anyone reaches for their political feelings, understand what this essay is not. A problem that has survived military rule, civil conflict, transitional governments, and successive elected administrations cannot be reduced to the failure of any president, past or present. It is an operating logic, diagnosed repeatedly in our own plans and never operationally corrected. Corruption is real, and it is a crime against this country. But in Liberia it is also partly a function of that same incoherence: where nothing is organized toward a defined national outcome, resources are easier to divert and far harder to miss.

Development is what accumulates

We have mistaken the ingredients of development for development itself. Foreign investment, roads, schools, agriculture, digital skills: these can improve lives directly, and that matters. But they are inputs, and the question is what the country does with them.

Here is the distinction six decades keep teaching and we keep refusing to learn. Investment, aid, public expenditure, exports, construction, and training are flows: things entering, moving through, or occurring within the country. Development is the accumulation of stocks: capable people, productive firms, domestic capital, functioning institutions, technical knowledge, and state capacity.

An economy compounds when today’s production becomes tomorrow’s productive capacity. Production creates wages, profits, and taxes; part of those flows must become savings, stronger firms, knowledge, infrastructure, and new investment.

Liberia’s cycle runs differently. Foreign capital finances production, but much of the equipment, expertise, contracting, and finance is imported. Commodities and a substantial share of the value leave. Wages and revenue enter an import-dependent economy and a recurrent budget. Too little becomes locally owned productive capital. The activity is real; the accumulation is weak. A new concession can therefore begin twenty years after the last one and meet the same shortage of Liberian engineers, suppliers, finance, and technical institutions that existed before.

That is the development gap: the failure to convert economic flows into accumulating national capability.

The evidence is not subtle. A child born in Liberia can expect to achieve roughly 32 percent of the productivity she would attain with full health and education, according to the World Bank’s Human Capital Index. Real income per person remains below its pre-war peak. After sixty years of flows, we are behind where we started.

Everything ends at its first output

Watch how development actually works here, and you will notice a pattern so common it has become invisible.

The road ends at the road. The training ends at the certificate. The project ends at the report. The study ends at the study. The concession ends at extraction and revenue. The education ends at the degree. The identity card ends at the card.

We complete the first output, hold the ceremony, and move on. But development lives in what the output enables. So does every government’s account of itself: kilometers paved, budgets grown, buildings dedicated, graduates counted, jobs announced. We have reduced development to new hospitals, new schools, new light posts. It is why the country feels the way it does, undirected and confused, a place where things are thrown at the wall to see what sticks.

The question we never ask

There is one question Liberia has never put at the center of its development, and everything else follows from its absence: what should our people become capable of doing?

Ask it of education first. In China, between 2021 and 2025, universities eliminated or suspended more than 12,000 undergraduate degree programs, over 30 percent of all offerings, and created 10,000 new ones, realigning higher education with where the economy is going. Set aside every debate about China’s model and notice only what the act reveals: a state that has decided what its people must become capable of doing, and treats education as the instrument for producing it.

Now ask it here. Not how many are enrolled, or how many graduated, but what can a Liberian high school graduate actually do on the day she finishes, and what should she be capable of doing? No government has produced and enforced an answer specific enough to govern what programs are authorized, what public money funds, or who receives a scholarship. Universities open programs based on what they can staff and what students will enroll in. Students choose qualifications in a labor market the country does not measure, and they carry all the risk of guessing wrong. We are expanding an academic model inherited from the 1960s without deciding what the expansion is for. And this in a country of five and a half million people, small enough to know its own labor market. We graduate her into a void and call the ceremony an outcome. Education without an answer to what our people should be able to do is not education. It is attendance.

Now ask it of mining, where the answer has had sixty years to arrive. Visit any major concession and watch who does what. The machines are imported, and so, overwhelmingly, are the people who operate at the top of them: the engineers, the technicians, the laboratory and logistics contractors. Liberians are present, and mostly at the bottom of the ladder, in a country that has been mining iron ore since before their grandfathers were born. So what mining capability does Liberia now possess? How many mining engineers, geologists, and certified technicians has this country deliberately produced? Which categories of mining procurement can Liberian firms reliably supply?

The answers embarrass us, and the blame is not where we usually put it. Mining companies cannot be expected to design Liberia’s national capability system; that responsibility belongs to the state. In the absence of credible Liberian pipelines, a company will import engineers and contractors because it must operate. Government presses episodically, scholarships this year, employment numbers next, and companies comply with the demand of the moment. The demands change. Nothing connects. Extraction continues, accompanied by activities. When the ore runs out, and ore always runs out, we will convene conferences on diversification and discover what sixty years of extraction left behind.

Employers complain constantly about workforce quality, and the answer is always more training. But a workforce employers can rely on is built deliberately, occupation by occupation, against real demand. It is not a social program. It is a foundation of production.

The same missing answer explains why agriculture, our announced salvation in every plan since independence, still does not feed us. And it explains the hollowness of our newest prescription. Entrepreneurship at scale is not a trait to be trained into a population; it is an outcome of an economy, of paying customers, working capital, and reachable markets. Where those are absent, we rebrand survival self-employment and ask young people to absorb the risk of a missing economy while calling it empowerment.

A country of projects without a national project

Someone will object that Liberia has a plan. Liberia has always had a plan. That is the evidence, not the defense.

We have produced five major strategies since the war, from the interim poverty-reduction strategy through the Agenda for Transformation to the Pro-Poor Agenda and now the ARREST Agenda. Each diagnosed us honestly. The PAPD said it plainly in 2018, in the government’s own words: Liberia is rich in human and natural resources but deprived of development because its people lack the capability to transform those resources into wealth. That is this essay’s argument, published by the state itself, eight years ago. It described the country. It did not govern the country. On the present trajectory we will not meet Vision 2030 either, and nothing in our planning culture guarantees the public autopsy such a failure should require. We do not learn from our plans. We replace them.

The ARREST Agenda deserves a fair reading, because its own arithmetic is the X-ray. It requires US$8.38 billion over five years. Government expects to finance roughly 30 percent; the rest is expected from private investment, development partners, and diaspora remittances. That does not make the plan unserious; most national strategies depend partly on capital beyond the budget. But it makes alignment the decisive test. Seventy percent of the plan depends on actors government cannot command. Unless their investments are connected to a governing national architecture, the plan remains a destination whose vehicle belongs to someone else.

Beneath every plan sits the same structural silence. Education manages education. Mines manages mining. Public Works builds roads. Partners fund projects. Every actor owns a component and can defend it. But who is accountable for whether the components add up to a different country? Who ensures a thirty-year concession changes what our technical colleges teach? Who decides that scarce capital will complete one system before starting five others? No one. Everyone is accountable for activity. No one is accountable for accumulation.

Our development partners are trapped inside this same gap, and they should hear this as a plea, not an accusation. In the absence of a national architecture, each partner rationally builds a project-level one: its own unit, database, consultants, and indicators. Local rationality, national irrationality. When implementation skills cannot be found locally, partners procure international firms, because the project window leaves no time to build local capacity to do the work. The work gets done. The capability leaves on the same flight as the consultants. The next project reassembles everything from zero. Knowledge behaves the same way: two decades of assessments, baseline surveys, and value-chain studies, one set per project, often covering the same sectors and the same farmers. Liberia may be among the most studied and least known countries on earth, because the studies function as project products rather than national assets. Knowledge, too, is a flow here. We have never let it become a stock.

So the question must be asked directly, with respect: if project cycles cannot absorb the time and risk required to build local delivery capacity, then who will? The projects are not more important than the levers required to deliver them.

Direction, conversion, accumulation

The answer is not another plan. God spare us another plan. It is three disciplines, applied without mercy.

Direction. A short list of concrete national capabilities we are deliberately building, so short that it forces exclusion. Everything is a priority in Liberia, which is how the budget gets spread until nothing we fund is ever finished, foundational, and usable. We have to stop trying to do everything and nothing.

Conversion. Design the connections, not just the components. Every road answers: what production does it unlock? Every concession answers: which occupations and suppliers, on what schedule? Every degree program answers: what demand? Every donor program answers: which national system does it strengthen?

Accumulation. Measure what remains, not what moved. Firms that survived. Occupations localized. Systems still operating. Value retained and reinvested. One question before every major intervention is approved, and again after it closes: what will Liberia permanently be able to do because this existed?

The question of 2040

Countries do not purchase direction. They choose it, and then organize institutions, capital, and public authority around the choice. Decisions of that kind are not imported. They are made.

So let us be honest about time. 2030 is around the corner, and the dream attached to it will not be met. The more important question is the one nobody is asking: what are we doing today that should make anyone believe 2040 will be substantially different? By 2040 we will certainly have more roads, more graduates, more agencies, more completed projects. More flows. The question is which stocks. What will Liberia be able to do in 2040 that it cannot do now, and can anyone name the mechanism currently building that capability? If the answer is silence, then 2040 is already written, and it looks like 2026, which looked like 1966.

I ended The Death of Potential with the warning that the greatest danger was not what Liberia lacked but what we had learned to accept. We have learned to accept activity as achievement. We have learned to celebrate what enters and never audit what remains. Sixty years ago, economists looked at booming Liberia and named our condition: growth without development. Their book should have been our warning. We made it our biography.

But a biography is not a destiny. We are 179 years old, small enough to know ourselves, young enough to redirect ourselves, and rich enough, in ore, in land, and in the ferocious untapped intelligence of our children, to build an economy that compounds within a generation. It begins the day this country answers, operationally and out loud, the question it has avoided since 1847:

What are we deliberately trying to become able to do?

Everything we build before answering that question is furniture.

Everything we build after it is a nation.

World.title: Tonse-Pamodzi raises conflict-of-interest concerns over AU-COMESA election mission chief
World.content:
Tonse-Pamodzi raises conflict-of-interest concerns over AU-COMESA election mission chief

The Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance has asked the head of the joint African Union and COMESA Election Observation Mission, former Ethiopian Prime Minister Hailemariam Dessalegn Boshe, to disclose his association with the Brenthurst Foundation and recuse himself from leading the mission’s assessment of Zambia’s August 13 general elections.

The request comes after the opposition alliance raised concerns that Dessalegn’s membership of the Brenthurst Foundation’s Advisory Board could create an appearance of a conflict of interest because of the Foundation’s reported historical relationship with President Hakainde Hichilema.

Publicly available biographical information identifies Dessalegn, who served as Ethiopian Prime Minister from 2012 to 2018 and chaired the African Union from 2013 to 2014, as an Advisory Board member of the Brenthurst Foundation. (African Parks)

The AU and COMESA have deployed 93 observers across Zambia’s 10 provinces for the August 13 elections, with Dessalegn heading the mission and Ambassador Marie-Pierre Lloyd serving as Deputy Head of Mission. The observers have been drawn from 29 African countries and include representatives of election management bodies, civil society organisations and specialists in human rights, gender and media. (ZNBC)

The Alliance’s concerns have also drawn attention to President Hichilema’s previous interactions with senior figures associated with the Brenthurst Foundation. In July 2022, Hichilema conferred the Order of the Eagle of Zambia, First Division, on former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, former Liberian President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf and former Sierra Leone President Ernest Bai Koroma.

The Brenthurst Foundation itself reported at the time that the three former presidents were members of its board and that, following the investiture ceremony in Lusaka, they were due to attend the Foundation’s annual board meeting in Livingstone. Its current profiles identify Johnson Sirleaf and Koroma as members of its Advisory Board. (The Brenthurst Foundation)

The Foundation’s own account said the awards recognised the former presidents’ lifetime work supporting democracy in Africa. Koroma had also headed the African Union Election Observation Mission during Zambia’s 2021 election, which resulted in the transfer of power from former President Edgar Lungu to Hichilema. (The Brenthurst Foundation)

The latest concerns follow a July 2026 investigation by Global Witness which reported allegations of a longstanding relationship between the Brenthurst Foundation and Hichilema dating to his years in opposition. The investigation also reported that Greg Mills, the Foundation’s founding director, was involved in Hichilema’s 2026 election campaign in a personal capacity. Those assertions form part of the basis cited by Tonse-Pamodzi in its demand for disclosure and recusal. (allAfrica.com)

In a letter dated August 12, 2026, signed by Ambassador Emmanuel Mwamba on behalf of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance/NRPUP, the opposition grouping said it was not questioning Dessalegn’s personal integrity but was concerned about the perception of impartiality surrounding the leadership of the observation mission.

The Alliance has asked Dessalegn to publicly disclose his Brenthurst Foundation association and any other relationships relevant to the perception of impartiality. It has further requested that he recuse himself from chairing, directing and publicly pronouncing the mission’s assessment, with those responsibilities transferred to Ambassador Lloyd.

It has also asked the AU-COMESA mission to disclose the conflict-of-interest screening applied to its leadership and observers and requested a response before polling begins.

The concerns and requested recusal are allegations and demands made by the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance; the documented membership of the Brenthurst Foundation’s Advisory Board does not by itself establish that Dessalegn is biased in carrying out his election-observation responsibilities.

FULL STATEMENT

Below is the full letter issued by the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance which triggered the concerns over the leadership of the AU-COMESA Election Observation Mission:

12 August 2026

H.E. Hailemariam Dessalegn Boshe

Head of Mission, AU–COMESA Election Observation Mission to Zambia

Lusaka, Republic of Zambia

H.E. Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, Chairperson, African Union Commission, Addis Ababa

The Secretary General, Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa, Lusaka

Your Excellencies,

RE: REQUEST FOR DISCLOSURE AND RECUSAL — APPEARANCE OF A CONFLICT OF INTEREST IN THE LEADERSHIP OF THE AU–COMESA ELECTION OBSERVATION MISSION TO THE 13 AUGUST 2026 GENERAL ELECTIONS

We write on behalf of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance and its presidential candidate, Hon. Brian Mundubile, first to welcome the deployment of the AU–COMESA Election Observation Mission and to affirm our full respect for the African Union, COMESA, and the ninety-three observers drawn from twenty-nine African nations now deployed across all ten provinces of our Republic. Zambia’s democratic tradition has long been strengthened by continental observation, and we are committed to full cooperation with the Mission.

It is precisely because the Mission’s findings will carry such weight in Zambia and before the world that we are compelled to place on record, before polling commences, a matter that bears directly on the perceived impartiality of the Mission’s leadership.

The public record establishes the following. First, His Excellency Hailemariam Dessalegn Boshe has served since August 2018 as a member of the Advisory Board of the Brenthurst Foundation, an appointment announced by the Foundation itself and reflected on its website and in His Excellency’s public biographies to date. Second, the published record – including a detailed investigative report issued by Global Witness in July 2026 – documents a close and sustained relationship between the Brenthurst Foundation and His Excellency President Hakainde Hichilema, reported to span from approximately 2008 to the present, encompassing policy support and the authorship of economic policy adopted by the present administration. Third, it is publicly reported that the Foundation’s founding director, Dr Greg Mills, is presently serving as a leading figure in President Hichilema’s 2026 re-election campaign in a personal capacity.

We wish to be unambiguous: we do not impugn the personal integrity of His Excellency Hailemariam Dessalegn Boshe, whose service to Ethiopia and to this continent commands respect. Our concern rests on the settled principle reflected in the Declaration of Principles for International Election Observation (2005), the OAU/AU Declaration on the Principles Governing Democratic Elections in Africa, and the African Charter on Democracy, Elections and Governance, the very instruments the Mission has cited as the basis of its assessment that election observation must not only be impartial but be seen to be impartial, and that observers should be free of any association that may give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias.

A Head of Mission who has served for years on the advisory board of an institution so closely identified with one contesting candidate – an institution whose founding director presently directs that candidate’s campaign – presents, at minimum, such an apprehension. Left unaddressed, it would place an unnecessary question mark over whatever findings the Mission announces on 15 August, to the detriment of the Mission, the African Union, COMESA, and the Zambian people, whichever way the electorate decides.

We therefore respectfully request:

That His Excellency the Head of Mission publicly disclose his Advisory Board association with the Brenthurst Foundation, and any related associations material to the perception of impartiality; That, in keeping with best practice, His Excellency recuse himself from the chairing, direction, and public pronouncement of the Mission’s assessment, and that these functions pass to the Deputy Head of Mission, Ambassador Marie-Pierre Lloyd of the COMESA Committee of Elders, in whom we repose full confidence; That the Mission confirm, for the public record, the conflict-of-interest screening applied to its leadership and observers, in accordance with the Declaration of Principles; and That, given polling commences within twenty-four hours, this request be acknowledged and addressed before the close of business today.

We reiterate our respect for the Mission and our full cooperation with its ninety-three observers. Nothing in this letter seeks to diminish the Mission’s work; on the contrary, it seeks to place its eventual findings beyond reproach. An election verdict, like a judicial one, draws its force from the undisputed impartiality of the hand that delivers it.

Please accept, Your Excellencies, the assurances of our highest consideration.

___________

Ambasador Emmanuel Mwamba

For and on behalf of the Tonse-Pamodzi Alliance / NRPUP

cc:

Ambassador Marie-Pierre Lloyd, Deputy Head of Mission, AU–COMESA EOM

The Chairperson, Electoral Commission of Zambia

Head of the European Union Election Observation Mission to Zambia

Heads of other accredited international observation missions

Dean of the Diplomatic Corps, Lusaka

Annexes:

A. Brenthurst Foundation announcement of Advisory Board appointments, August 2018

B. Brenthurst Foundation website, “Our People” — Advisory Board listing (print-out, dated)

C. Global Witness, “How a Canadian Mining Giant Infiltrated Zambia’s Democracy”, July 2026 (relevant extracts)

D. AU–COMESA EOM Arrival Statement, August 2026

World.title: Govt. dismisses abduction allegations
World.content:
Government has dismissed allegations circulating on various media platforms suggesting that it has abducted individuals connected to some political parties.

Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security Permanent Secretary Dickson Matembo has clarified that several suspects, among them, three former senior government officials have been apprehended over an alleged plot to interfere with the 2026 general elections.

Speaking during a joint media briefing, Mr Matembo clarified that no abductions have taken place, stressing that all actions undertaken by the state are within the confines of the law.

Mr Matembo emphasised that contrary to speculation, individuals such as former Ambassador Martha Lungu and journalist Hannah Katontoka were not abducted, but lawfully apprehended to assist with investigations and have since been released.

And government has commended members of the public for their cooperation in providing information that aided law enforcement and urged citizens to remain vigilant, reporting any activities that may threaten national security, public safety, or peace.

“The government’s position is clear. The security of the Republic of Zambia is a responsibility of the state and must be protected through lawful, accountable and constitutionally established institutions,” he emphasised.

Mr Matembo also confirmed the arrest of businessman Valden Findlay in connection with investigations into alleged military-related training undertaken by Zambian nationals abroad.

The arrest follows the earlier interception of three Zambian nationals at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport on August 1st, 2026 who have since been arrested and charged with unlawful drilling, unauthorised use of uniform and prohibition of terrorism.

He explained that a joint intelligence-led operation involving defense and security agencies culminated in the apprehension of several suspects linked to attempts to interfere with the electoral process.

He added that the three former senior government officials are currently in lawful custody for allegedly providing technical services aimed at undermining the electoral system.

The Permanent Secretary revealed that Investigators have also extended invitations to Japhen Mwakalombe, Mwila Kakana and Sessho Banda to assist with ongoing inquiries after they were found in possession of over K7.3 million.

He explained that the source and intended purpose of the funds remains unclear, noting that the trio, however, have communicated through their lawyers that they will only be available after August 14th, 2026.

Mr Matembo further disclosed that sensitive military intelligence information was discovered on electronic devices seized from the suspects, raising concerns about unauthorised access to protected data.

In a related development, Mr Matembo also disclosed that a Kenyan national, Michael Juka, aged 56, has been apprehended for allegedly being contracted to carry out cybercrimes targeting the State.

And Ministry of Information and Media Permanent Secretary Thabo Kawana warned that anyone attempting to disrupt elections, peace, or national security will face the wrath of the law.

He noted that some political leaders had admitted to sending people abroad for training and later declared readiness to kill or be killed during elections, warning that such actions would not be tolerated.

Mr Kawana added that foreigners linked to treasonous activities were among those arrested, while others fled.

He reiterated that the government would not allow desperate individuals to endanger peace and security in pursuit of political power.

“We are aware of some individuals that also have finished their so-called training and would want to get back into the country to implement that which they want to come and do on the soil of this country. We want to say we welcome them. The law enforcement agencies are ready”, the Permanent Secretary warned.

World.title: ECZ deploys Poll staff in Chilubi
World.content:
The deployment of poll staff by the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) in Chilubi District ahead of the August 13 General Election has reached an advanced stage.

The exercise, which began yesterday, is scheduled to be completed today.

Chilubi District Electoral Officer Kenneth Kafumbwe says poll staff that have been deployed to swamp areas are being airlifted using a Zambia Air Force (ZAF) chopper, while those assigned to the mainland are being transported by boats, before continuing their journey on vehicles and motorbikes.

Speaking in an interview with the media today in Chilubi today, Mr Kafumbwe expressed optimism that the deployment exercise will be completed before the close of business today.

Meanwhile, stakeholders observing the electoral process have welcomed the timely deployment of poll staff noting that the Electoral Commission of Zambia has taken into account Chilubi’s unique geographical challenges.

New Buyantanshi Village Headman, David Mwaba said the Commission’s proactive approach has ensured that staff reach their destinations on time.

Mr Mwaba further expressed happiness for the peaceful atmosphere that has characterised the electoral process in the area.

World.title: Zambians urged to be peaceful- Haamaundu
World.content:
Government has called on members of the public to uphold peace during elections, stating that continued peace in the country acts as an asset in promoting investor confidence and economic development.

Ministry of Defence Permanent Secretary, Maambo Haamaundu, says that his ministry is committed to ensuring continued peace that can be exported to other countries in leadership and peace keeping missions.

Mr Haamundu added that despite crowd management falling under the Ministry of Home Affairs and Internal Security, the Ministry of Defence has its services on standby, should they be called upon due to a situation that demands their attention.

“We must continue to maintain the peace of our country, because like I said, it is the foundation for economic and social development,” he said.

Mr Haamaundu has since appealed to members of the public to refrain from the temptation of wanting to cause violence, as they remain as key stakeholders of championing peace in the country.

He said that the government will work with a government approach that will involve key collaborations with stakeholders such as correctional services and immigration, in order to maximize peace.

Mr Haamaundu expressed that he is hopeful of a peaceful environment as the people go about casting their votes and that individuals who want to cause unnecessary trouble will be dealt with accordingly.
