Through its Credicasa program, Biess has channeled tens of millions of dollars into home loans for ordinary families. Ecuador’s state pension bank does not usually make headlines, but its mortgage desk has been busy.

Part of a wider lending push that is quietly shaping the country’s housing market this year.

What Credicasa is doing

The immediate news is a program called Credicasa, Biess’s housing-finance line for the people it serves. According to reporting, it has disbursed more than US$53.69 million to over 1,030 families seeking to buy a home.

The draw is a preferential interest rate of 2.99%, offered to the bank’s affiliates and retirees.

Why the rate matters

In a market where mortgage rates can run much higher, 2.99% is a meaningful advantage for a borrower. Over the life of a home loan, a few percentage points translate into thousands of dollars saved.

That gap is precisely what makes a state-backed lender like Biess attractive to working families.

The bigger lending picture

Credicasa is one thread in a larger story about how much Biess is lending for housing this year. In the first half of 2026, the bank made US$263.4 million in housing loans across 4,192 separate operations.

That is a clear step up from the same period in 2025, when it lent US$237.4 million over 3,796 operations.

A strong first half

The momentum built as the half went on, rather than fading. June was the standout month.

In that single month, Biess approved 869 operations and disbursed US$54.25 million for housing. That kind of monthly pace suggests steady, resilient demand from Ecuadorians looking to buy.

Where the money goes

Not all mortgage lending is the same, and Biess’s mix leans heavily in one direction. About 89.8% of its first-half housing disbursements, some US$236.5 million, went toward buying finished homes.

That points to families purchasing completed housing rather than financing construction from the ground up.

Biess and the private banks together

The state bank is a big player, but it is not the only one writing mortgages in Ecuador. Private-sector lenders disbursed roughly US$734 million in home loans over the same first half of 2026.

Add Biess’s US$263 million, and total housing finance in the country reached about US$997 million.

Why a pension bank lends for homes

It can seem odd that a social-security institution is in the mortgage business at all. But lending members’ pension savings for housing is a way to put that money to work while serving affiliates.

A home loan is a relatively safe, long-term asset, and it directly benefits the workers whose funds back it.

A read on the housing market

Taken together, these numbers offer a useful snapshot of Ecuador’s housing demand right now. Rising loan volumes at both public and private lenders suggest appetite for home ownership is holding up.

In an uncertain economy, a steady flow of mortgages is a modestly encouraging sign.

A note on the figures

One caveat is worth flagging for readers who like their numbers airtight. The broad half-year lending totals are backed by more than one source, but the specific Credicasa figure comes from a single report.

The direction of travel is clear, even if the exact Credicasa total awaits fuller official confirmation.

What to watch next

The thing to follow is whether Biess keeps up this pace through the second half of the year. Watch, too, for any change in its preferential rate, which is what makes the offer so appealing.

For now, the state bank is lending briskly, and thousands of Ecuadorian families are the direct beneficiaries.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Biess?

Biess is Ecuador’s state pension bank, the Banco del Instituto Ecuatoriano de Seguridad Social, which lends members’ social-security savings, including for housing.

What is Credicasa?

Credicasa is Biess’s housing-finance program. Reporting says it has disbursed over US$53.69 million to more than 1,030 families at a preferential 2.99% rate.

How much did Biess lend for housing in early 2026?

US$263.4 million across 4,192 operations in the first half of 2026, up from US$237.4 million and 3,796 operations a year earlier.

How big is Ecuador’s mortgage market overall?

Adding private lenders’ roughly US$734 million to Biess’s US$263 million. Total housing finance reached about US$997 million in the first half of 2026.

Sources: La Hora; Ecuadorian financial press.

World.title: A ‘Grotesque’ Failure: Fraga’s Verdict as the Banco Master Case Widens
World.content:
Business

Key Facts — The verdict Armínio Fraga called the Banco Master episode a ‘grotesque failure’ in how regulation was applied, on August 11, 2026.

— His point Fraga said the flaw was in enforcement, not in the design of the rules.

— The raid Federal Police searched Iprev de Maceió on August 10, in the widening probe.

— The money Two investments in Banco Master financial letters, totaling R$97 million (about US$19 million), are under scrutiny.

— The operation The Maceió action is part of Operation Compliance Zero, authorized by Supreme Court Justice André Mendonça.

A respected former central banker says the rules were fine; it was the enforcement that broke down.

A ‘Grotesque’ Failure: Fraga’s Verdict as the Banco Master Case Widens. (Photo internet reproduction)

Armínio Fraga used exactly that word this week to describe the Banco Master affair. When one of Brazil’s most respected former central bankers reaches for the word ‘grotesque’, people tend to listen.

And his verdict landed just as police widened a probe into how public pension money ended up tangled in the case.

What Fraga actually said

Speaking at a roundtable in São Paulo on August 11, Fraga did not mince words about the Banco Master saga. He called it a ‘grotesque failure’, but he was careful about where he aimed the blame.

In his telling, the problem was not the design of Brazil’s banking rules. It was the way those rules were applied, or not applied, in practice.

Why the distinction matters

That difference between rules and enforcement is more than a debating point; it shapes what fixing the problem looks like. If the rulebook is sound, the answer is sharper supervision, not a wholesale rewrite of regulation.

Coming from a former central bank president, that framing carries real weight in Brasília’s ongoing debate.

The deposit guarantee problem

Fraga pointed to one distortion in particular, tied to Brazil’s deposit guarantee fund, known by its initials FGC. Banco Master had been able to hoover up deposits by paying unusually rich returns, reportedly the CDI benchmark plus six percent.

Because those deposits were covered by the guarantee, savers took the high yield without feeling the risk that came with it.

A guarantee that can backfire

Deposit guarantees exist for good reason: they stop panics and protect ordinary savers when a bank fails. But Fraga’s example shows how the same safety net can quietly encourage reckless behaviour if no one is watching.

A bank that knows its depositors are protected can chase growth aggressively, pushing risk onto the system as a whole.

The raid in Maceió

As Fraga spoke, the investigation itself was moving. A day earlier, Federal Police searched a pension body in the northeast.

The target was Iprev de Maceió, the municipal pension fund, in a line of inquiry connected to Banco Master. The warrants were authorized by Supreme Court Justice André Mendonça, a sign of how high up the case now reaches.

Following the Banco Master money

At the centre of the Maceió inquiry are two investments the pension fund made in Banco Master financial letters. Together they total around R$97 million, roughly US$19 million, placed in 2023 and 2024.

The action forms part of a broader investigation that carries the pointed name Operation Compliance Zero.

The fund’s response

For its part, the Maceió pension body has pushed back gently rather than gone silent. Iprev said it has been cooperating with authorities since the beginning of the inquiry.

It added that it is handing over the information investigators have requested, a fairly standard line in cases like this.

Why public money raises the stakes

The Banco Master story would matter even if only private investors were exposed, but public pension money changes the temperature. Money meant to pay municipal workers’ retirements is exactly the kind of savings the system is supposed to shield.

When it turns up inside a troubled bank, the political and legal pressure rises sharply.

A test for Brazil’s watchdogs

Taken together, Fraga’s critique and the widening raids put Brazil’s financial supervisors under an uncomfortable spotlight. The core question is whether regulators had the tools to catch this earlier and simply failed to use them.

How that question is answered could shape reforms to supervision and to the guarantee system Fraga singled out.

What to watch next

The immediate thread to follow is where Operation Compliance Zero leads and who else it touches. Beyond the raids, watch whether Fraga’s call for a rethink of the guarantee fund gains traction in Brasília.

A case that began as one troubled bank is fast becoming a broader argument about how Brazil polices its financial system.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Armínio Fraga say about Banco Master?

At a São Paulo roundtable on August 11, 2026. The former central bank president called the episode a ‘grotesque failure’ in how regulation was applied, not in the rules themselves.

What happened in Maceió?

On August 10, Federal Police searched the Iprev de Maceió pension fund. In a probe authorized by Supreme Court Justice André Mendonça and tied to Banco Master.

How much money is under investigation there?

Two investments in Banco Master financial letters, made in 2023 and 2024 and totaling around R$97 million (about US$19 million).

Why did Fraga mention the deposit guarantee fund?

He argued the FGC let Banco Master attract deposits at very high rates without savers feeling the risk. Distorting incentives and encouraging aggressive risk-taking.

Sources: O Globo; Folha de Pernambuco; Estado de Minas.

World.title: Brazil’s Top Court Begins Judging Its Environmental Licensing Law
World.content:
Business

Key Facts — The case The Supreme Federal Court began judging the general environmental licensing law, Law 15.190/2025, on August 12, 2026.

— The stakes The outcome could affect how infrastructure, agribusiness, energy, mining and construction projects are approved.

— The change The law eases or removes licensing for some activities and expands self-declared permits.

— The critics The Federal Public Defender’s Office argues parts of the law are unconstitutional.

— The nuance The court could uphold some provisions and strike others, rather than voiding the whole law.

A quiet-sounding case about permits could reshape the pace of roads, dams and mines across the country.

Brazil’s Top Court Begins Judging Its Environmental Licensing Law. (Photo internet reproduction)

On August 12, the justices began weighing the country’s general environmental licensing law. It does not sound like a blockbuster case.

But it may be one of the most consequential things Brazil’s Supreme Court does this year. And the ruling could quietly reset how quickly roads, dams, mines and farms get the green light.

Why the environmental licensing law matters so much

Environmental licensing is the gate every large project in Brazil has to pass through before a single shovel hits the ground. It decides how long approvals take, how much they cost and how solid they are once granted.

Change the rules of that gate, and you change the economics of everything from a highway to a hydroelectric dam.

What the court is actually judging

The case centres on the general environmental licensing law, formally Law 15.190/2025, passed last year after a long fight in Congress. The Supreme Federal Court took it up in a bundle of constitutional challenges, so several disputes are being heard together.

At its heart is a simple question: how much of this new, looser licensing regime is compatible with Brazil’s constitution.

What the law changes in practice

The law’s supporters pitched it as a way to cut red tape that had bogged down worthwhile projects for years. It broadens the activities that can skip full licensing altogether, in some cases including certain farming operations.

It also expands a mechanism known as licensing by adhesion and commitment, a form of faster, largely self-declared permit.

The role of the watchdog agencies

Part of what makes the law contentious is how it treats Brazil’s federal technical agencies. Critics say it narrows the say of bodies like Ibama, ICMBio, Funai and Iphan, which review environmental and indigenous impacts.

Trim those agencies’ role, and you speed things up, but you also thin out the scrutiny that permits are supposed to carry.

Who is for it, and who is against

Industry groups have lined up firmly behind the law, and one construction association even filed to defend it before the court. For builders and developers, faster, cheaper permitting is close to a permanent wish-list item.

On the other side, the Federal Public Defender’s Office argues the law weakens environmental safeguards enough to be unconstitutional.

The Amazon in the background

This is not an abstract legal debate; it lands in a country where the Amazon is under constant pressure. Looser licensing raises the stakes for sensitive regions, where a shortcut in review can carry lasting consequences.

That is why environmental groups are watching the case as closely as any single deforestation ruling.

What a ruling could look like

One important nuance is that this is not an all-or-nothing decision, whatever the headlines might suggest. The court can uphold some provisions of the law while striking down others it finds unconstitutional.

Reporting also indicates the justices are unlikely to automatically cancel permits already issued under the current rules.

Why business is paying attention

For companies, the value of a permit lies in its legal durability as much as in how fast it arrives. A licence that might be challenged or unwound later is a shaky foundation for a multi-year investment.

The court’s ruling will shape the timing, cost and legal security of projects across several major sectors.

A balancing act, not a switch

Underneath the legal arguments sits an old tension between growth and protection that no ruling fully resolves. Brazil wants to build faster, but it also carries unique responsibility for some of the planet’s most important ecosystems.

Where the court draws that line will echo well beyond this single law.

What to watch next

The immediate thing to follow is how far the justices go in trimming or preserving the law’s provisions. Watch, too, for how quickly any decision translates into new guidance for projects already in the pipeline.

Either way, a case that sounds technical could end up steering years of construction and investment.

Frequently Asked Questions

What law is the Supreme Court judging?

Brazil’s general environmental licensing law, formally Law 15.190/2025, which sets the rules for permitting large projects. The court began hearing constitutional challenges on August 12, 2026.

What does the law change?

It eases or removes licensing for some activities, including certain farming. And expands a faster, largely self-declared permit known as licensing by adhesion and commitment.

Why do critics oppose it?

The Federal Public Defender’s Office and environmental groups argue it weakens safeguards and narrows the role of agencies like Ibama. ICMBio, Funai and Iphan, making parts of it unconstitutional.

Could the whole law be struck down?

Not necessarily. The court can uphold some provisions and strike others, and reporting suggests permits already issued are unlikely to be automatically cancelled.

Sources: Jota; O Globo; Poder360; Agência Brasil; Al Jazeera.

World.title: García Márquez’s Mexico City Home Closes for Lack of Money
World.content:
Mexico · Culture

Key Facts — The closure Gabriel García Márquez’s house in Mexico City has closed to the public for lack of funds.

— The home He lived there for 39 years, until his death in 2014.

— The opening It had been open to visitors since 2021.

— The reason Maintenance costs could not be covered.

— The ticket Entry had cost 400 pesos, about US$23, which still did not cover upkeep.

The house where the Nobel laureate lived and wrote for decades has shut its doors to the public. Unable to cover its own upkeep.

García Márquez’s Mexico City Home Closes for Lack of Money. (Photo internet reproduction)

The house where Gabriel García Márquez lived, wrote and dreamed for nearly four decades has fallen quiet. The Mexico City home of the Nobel-winning author has closed its doors to the public.

Undone not by scandal or neglect but by something stubbornly mundane: it could no longer pay for its own upkeep.

A literary landmark goes dark

For readers who make quiet pilgrimages to the homes of favourite writers, this was always a special address. It was where García Márquez, the towering figure of Latin American letters, lived for 39 years until his death in 2014.

Now, according to reporting, it has closed to visitors for the simplest of reasons: the money to maintain it ran out.

From private home to public shrine

The house opened its doors to the public in 2021, inviting ordinary readers into the private world of a literary legend. Wandering the rooms of a beloved author is one of the few ways to feel physically closer to the books that shaped you.

For devotees of ‘One Hundred Years of Solitude’, the place offered a tangible link to the man behind the myth.

The unglamorous problem of upkeep

The cause of the closure is painfully ordinary, and all the more relatable for it. Old houses are expensive to keep standing.

Reporting says maintenance costs simply could not be covered by the operation running the site. Even a shrine to literary genius is, in the end.

A building that needs a sound roof, working systems and a real budget.

When a ticket is not enough

The house charged an entry fee of 400 pesos, roughly US$23, which is hardly a trivial or token sum. Yet even at that price, ticket sales were not enough to keep the doors open on a sustainable footing.

It is a pointed reminder of how thin the finances of many cultural sites really are behind the scenes.

A wider strain on culture

The story echoes a much broader struggle facing museums and heritage homes all over the world. Cultural institutions frequently run on tight budgets, leaning on grants, private donors or steady support from the state.

When any one of those props weakens, even famous and well-loved sites can suddenly find themselves shuttered.

Why García Márquez still matters

García Márquez did not merely write bestsellers; he changed the way the entire world reads Latin America. His magical realism transformed the region’s history, politics and folklore into something universal and enduring.

Against that backdrop, a closed house feels like a small dishonour to an author of such outsized legacy.

A shared regional heritage

Though the house sits in Mexico City, García Márquez was Colombian, and his legacy belongs to the whole region. His work remains a genuine point of pride across Latin America and far beyond its borders.

That sense of shared ownership is exactly why the closure resonates well past Mexico’s own frontiers.

Where the money usually comes from

Writers’ houses rarely pay for themselves on ticket sales alone, wherever in the world they happen to sit. Most rely on some blend of public funding, foundation grants and the loyalty of a few committed patrons.

When that mix is absent or too thin, the gap between visitor income and running costs quickly becomes fatal.

The question of rescue

A closure of this kind is not always permanent, and history offers a few hopeful precedents. Governments, foundations or private patrons could still step in to preserve and eventually reopen the site.

Whether anyone actually does may depend on how loudly readers and institutions choose to object.

What to watch next

The immediate question is whether the closure prompts a public offer of support from any quarter. Watch for any move by Mexican or Colombian cultural authorities, or by donors, to secure the house’s future.

For now, one of literature’s warmest addresses stands empty and silent, simply waiting.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened to the house?

Gabriel García Márquez’s home in Mexico City has closed to the public because it could not cover its maintenance costs.

How long did he live there?

For 39 years, until his death in 2014. The house opened to the public in 2021.

Why did it close?

According to reporting, upkeep costs could not be covered, even with an entry fee of 400 pesos, about US$23.

Why does it matter?

García Márquez reshaped world literature with his magical realism. His home was a cherished link to his life and work.

Could it reopen?

Possibly. Public attention or support from governments, foundations or private patrons could help secure its future.

Sources: Clarín; Mexican and Colombian press.

World.title: Medellín Throws a Benefit Concert for Colombia’s Earthquake Victims
World.content:
Colombia · Culture

Key Facts — The event Medellín will host a charity concert, ‘Colombia, Medellín te quiere’, on August 15.

— The venue It takes place at the Centro de Eventos La Macarena.

— The cause It is a donation drive for families affected by the western Colombia earthquake.

— The lineup Artists include Luis Alfonso, Kapo, Pipe Bueno, Westcol, Andy Rivera and Felipe Peláez, among more than 25.

— The companion show A separate Miami benefit, ‘Unidos por los nuestros’, follows on August 16 with stars like Marc Anthony.

Colombia’s music world is rallying for families hit by the quake, with a hometown show and a star-studded companion concert in Miami.

A concert crowd. Medellin hosts ‘Colombia, Medellin te quiere’ on August 15 to raise aid for the western Colombia earthquake victims. (Photo: Shixart1985, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

And Medellín is turning a single night of music into a lifeline for the families left reeling. When disaster strikes Colombia, its musicians tend to answer, and quickly.

After an earthquake battered the country’s west, the industry is rallying once again.

Medellín opens its arms

The centrepiece is a charity concert in Medellín titled ‘Colombia, Medellín te quiere’, a name that doubles neatly as a message. It is set for August 15 at the Centro de Eventos La Macarena, one of the city’s best-known venues.

The goal is simple and direct: gather donations and practical aid for the families hardest hit by the earthquake.

Who is performing

The lineup leans on homegrown talent rather than a parade of global megastars, and that is part of its charm. Artists named so far include Luis Alfonso, Kapo, Pipe Bueno, Westcol, Andy Rivera and Felipe Peláez.

Organizers say more than 25 performers will take part, turning the night into a broad, cross-genre show of solidarity.

A companion concert in Miami

Medellín is not the only stage carrying this effort. A separate benefit is planned in Miami the following day, on August 16.

Called ‘Unidos por los nuestros’, it draws bigger international names, with reporting pointing to stars like Marc Anthony. Together, the two shows widen the net, reaching both Colombians at home and the large diaspora living abroad.

Why the earthquake hit so hard

The quake struck western Colombia, damaging homes and upending daily life across several different regions. Coverage has pointed to affected areas including Chocó and parts of the country’s coffee-growing zone.

For many families, the loss is not an abstraction; it is a roof, a livelihood and a hard-won sense of safety.

Music as a relief machine

Benefit concerts are more than feel-good gestures, whatever the cynics might say. They are efficient fundraising engines.

A single well-publicized night can channel the attention of millions toward one specific, urgent and immediate need. In Colombia, where music is woven deeply into national identity, popular artists carry real convening power.

The reach of Colombian stars

Colombia’s artists have become a genuine cultural export in recent years, spanning reggaeton, pop and vallenato. That global profile means a local tragedy can command international attention the moment those artists choose to speak up.

Turning hard-won fame into fundraising is a role many Colombian musicians appear to embrace readily and without fuss.

More than one way to give

The concerts are one clear channel for help, but the wider effort extends well beyond the ticketed shows themselves. Some artists are reportedly gathering relief supplies and donations around their scheduled performances.

The combined push blends straightforward cash donations with practical, on-the-ground aid for affected families.

A tradition of showing up

This is not the first time Colombia’s music scene has mobilized in the wake of a national emergency. Artists there have a long habit of lending their platforms to relief drives when floods, quakes or violence strike.

That track record is part of why the public tends to trust these events to actually deliver help.

A test of solidarity

Disasters have a way of revealing how a society responds, and Colombia’s cultural sector is answering loudly. The scale of the turnout, in both artists and audiences, will signal the real depth of national solidarity.

For the families still waiting on help, that solidarity is not symbolic at all; it is closer to survival.

What to watch next

The immediate measure of success is how much the concerts raise and how quickly the aid actually reaches victims. It is worth watching, too, whether the momentum sustains itself beyond a single busy weekend of shows.

Relief is a marathon rather than a sprint, and the hardest work often begins after the music stops.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Medellín concert?

A charity event called ‘Colombia, Medellín te quiere’. On August 15 at the Centro de Eventos La Macarena, raising aid for earthquake-affected families.

Who is performing in Medellín?

Artists including Luis Alfonso, Kapo, Pipe Bueno, Westcol, Andy Rivera and Felipe Peláez, among more than 25 performers.

Is there another concert?

Yes. A separate Miami benefit, ‘Unidos por los nuestros’, is planned for August 16 with bigger international names, reportedly including Marc Anthony.

What is the cause?

Both events raise donations and aid for families affected by the earthquake in western Colombia.

Which areas were hit?

Coverage points to affected regions including Chocó and parts of the coffee-growing zone.

Sources: Colombian press; concert organizers.

World.title: Venezuela’s Oil Output Inches Up, but India Turns Away
World.content:
Venezuela · Oil

Key Facts — The output Venezuela’s July oil production came in around 1.12 million barrels a day, according to OPEC-based data.

— The range Other trackers put it higher, between roughly 1.16 and 1.22 million barrels a day.

— The India shift Venezuelan crude exports to India fell to about 178,000 barrels a day in July.

— The drop That was down from around 277,000 barrels a day earlier in the year.

— The backdrop Venezuela’s oil industry is still recovering slowly under the weight of US sanctions.

The numbers point to a slow, grinding recovery under sanctions, even as one of the country’s newer customers quietly pulls back.

Venezuela’s Oil Output Inches Up, but India Turns Away. (Photo internet reproduction)

Venezuela’s oil industry, once the envy of the region, now measures progress in small, careful steps. Its July output edged up to roughly 1.12 million barrels a day.

A modest gain that underlines both a slow recovery and the country’s still-diminished place in the world market.

What the production numbers say

Pinning down how much oil Venezuela pumps is harder than it should be, mainly because the sources rarely agree with one another. OPEC-based figures put July production at about 1.12 million barrels a day, a slight improvement on the month before.

Other trackers, including ship-watchers and Venezuela’s own state producer PDVSA, place it higher, somewhere between 1.16 and 1.22 million barrels a day.

Why the sources diverge

The gaps are not random, and they are not evidence of anyone fudging the books. They reflect how each source chooses to measure the oil.

Some counts fold in condensates and natural-gas liquids, while others track only the crude actually loaded onto departing tankers. For a country as opaque and heavily sanctioned as Venezuela, a single agreed figure is a luxury that simply does not exist.

A shadow of its former self

Whatever the exact number turns out to be, the deeper story is one of dramatically diminished scale. Venezuela once pumped more than three million barrels a day and sat comfortably among the world’s major oil exporters.

Years of underinvestment, mismanagement and American sanctions hollowed out the industry, leaving today’s output at a fraction of that former peak.

Where Venezuela’s oil goes now

With few open markets available, every barrel has to find a willing buyer, and the list of them is short. In July, Reuters-based reporting put shipments to Europe at about 82,200 barrels a day and Chevron-linked volumes at roughly 293,000.

The rest leans heavily on China and a handful of intermediaries, which is exactly why any lost customer is felt so sharply.

India steps back

The more striking shift in July came on the demand side, and specifically in India. Venezuelan crude exports to India fell to about 178,000 barrels a day, down from around 277,000 earlier in the year.

India had quietly become a meaningful buyer of discounted Venezuelan oil, so a pullback of that size genuinely matters.

Why India’s move stings

Given how few markets remain open to it, every barrel Venezuela manages to sell is precious to the government’s finances. Losing volume to a growing customer like India tightens an already narrow commercial space with little room to spare.

It also leaves the country more dependent on a shrinking group of buyers, chief among them China.

The sanctions squeeze

US sanctions remain the single defining constraint on Venezuela’s oil trade, shaping almost every deal. They complicate payments, frighten off cautious buyers and force sales at steep discounts through layers of intermediaries.

Any recovery in the volume pumped runs straight into the same wall: restricted, nervous access to actual customers.

The economics of a discount barrel

Because of the legal and reputational risk, Venezuelan crude typically sells well below global benchmark prices. That discount means the country earns less per barrel than its rivals, even in months when it manages to pump more.

Volume gains, in other words, do not translate cleanly into revenue gains for a state that badly needs the cash.

A slow, uneven rebuild

Reporting suggests PDVSA has been cutting some traders out of the chain and dealing more directly with returning refiners. That shift could tighten margins in the company’s favour, but it does little to change the underlying ceiling on sales.

Rebuilding a hollowed-out industry takes sustained investment, and sanctions keep much of that investment on the sidelines.

Why it matters beyond Venezuela

Venezuela sits on some of the world’s largest proven oil reserves, so its trajectory carries weight far beyond its borders. Any easing or tightening of sanctions can ripple through global oil markets and reshape regional politics.

Neighbours and investors alike watch these monthly figures for clues about where the country, and its oil, are heading.

What to watch next

The near-term question is whether output can hold above the one-million-barrel mark and keep climbing. On the demand side, the thing to watch is whether India’s pullback proves temporary or hardens into a lasting trend.

And, as ever with Venezuela, the biggest single variable remains what Washington decides to do about sanctions.

More: Brazil news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much oil is Venezuela producing?

Around 1.12 million barrels a day in July per OPEC-based data, though other trackers put it between roughly 1.16 and 1.22 million.

Why do the figures vary?

Different sources measure differently; some include condensates and gas liquids, others count only crude on tankers. Venezuela’s opacity adds uncertainty.

What happened with India?

Venezuelan crude exports to India fell to about 178,000 barrels a day in July, down from around 277,000 earlier in the year.

Why is output so low historically?

Venezuela once pumped over three million barrels a day. Underinvestment, mismanagement and US sanctions cut that to just above one million.

Why does it matter globally?

Venezuela holds some of the world’s largest oil reserves, so its output and any sanctions changes can move markets and regional politics.

Sources: OPEC; Reuters; Argus; PDVSA data.

World.title: US Puts US$2 Million Into Guyana’s Skies as It Watches Venezuela
World.content:
Guyana · Security

Key Facts — The funding The US announced US$2 million to boost Guyana’s air surveillance and drone capabilities.

— The trigger It followed an August 11 meeting between US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and President Irfaan Ali.

— The purpose To help Guyana monitor its airspace and build unmanned-aircraft capacity.

— The uses It is tied to counternarcotics, border security and other priorities.

— The framework It builds on a US-Guyana security cooperation agreement signed in March 2025.

Washington is helping Georgetown see what flies over its territory, a modest sum with an outsized strategic message.

A surveillance drone. The US pledged US$2 million to strengthen Guyana’s air surveillance and drone capabilities. (Photo: AMISOM Public Information, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The United States is putting that amount into helping Guyana watch its own skies. Two million dollars is a small sum in geopolitics, but where it is spent can matter more than how much.

A modest investment loaded with strategic meaning as tensions with neighbouring Venezuela simmer.

What the US announced

The United States said it would provide US$2 million to strengthen Guyana’s air surveillance and drone capabilities. The aim is to help the small country monitor its airspace and develop unmanned-aircraft systems.

It is about awareness: knowing what enters and moves through Guyanese skies.

The meeting behind it

The announcement followed a high-level visit. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau met President Irfaan Ali in Georgetown on August 11.

Landau’s trip also took in Trinidad and Tobago, underscoring Washington’s regional focus. Such visits are how security relationships are cemented and funding is unveiled.

The uses for the money

The funding is explicitly linked to several security priorities. These include counternarcotics, border security and broader national defense.

In a region where trafficking routes cross porous borders, air awareness is valuable.

The Venezuela shadow

The strategic backdrop is impossible to ignore. Guyana and Venezuela are locked in a dispute over the Essequibo region.

Caracas has revived old claims to territory that makes up much of Guyana. Any US help to Guyana’s defenses is read, in part, through that lens.

Why airspace matters most

Of all the domains to watch, airspace is telling. Drones, aircraft and incursions all reveal intent.

For a country with a long, thinly monitored frontier, seeing the sky is a force multiplier. Modern surveillance lets a small nation punch above its weight.

Building on an existing pact

This is not a one-off gesture. It builds on a US-Guyana security cooperation agreement signed in March 2025.

That framework has steadily deepened defense ties between the two countries. Each new tranche of support tightens the relationship.

A small sum, a clear signal

The dollar figure is deliberately modest, but the message is not. Washington is signalling that it is paying attention to Guyana’s security.

In deterrence, being seen to care can matter as much as the hardware.

Guyana’s balancing act

Newly oil-rich, Guyana is courted by many and wary of over-reliance on any one partner. Deeper US ties bring protection but also expectations.

Georgetown must weigh security benefits against strategic entanglement.

What to watch next

Watch whether US support scales up from this modest start. The Essequibo dispute remains the wildcard that could accelerate cooperation.

For now, Guyana gains a sharper view of its own skies.

A frontier hard to watch

Guyana’s territory is vast, forested and thinly populated, a nightmare to monitor from the ground. Aircraft and drones can cover in hours what patrols would take weeks to reach.

That is why air-domain awareness is such a force multiplier for a small state.

Oil wealth raises the stakes

Guyana’s new oil riches have made it far more strategically important than its size suggests. Wealth attracts both investment and unwanted attention, from traffickers to a covetous neighbour.

Protecting that wealth is now a national priority, and a shared interest with partners like the US.

The limits of US$2 million

It would be easy to oversell a two-million-dollar programme. On its own, it buys capability, not security.

Real air defense would require far larger, sustained investment over years. This is a foundation and a signal, not a finished shield.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the US fund?

US$2 million to strengthen Guyana’s air surveillance and drone capabilities, helping it monitor its airspace.

When was it announced?

After an August 11 meeting between US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and President Irfaan Ali in Georgetown.

What is it for?

Counternarcotics, border security and broader national-security priorities, all tied to air-domain awareness.

How does Venezuela factor in?

Guyana and Venezuela are locked in a dispute over the Essequibo region, so US support for Guyana’s defenses carries strategic weight.

Is this new cooperation?

No. It builds on a US-Guyana security cooperation agreement signed in March 2025.

Sources: US Embassy Georgetown; US State Department; Guyanese presidency.

World.title: Records Show the MV Barima’s Faults Were Flagged Months Before It Sank
World.content:
Guyana · Accountability

Key Facts — The disaster The MV Barima sank on July 18 with 179 people aboard.

— The toll Reporting cited 76 rescued, 72 dead and 30 missing by early August.

— The records Maintenance logs from November 2025 to March 2026 documented serious defects.

— The faults They included an out-of-service generator, overheating machinery and a leaking engine exhaust.

— The question Some entries were marked urgent, raising why the vessel kept sailing.

Maintenance logs describe urgent, unfixed defects on the Guyanese ferry long before the disaster that killed dozens.

Records Show the MV Barima’s Faults Were Flagged Months Before It Sank. (Photo internet reproduction)

When the MV Barima went down off Guyana on July 18, it looked like a sudden tragedy. Maintenance records tell a slower, harder story: the ferry’s serious faults were documented for months before it sank.

Some of them flagged as urgent.

What happened to the MV Barima

The MV Barima sank on July 18 with 179 people aboard, one of Guyana’s worst recent maritime disasters. By early August, reporting cited 76 people rescued, 72 confirmed dead and 30 still missing.

The scale of loss turned attention quickly to how such a thing could happen.

A paper trail of problems

The most troubling evidence sits in the vessel’s own maintenance records. Logs covering November 2025 to March 2026 describe a string of mechanical failures.

This was not a boat in sudden distress; it was one with a documented history of trouble.

The defects on the list

The records paint a grim picture of the ferry’s condition. They describe an out-of-service generator, overheating machinery, a leaking main-engine exhaust and defective cooling equipment.

Electrical failures also featured, and several entries were marked urgent.

The word that changes everything: ‘urgent’

A defect noted in passing is one thing. A defect marked urgent is another.

It implies someone knew the problem was serious and pressing. That is what turns a maintenance file into a question of accountability.

What is verified, and what is not

It is important to be careful here. The records themselves are documented, and the sinking is beyond dispute.

But whether warnings were deliberately ‘ignored’ depends on who received them and what they decided. That is a question for an official investigation, not a maintenance log alone.

A familiar pattern in transport disasters

Sadly, the shape of this story is common. Many transport tragedies are preceded by documented, unheeded warnings.

Cost, pressure to keep services running and diffuse responsibility often combine. The result is a known risk that is tolerated until it becomes a catastrophe.

Why it matters for Guyana

Guyana is booming on oil wealth, but ferries remain a lifeline for many communities. Public trust in that transport depends on knowing safety is taken seriously.

A disaster tied to ignored defects strikes at that trust directly.

The push for answers

Families of the victims are owed a clear account of what went wrong. An honest inquiry would establish who saw the warnings and why the vessel kept sailing.

Accountability is not only about blame; it is about preventing the next disaster.

What to watch next

The key is the official investigation and whether it confirms the maintenance findings. Also watch for any changes to Guyana’s ferry oversight and inspection rules.

For the families, the priority is simpler: the truth, and that it never happens again.

A lifeline turned deadly

For Guyana’s riverine and coastal communities, ferries are not a convenience but a necessity. They carry people, goods and vehicles where roads simply do not reach.

That dependence is exactly why safety failures on such vessels carry such a heavy human cost.

The oil-wealth contrast

The tragedy lands amid a jarring contrast. Guyana is suddenly one of the world’s fastest-growing economies, thanks to offshore oil.

Yet the everyday infrastructure many citizens rely on has not kept pace with that windfall. A nation earning billions from crude still lost dozens of people on an ageing ferry.

From records to reform

Documented defects are only useful if they drive change. The value of a maintenance log is in acting on it.

Investigators will now ask whether Guyana’s inspection and oversight system failed alongside the vessel. The answer will shape how the country protects passengers in the future.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the MV Barima?

It was a Guyanese ferry that sank on July 18 with 179 people aboard. In one of the country’s worst recent maritime disasters.

How many people died?

Reporting cited 76 rescued, 72 dead and 30 missing by early August.

What did the records show?

Maintenance logs from November 2025 to March 2026 documented serious defects. Including an out-of-service generator and a leaking engine exhaust, some marked urgent.

Were the warnings ignored?

That specific claim is not yet proven. It depends on who received the reports and chose to keep the vessel sailing, a question for an official inquiry.

Why does it matter?

Ferries are a lifeline in Guyana, and a disaster tied to documented, unheeded faults undermines public trust in transport safety.

Sources: Kaieteur News; Guyanese authorities; local reporting.

World.title: Lionel Messi Says He May Not Play Much Longer After Father’s Death
World.content:
Argentine soccer star Lionel Messi said Wednesday that he has “a lot of doubts” about whether he will continue playing football “for much longer,” in an emotional farewell letter to his father and agent, Jorge Messi, who died Friday at the age of 68. In his first public reaction since his father’s death, the 39-year-old star reflected on the final months of his father’s life, which were marked by the worsening cancer that ultimately killed him, according to media reports.



Jorge Messi’s declining health, after playing a central role throughout his son’s brilliant career, coincided with the 2026 World Cup in North America. Argentina lost the final 1-0 to Spain on July 19 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. “I don’t know what I’m going to do without you, I don’t know how to go on. All I ever did was play football, and now I have a lot of doubts about whether I’ll keep doing it for much longer,” Messi wrote in a letter posted on Instagram alongside photographs of himself with his father.

“You kept asking me to play in one last World Cup, and just days before it started was when you got much worse. It was the first time you weren’t going to be at a tournament,” the Argentina captain added. “I kept telling you we were going to reach the final so you could travel.”

I Never Managed to Feel Right

The former FC Barcelona forward, whose contract with Inter Miami runs through 2028, said he wanted to win the World Cup so he could take the trophy to his father. But he acknowledged that he was unable to do so because his body failed him in the title match against a Spain side that overwhelmed Argentina.

“A huge hug to you and your family during these difficult moments, Leo. Stay strong,” Cristiano Ronaldo, Messi’s longtime rival in the debate over the world’s best player, replied to Wednesday’s post. Jorge Messi’s poor health, which became public during the World Cup, ended with his burial Sunday near Rosario.

In Argentina’s opening match against Algeria, Messi cried after scoring one of his three goals in a 3-0 victory. Afterward, he acknowledged that the unusual display of emotion was connected to his father’s condition. “Every time a match ended, I waited for and missed your message. That was when I realized the situation was really serious. Even so, I couldn’t stop thinking about going as far as possible, to give you time and so you could see one of the matches,” Messi wrote.

“We reached the final and you couldn’t be there. I wanted to win it so I could take it to you and show you another one. I couldn’t. My legs had nothing left. This time I tried to fight against my body, but I couldn’t. I never managed to feel right,” he added. After losing the final in his sixth and final World Cup, Messi returned to Argentina to visit his father. He realized that Jorge had been unable to follow much of the tournament. “When I arrived, you thought we had lost the final on penalties.

We couldn’t talk about anything that had happened. You weren’t able to enjoy any of it,” Messi wrote. “We weren’t champions, but you have no idea how much we enjoyed every match. Once again, you were right: I had to be there and play in it,” he added.

Father, Friend and Agent

Messi, who has yet to define his international future, produced an exceptional World Cup at the end of a career that many believe has established him as the greatest footballer in history. With eight goals and performances reminiscent of his peak years, he was the driving force behind Argentina reaching a second consecutive World Cup final.



Jorge Messi is widely regarded as a fundamental figure in the career of the most decorated footballer in history. Demanding and critical of his son, but also his most constant source of support, he accompanied Lionel from the modest football fields of Rosario to the highest levels of the sport.

“You were always like that from the time I was little. You took me to every training session as soon as you got home from work,” Messi recalled. “You never missed a match. How much you suffered watching me and how much you enjoyed it, even though you never gave me many compliments.”

The eight-time Ballon d’Or winner emphasized his father’s importance both on and off the field. “You were a father, a friend and an agent. You were always the person you needed to be at every moment, and you never got anything wrong,” he wrote. “Rest in peace and look after us from above the way you did here. Thank you for everything.”

Messi left Argentina for the United States on Tuesday night, according to local media. Neither he nor Inter Miami has said when he will return to competition.

World.title: Is Panama the New Costa Rica? A 2026 Expat & Real Estate Investor Comparison
World.content:
For decades, Costa Rica was the undisputed poster child of Central American expat life. However, a quiet reshuffling of priorities is underway, and a growing number of (Real Estate) investors, immigrations and retirees are now asking: Is Panama the new Costa Rica?

Fresh residency data, shifting visa requirements, and a surge in real estate acquisitions suggest the question is not just rhetorical. Panama’s streamlined immigration framework, its use of the US dollar, and a territorial tax system are redrawing the map for those seeking a second home in the tropics.

To understand the ground reality, we spoke with the team at Expat-Tations, a relocation advisory firm operating in both Panama and Costa Rica, along with their in-house law division who process residency applications daily in both countries. As well as their Real Estate division in Panama that handles property acquisitions, often to align legal residency. Their insights reveal a clear trend: more expats are crossing the border, and the numbers don’t lie.

Quick Takeaway

For investors and retirees seeking speed and a straightforward path to permanent residency, Panama is pulling ahead in 2026. Costa Rica retains its biodiversity and established expat communities, but its slower immigration processing and temporary-to-permanent residency ladder are pushing many toward Panama.

According to senior attorney, Ricardo Batres, at the law firm Expat-Tations in Panama:

“We’re seeing a 40% increase in inquiries from people who were originally targeting Costa Rica. They’ve done their research and realized Panama offers them a permanent solution in a fraction of the time.”

At a Glance: The 2026 Comparison

Feature Panama Costa Rica Permanent Residency Timeline 30–90 Days (Golden Investor Visa), 3–5 Years (Temporary to Permanent) on most programs with several complicated renewals Minimum Real Estate Investment $300k Gold Investor, $200k if Friendly Nations Residency $150,000 (Temporary residency only at first) Path to Citizenship 5 years 7 years (for most nationalities) Forced Social Security Payments Not required A requirement for residency with a monthly fee reaching often hundreds of dollars Residency Type Granted Direct Permanent in most cases (Golden Investor, Retiree) Temporary first, then Permanent Property Ownership Via corporation allowed Personal name only Currency US Dollar Costa Rican Colón Infrastructure Modern metro, fiber-optic, global airport Poor roads, power outages Cost of Living ~15% cheaper than San José Highest consumer prices in Central America Processing time of residency 3 to 6 months on all, except Golden Investor 45 days 1 to 3 years until you have a status

Residency Timelines: Speed vs. Patience

The sharpest contrast between the two neighbors lies in how quickly a foreigner can secure permanent status. According to the legal experts at Expat-Tations, this is the number one factor driving the shift toward Panama. In both countries the law sets a maximum timeline of 6 months, but Costa Rica hasn’t been able to keep that timeline ever, resulting in many cases the process taking up to 3 years.

Panama’s Qualified Investor Residency

In Panama, the Qualified Investor Visa, also called the Golden Visa, delivers permanent residency in as little as 30 to 90 days. A buyer who puts $300,000 into approved real estate walks away with permanent residency almost immediately, without any obligation to live in the country first.

The team at Expat-Tations notes that their Panama-based law firm have streamlined the process to near perfection. Applicants are often surprised at how efficient the system is compared to other countries in the region. Especially cause they also offer the required legal documents, like FBI background check with their digital fingerprint system.

Documents from Panama’s Ministry of Commerce and Industries confirm that real estate is the engine of this speed advantage. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the Qualified Investor program funneled $113.6 million into the economy. Nearly 87 percent of successful applicants chose property as their qualifying asset.

A government spokesperson familiar with immigration processing described the draw in blunt terms:

“Our Qualified Investor program is designed to provide certainty and speed. People don’t want to wait half a decade for a piece of paper when they’re ready to build a life.” [Translated from Spanish]

Costa Rica’s Inversionista Residency

Costa Rica’s main investor category, the Inversionista Residency, tells a different story. A $150,000 investment in real estate, stocks, or a productive project opens the door, but only to temporary residency at first. Holders must renew that status for three years before they can even apply for permanent residence. Many expats end up waiting five years or longer.

This is where Expat-Tations sees the most frustration among their clients. Relocation advisor and Real Estate Broker, Ismael Arcia shared: “People come to us thinking Costa Rica is the easy option. They don’t realize they’re signing up for years of renewals, paperwork, and uncertainty. In Panama, they can get the final stamp in a matter of months with the right property.”

Costa Rica’s migration authorities have been grappling with backlogs. Routine residency renewals can stretch for months, and the path from temporary to permanent status remains a bureaucratic marathon. That sluggishness, combined with a 2024 tax overhaul that began treating worldwide income often as taxable for residents, has pushed many long-time expats to explore alternatives just across the border.

Real Estate Investment: What Your Money Actually Buys

Cost-conscious buyers who compare the two markets often fixate on entry prices, yet the raw numbers rarely tell the whole story. The Expat-Tations real estate team emphasizes that buyers need to look beyond the dollar figure and understand what each investment actually secures.

Panama’s Real Estate Residency Pathway

Current minimum: $300,000 ( For Friendly Nations Residency only $200,000 )

**After October 2026 possible:** $500,000

The impending hike has lit a fire under the market. Agents and the Expat-Tations team report a frenzy of pre-qualification requests from buyers who want to lock in the lower threshold before it vanishes.

What $300,000 buys you in Panama: Direct permanent residency, no waiting period, and the freedom to live in the country immediately.

Costa Rica’s Real Estate Residency Pathway

Minimum: $150,000

Costa Rica’s $150,000 Inversionista line looks cheaper on paper, but it does not buy permanence. It buys a renewable temporary permit. The property must be registered in the applicant’s personal name, a restriction that can complicate estate planning and asset protection.

What $150,000 buys you in Costa Rica: Temporary residency with renewals for 3+ years, no guarantee of permanent status, and personal-name registration only. After 3 years of renewals another application for permanent residency follows.

Property Ownership and Corporate Structures

Property rights also differ in ways that surprise newcomers. In both countries, foreigners enjoy the same ownership rights as locals, with one major exception:

Panama: The constitution prohibits non-citizens from owning land within ten kilometers of any international border.

The constitution prohibits non-citizens from owning land within ten kilometers of any international border. Costa Rica: The Maritime Zone Law creates a similar coastal restriction, though the mechanics are different.

However, the Expat-Tations legal team highlights a critical advantage in Panama: the ability to hold real estate through a Panamanian corporation and trusts, as long as the visa applicant is listed as the Ultimate Beneficial Owner. That corporate wrapper provides layers of privacy and asset protection that Costa Rica’s more rigid personal-name requirement does not easily match.

“This is often a game-changer for serious investors,” explains a Panama-based real estate attorney Luis Mon, from the Expat-Tations Real Estate devision. “You can structure your assets efficiently, protect your privacy, and still qualify for residency. Costa Rica doesn’t offer that flexibility.”

The Currency Advantage for Real Estate Buyers

Another structural difference is currency. Panama uses the US dollar. Buyers who wire funds from North America or Europe sidestep the exchange-rate anxiety that can come with Costa Rica’s colón. In 2024 and 2025, the colón’s volatility against the dollar whipsawed household budgets and made long-term financial planning a headache for retirees and investors alike.

Dollarized pricing in Panama eliminates that variable entirely; a factor that Expat-Tations brokers cite as a decisive tiebreaker for their clients.

The ‘Is Panama the New Costa Rica?’ Debate Gains Momentum

Shift the lens from investment math to daily life, and the conversation only intensifies. Costa Rica still holds a powerful brand built on eco-tourism, biodiversity, and a “pura vida” identity that no competitor can replicate. But expats who have lived in both countries, and the advisors at Expat-Tations who guide them, point to infrastructure and processing gaps that can erode the idyllic image.

Infrastructure: Urban Edge vs. Rural Challenges

Panama City offers a modern metro system, high-speed fiber-optic network, and Tocumen International Airport as a global flight hub connecting to over 80 destinations.

offers a modern metro system, high-speed fiber-optic network, and Tocumen International Airport as a global flight hub connecting to over 80 destinations. Costa Rica’s road network, especially outside the Central Valley, remains notoriously unreliable, and power brownouts are a recurring feature of the rainy season in some regions.

Cost of Living: Panama is More Affordable

United Nations and regional bank data consistently rank Costa Rica as having the highest consumer prices in Central America. Utilities, gasoline, and imported goods carry steeper price tags there than in Panama, where the Panama Canal and the Colón Free Zone keep supply chains humming.

A 2025 cost-of-living survey by a global relocation firm placed Panama City roughly 15 percent cheaper than San José for a comparable expat lifestyle, a gap that widens considerably when housing is factored in.

Tourist Stays and Immigration Enforcement

Tourist stay limits and their observations, have tightened in both countries. Panama recently standardized to 90-180 days per visit for visa-exempt nationalities (including Americans, Canadians, and Brits) with a mandatory 30-day gap before re-entry now often enforced more strictly. Costa Rica similarly enforces a up to 180-day stay, though its exit-and-return practice has long been treated with a wink.

The difference is Panama’s clearly signaled intent to digitize and tighten enforcement while simultaneously speeding up residency approvals for those who commit to investment. The message is clear: short-term tourists are welcome, but people who want to stay should do so through formal channels, and those channels have been polished to work fast.

Junior Attorney and Legal Aid Edgar Landazuri at Expat-Tations sums it up: “Panama is saying, ‘If you’re serious about moving here, we have a fast lane for you.’ Costa Rica is still treating everyone the same, whether you’re a backpacker or a million-dollar investor. That’s starting to frustrate the high-net-worth crowd.”

Pensionado Perks: Residency Without Real Estate

Not everyone wants to buy property, and both countries recognize that.

Panama’s Pensionado Visa

Panama’s Pensionado Visa has carved out a reputation among retirees. Anyone with a lifetime pension of at least $1,000 per month can obtain permanent residency, no real estate purchase required.

The program’s signature draw is a booklet of legally mandated discounts:

25% off domestic and international airline tickets

domestic and international airline tickets 50% off movie tickets and hotel stays during the week

movie tickets and hotel stays during the week 25% off restaurant meals

restaurant meals 15–20% off medical services and hospital bills

According to the Expat-Tations legal team, this visa is processed in approximately 3 to 6 months, significantly faster than Costa Rica’s equivalent.

Costa Rica’s Pensionado Regime

Costa Rica’s pensionado regime also requires a $1,000 monthly pension and offers similar discounts on health care, transportation, and entertainment. However, the scope and depth of Panama’s menu of perks is widely seen as more generous and better enforced.

Critically, Costa Rica’s pensionado process still involves a temporary-to-permanent ladder that can take years. Applicants receive temporary residency first, with no guarantee of permanent status down the line and the need of several renewals.

Processing Speed for Retirees

A digital overhaul at Panama’s immigration authority has shortened approval windows and reduced the number of in-person appointments required. Applicants routinely report that the entire procedure, from initial application to the issuance of a cedula (national ID), can be completed in three to six months.

Costa Rica’s understaffed migration offices have struggled to match that pace. Expat-Tations advisors regularly field complaints about delayed appointments, lost paperwork, and unclear timelines.

What the Data Shows

The cumulative effect of faster residency processing, real estate flexibility, dollarized stability, no social security payments and modern infrastructure is no longer a well-kept secret. Property transactions in Panama’s beach communities and mountain towns have climbed steadily through 2025 and into 2026, fueled partly by Costa Rican expats who are shedding their residency and buying anew.

The legal team at Expat-Tations has witnessed this firsthand. One partner commented: “Three years ago, 70% of our inquiries were about Costa Rica. Today, that number has flipped. People are doing the math on time and realizing Panama gives them more certainty, while Costa Rica gives them a waiting game.”

Not everyone will be convinced to leave behind Costa Rica’s cloud forests and conservation ethos, but the question itself is telling. When even loyalists begin asking “Is Panama the new Costa Rica?” , does that mean “The axis of Central American expat life has already begun to tilt?”

World.title: Costa Rica Wildlife Study Records 79 Species at Reserva Conchal
World.content:
A year-long wildlife study at Reserva Conchal in Guanacaste documented 79 species of mammals, birds and reptiles, nearly double the 40 recorded during the property’s previous monitoring period in 2023–2024. The research was carried out at the Conchal Mixed National Wildlife Refuge using 20 camera traps placed at different points across the property.

The cameras operated for a year, recording wildlife activity and providing researchers with a broader look at animal life within Guanacaste’s tropical dry forest. The monitoring identified 28 mammal species, 48 bird species and three reptile species. White-nosed coatis, white-tailed deer, raccoons, opossums and coyotes were among the animals recorded with the greatest relative abundance.

The most notable findings involved Costa Rica’s wild cats. Cameras confirmed the presence of pumas, ocelots, known locally as manigordos, and jaguarundis. The study reported three puma records, 14 ocelots and six jaguarundis, along with evidence of reproduction, including a female ocelot accompanied by a cub.

The presence of large and medium-sized predators is being viewed by Reserva Conchal as an encouraging sign for the refuge, particularly because wild cats depend on functioning habitat and adequate prey populations. “Each species recorded gives us valuable information about the health of the ecosystem,” said Gabriela Meza, Sustainability Manager at Reserva Conchal.

Meza said the monitoring gives conservation teams a stronger scientific basis for deciding where future protection efforts should be concentrated. The increase from 40 species in the previous monitoring period to 79 in the latest survey is substantial, although it should be interpreted as an increase in species detected rather than evidence that wildlife populations themselves nearly doubled.

The publicly available report does not provide enough methodological detail to determine how directly the two monitoring periods can be compared. Reserva Conchal carries out its wildlife work with the Tempisque Conservation Area, McGill University in Canada, the SalveMonos Foundation and the Baulas-Conchal Marine-Coastal Biological Corridor. The partnerships are focused on wildlife research and maintaining connections between habitat areas used by animals moving through this part of Guanacaste.

More than 60 wildlife crossings have also been installed on the property in recent years. The crossings are intended to reduce vehicle strikes and electrocutions, two threats that can become more serious where wildlife habitat overlaps with roads, power infrastructure and tourism development.

Reserva Conchal has also incorporated artificial intelligence into biodiversity analysis, using technology alongside camera-trap monitoring to help researchers process wildlife information and guide conservation decisions. Previous reports on the property’s environmental programs have also documented its use of camera traps, wildlife crossings and collaboration with McGill University and SalveMonos.

The refuge is officially listed by Costa Rica’s National System of Conservation Areas, or SINAC, as the Conchal National Wildlife Refuge under the mixed category. It is located in the Cabo Velas district of Santa Cruz, Guanacaste.

Conservation work at Reserva Conchal also extends to schools in surrounding communities. Since 2017, its Simbiosis environmental education program has reached more than 3,700 students through activities involving biodiversity, ecosystem conservation, pollinators, reforestation and sustainability.

The program brings children and young people into direct contact with the natural environment, rather than limiting environmental education to the classroom. For Reserva Conchal, the latest camera-trap results offer another measure of what wildlife continues to use a landscape that combines protected habitat with one of Guanacaste’s best-known tourism areas.

Continued monitoring will be especially important in determining whether the expanded species list represents a lasting trend and how wild cats and other animals move through the refuge as development continues along Costa Rica’s northern Pacific coast.

World.title: Costa Rica Free-Zone Growth Slows to Weakest Pace Since 2020
World.content:
Growth in Costa Rica’s free-zone economy slowed sharply in June, falling to its weakest pace since 2020 and extending a year-long deceleration in one of the country’s most important economic sectors. Economic activity among companies operating under Costa Rica’s special regimes, which include most free-zone companies, grew 2.9% in June compared with the same month a year earlier, according to the latest Monthly Economic Activity Index, or IMAE, from the Central Bank of Costa Rica.

That was down from 17.2% annual growth in June 2025 and marked the 12th consecutive month in which the sector’s growth rate slowed. The Central Bank attributed much of the slowdown to weaker growth among manufacturers, particularly medical-device producers, as well as lower output of metal products such as electronic components and circuit boards. Professional and administrative services, including advertising, also lost momentum.

Free-zone manufacturing grew just 1.2% year over year in June. Manufacturing outside the special regime performed even worse, contracting 0.9%. The numbers matter because Costa Rica has built much of its recent export and foreign-investment success around free-zone companies, particularly medical-device manufacturers, technology firms and business-service operations.

The latest data do not show that Costa Rica’s free-zone model is collapsing or that companies are leaving the country in large numbers. Much of the slowdown follows an unusually strong period of expansion in 2025. Earlier this year, the Central Bank warned that the pace of growth in the special regime could continue moderating because it was being compared with exceptionally strong results from the previous year.

Still, the speed of the slowdown is notable. Overall economic activity in Costa Rica grew 3% in June, 2.2 percentage points less than in June 2025. Businesses operating outside the special regimes grew 3.1%, meaning the domestic economy slightly outperformed the free-zone sector during the month.

That represents a significant reversal from much of the past several years, when free-zone companies were among the main engines pulling national growth higher. The softer free-zone performance has already affected the broader economic outlook. In April, the Central Bank projected that Costa Rica’s economy would grow 3.5% in 2026, down from an earlier forecast of 3.8%.

At the time, it projected 5.5% growth for the special-regime economy, compared with preliminary growth of 12.7% in 2025. Researchers at the University of Costa Rica were somewhat more cautious in June, forecasting overall economic growth of 3.4% this year and growth of about 4% in the special regime.

They identified slower free-zone activity as one of the main reasons for the weaker national outlook.Not every part of Costa Rica’s economy slowed in June. Construction expanded 9.5%, helped by private projects and a 12.2% increase in public works. The Central Bank pointed to road and bridge projects, emergency reconstruction work and improvements at Juan Santamaría International Airport as contributors to the increase.

Services grew 3.9%, while commerce expanded 2.7%. Hotels and restaurants were among the service activities that grew faster than a year earlier. Agriculture barely grew, at 0.1%, as stronger banana, root-crop, beef and egg production was offset by declines in pineapple and coffee.



For Costa Rica, the question over the coming months will be whether the slowdown in free zones settles at a more normal growth rate after the exceptional gains of 2025 or develops into a broader competitiveness problem. The June numbers alone do not answer that question. They do, however, show that the part of Costa Rica’s economy that has delivered some of its strongest growth in recent years is no longer expanding at anything close to the pace seen a year ago.

World.title: Costa Rica Looks to Ukraine for Drone Technology in Security Fight
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Costa Rican President Laura Fernández exchanged invitations for official visits during a phone call yesterday, as the two leaders also discussed possible security cooperation involving Ukraine’s experience with drone technology. Zelensky invited Fernández to visit Ukraine, while the Costa Rican president invited Zelensky to Costa Rica, according to Ukraine’s presidential office and reports on the conversation.



Zelensky used the call to thank Costa Rica for its support for Ukraine in international forums, including votes on United Nations General Assembly resolutions concerning the war with Russia. He also highlighted Costa Rica’s backing for efforts to return Ukrainian children taken to Russia and initiatives aimed at holding Russia accountable for the war.

Ukraine said it had recovered 2,368 children as of early July. For Costa Rica, however, one of the most significant parts of the conversation centered on security. In a video of the call released by the Costa Rican government, Fernández said Costa Rica has a strong interest in learning from Ukraine’s experience with drone-based defense technology.

She linked that interest to her government’s efforts to modernize Costa Rica’s security capabilities as the country confronts drug trafficking and transnational organized crime. Ukraine has become one of the world’s leading developers and users of drone technology during its war with Russia, using unmanned aircraft for surveillance, reconnaissance, communications and battlefield operations.

Zelensky said Costa Rica had expressed specific interest in Ukraine’s security experience. The two presidents agreed that their teams would continue discussions and explore a possible format for a future meeting. No date or location for such a meeting was announced.

The exchange of invitations does not necessarily mean either presidential visit is being actively planned. Invitations between heads of state are common diplomatic gestures, and neither government has announced a timetable, itinerary or formal preparations for a visit. A trip by Fernández to Ukraine would also involve substantial security and logistical considerations because of the ongoing war.

Costa Rica has not indicated that preparations for such a visit are underway. A Zelensky visit to Costa Rica would avoid those complications, but there is similarly no indication that a trip to San José is imminent. For now, the more concrete outcome of yesterday’s conversation appears to be the possibility of technical cooperation on security.

That could move forward through government ministries, security officials and technical teams without requiring either president to travel. For Costa Rica, Ukraine’s rapidly developed expertise with drones could be particularly relevant for surveillance of borders, coastlines and areas used by organized crime and drug trafficking networks.

The conversation also adds a new dimension to relations between Costa Rica and Ukraine. San José has consistently supported Ukraine diplomatically since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, while the Fernández government is now exploring whether that relationship can produce practical security cooperation at home.

World.title: Latin American Qualifiers Face Double-Duty Day at Cincinnati Open
World.content:
Latin America’s Cincinnati Open contingent faces a high-pressure Wednesday after severe weather disrupted the opening day of qualifying, leaving several players from the region with unfinished business and the possibility of playing twice in one day. Four Latin American players entered Wednesday still in contention for spots in the main draw: Argentina’s Marco Trungelliti and Nadia Podoroska, along with Colombians Nicolás Mejía and Emiliana Arango.

The most intriguing possibility comes on the women’s side. Arango and Podoroska were placed in neighboring sections of the qualifying draw, and both had first-round matches carried into Wednesday. If both advance, they are scheduled to face each other later in the day for a place in the Cincinnati main draw.

Arango, the No. 10 qualifying seed, faces Aliaksandra Sasnovich, while former French Open semifinalist Podoroska takes on No. 16 seed Ella Seidel of Germany. The winners are scheduled to meet no earlier than 4 p.m. Wednesday. That creates a straightforward scenario for Latin American tennis: victories by both would guarantee either Colombia or Argentina another representative when main-draw play begins Thursday.

The men’s qualifying picture offers its own storyline. Trungelliti survived one of Tuesday’s tightest completed matches, rallying past Austria’s Sebastian Ofner 4-6, 6-4, 7-6(4). The 36-year-old Argentine now gets one of the biggest names in qualifying, former world No. 4 Kei Nishikori, with a main-draw place at stake.

Nishikori had his own difficult opening round, defeating Argentina’s Francisco Comesaña 6-4, 1-6, 7-5. Their meeting with Trungelliti gives Argentina another chance to prevent the Japanese veteran from reaching the main draw. Colombia’s Mejía has an even longer potential Wednesday ahead of him.

His first-round match against Britain’s Jacob Fearnley was pushed onto the Wednesday schedule. The winner is then scheduled to return after suitable rest to face either American Marcos Giron or Portugal’s Henrique Rocha for a place in the main draw. The compressed schedule is a direct consequence of Tuesday’s weather.

Severe storms delayed qualifying at the Lindner Family Tennis Center, where 48 men’s and 48 women’s qualifying matches had originally been scheduled across the two-day preliminary event. Twelve qualifiers from each draw will advance into the 96-player main draws. Several Latin American players have already been eliminated. Brazil’s Gustavo Heide fell 6-3, 6-4 to top qualifying seed Luca Van Assche, while Bolivia’s Hugo Dellien lost 6-3, 6-1 to Sho Shimabukuro. Comesaña’s narrow loss to Nishikori also ended his attempt to qualify.

On the women’s side, Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa and Argentina’s Solana Sierra were eliminated in the first qualifying round. Zarazúa, the No. 2 seed, lost to China’s Yue Yuan, while Japan’s Aoi Ito defeated sixth-seeded Sierra. Regardless of Wednesday’s qualifying results, Latin America already has several players waiting in the main draw. Brazil’s João Fonseca and Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo are among the men entered directly, while Colombia’s Camila Osorio opens against American Taylor Townsend.

The Osorio-Townsend winner would move on to face No. 2 seed Elena Rybakina. Main-draw play begins Thursday at the Cincinnati Open, one of the final major hard-court events before the U.S. Open.

World.title: Costa Rica Named Among Top Destinations for Solo Travelers
World.content:
Costa Rica has been included among 25 of the world’s best destinations for people traveling alone in a 2026 selection by Travel + Leisure, which highlighted the mix of outdoor adventure, beaches and places where visitors can slow down between activities. The list, published June 11, describes Costa Rica as particularly well suited to adventurous solo travelers.

Among the experiences singled out are whitewater rafting on the Reventazón River, ziplining through rainforest, waterfall rappelling and hiking around Arenal Volcano National Park. Travel + Leisure also points to the hot springs around Arenal as an option for travelers looking for a quieter break and highlights Pacific beaches near Manuel Antonio as popular choices for women traveling alone.

Costa Rica was one of 25 countries selected for the list alongside destinations including Thailand, Albania, Germany, Vietnam, Iceland, Japan and Denmark. The publication did not present the countries as a numbered ranking, meaning Costa Rica was included among the recommended destinations rather than assigned a specific position.

The recognition fits Costa Rica’s long-established tourism pitch: a relatively small country where travelers can move between volcanoes, rainforests and beaches while choosing from activities ranging from wildlife watching and hiking to surfing and rafting.

For solo visitors, that variety can be especially attractive because many of the country’s most popular activities are offered as guided day trips.
