World.title: 1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.content:
On a rain-washed weekend morning, mist clings to the peaks surrounding Ze’e Village in the southwestern Sichuan province. Over the sound of a rushing mountain stream, 24-year-old Jifu Lama leads a procession of children in matching kits. They navigate through rice paddies, along irrigation canals and over earthen mounds until they reach their destination: a soccer pitch carved out of a former cornfield.

Perched halfway up a mountain at an altitude of 1,300 meters, Lama’s pitch looks like a vibrant green terraced field folded into the sweeping landscape of Sichuan’s Daliangshan region. Standing in the center circle, the young coach directs his players — mostly children aged 6 to 13 from six neighboring Yi ethnic villages — to lace up their boots, arrange the cones and begin their warm-ups.

Ze’e Village is remote, accessible only by winding mountain roads, but the children’s imaginations stretch far beyond the peaks. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, the young athletes devoured match highlights on smartphones. Winning and losing are secondary to the star players: the children argue passionately over the goals scored by superstars like Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi and Harry Kane.

Seven-year-old Aluo, a first-grader with lightning-fast footwork, idolizes France’s Mbappé. His cousin, Yang Xiaojun, a skinny third-grader, became a die-hard Gareth Bale fan after watching a clip of the Welshman’s legendary bicycle kick.

When they score on this mountain pitch, the kids leap into the air, spinning to land in Cristiano Ronaldo’s iconic, arms-down “Siu” celebration.

For these children, soccer is bright spot in childhood marked by economic hardship. Local data shows rural per capita income in Daliangshan is around just 12,700 yuan ($1,770) a year. To make a living, parents migrate to factories in the southern Guangdong province, Wuhan in the central Hubei province, and the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, returning only once a year for the traditional Yi New Year.

Raised by aging grandparents in households with multiple siblings, these “left-behind” children have few outlets for their energy. A piece of candy or a lucky draw at the school gate used to be the highlight of their week. Now, soccer offers them friendship, structure and a window to the outside world.

To keep them invested, Lama implemented a reward system. Players earn four points for every practice they attend, which they can exchange for free gear. That is how Hu Feifei, one of the girls who recently joined the squad, earned her jersey, socks and boots.

Hu remembers when the pitch was nothing but sand dumped over uneven soil. When it rained, they played in puddles and went home with scraped knees, but they were happy. Today, thanks to a corporate sponsor moved by the team’s story, they play on an artificial turf pitch that Lama proudly claims is “better than the ones in the county town.”

The sponsor discovered them because of Lama, who is no stranger to the spotlight. But his viral fame is a chapter of his life tinged with both pride and heartbreak.

Lama’s obsession began in middle school when a friend gifted him a Neymar Barcelona jersey. The self-described rebellious teen found his anchor in soccer. To play, he transferred to a vocational school with a pitch.

To master the game, he did the unthinkable and dropped out, hiked to an altitude of 2,000 meters, and built a wooden hut on a flat peak. There, with no electricity and relying on a wood fire to cook, he trained alone for days at a time. His goal was to become a professional soccer player within five years.

He documented his solitary, high-altitude drills on short-video platforms. The stark contrast between the primitive, breathtaking environment and the boy’s fluid footwork captivated the internet. He amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, drawing the attention of FIFA on the eve of the 2022 Qatar World Cup. At his peak, he was earning up to 6,000 yuan a month from his videos.

But soon this felt wrong, money was not why he played soccer. “It felt like I was using soccer to make a profit,” Lama says. “It betrayed my original love for the game.”

However, his online presence earned him a spot in professional tryouts. It was here that Lama’s dream collided with reality. “My technique was too poor, I couldn’t understand the tactics, and my receiving and passing were all wrong,” he said.

In May 2023, he finally earned a spot with Jingchuan Wenhui, a fourth-tier club in the Chinese Champions League. Stepping onto the pitch, the cheers of the fans made the experience feel unreal.

It lasted exactly 45 minutes. Half a match that Lama doesn’t dare to rewatch. “My muscles were constantly tense, and I felt I performed too poorly,” he said.

The experience made clarified the insurmountable chasm between himself and real professional players, he said he could “never keep up with the rhythm and physical confrontation.”

The failure was a brutal watershed moment. But instead of continuing to chase trials across the country, Lama packed his bags and looked back to the dirt fields of Ze’e Village.

Today, he serves as an unpaid, unofficial soccer coach for two local primary schools. He runs training sessions five days a week and spends his weekends driving his minivan across the mountains to ferry kids to and from practice.

The transition from viral star to grassroots coach hasn’t been easy. The internet money has dried up, and his public welfare coaching model is financially unsustainable. He is considering charging a modest annual fee of 1,200 yuan for new recruits this fall, but he agonizes over whether the cost will price out the very kids who need the game most. He regularly visits skeptical parents, trying to convince them that soccer isn’t a distraction, but a vital tool for development.

“I want these children to start changing from this generation,” Lama said. “I want them to learn manners and be driven.”

In a region where educational resources are sparse and academic struggles are common, Lama sees soccer as a safety net. His vision is already bearing fruit: four of his sixth-graders recently passed a specialized sports exam, securing them spots in a superior middle school in the county town.

Eventually, Lama plans to build a fully registered professional club. He has already chosen the name: Leke, the Yi word for plowshare.

It is a fitting moniker for a young man breaking tough ground. “I don’t even have a first team yet,” Lama said, looking out over the mist-covered pitch. “I’ve only just lifted my foot to take the first step, and it hasn’t even landed yet.”

This piece was originally published by Caixin Global. It is republished here with permission.

Reporter: Zheng Haipeng.

(Header image: Players from Jijia Primary School pose for a group photo, imitating the signature moves of their favorite soccer stars, Ze’e Village, Sichuan province, June 2026. Zheng Haipeng/Caixin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Saving China’s Vanishing Fields of Knowledge
World.content:
Every summer, millions of Chinese high school students who have just completed the national college entrance examination, or gaokao, face a pivotal decision: which university and major to choose. At the same time, media outlets and social platforms fill with debate over which fields of study offer the best employment prospects and financial returns. Driven by pragmatism, students tend to favor majors that lead to well-paid or stable careers, such as computer science, software engineering, medicine, and accounting.

At the other end of the spectrum are disciplines that appear to have little practical value and remain unfamiliar to most people, including Western Xia studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, silk manuscript studies, and Dunhuang studies. In recent years, these fields have come to be grouped under the poetic term “lengmen juexue,” often translated as “niche and endangered disciplines.”

The phrase combines two concepts. Lengmen, or “niche disciplines,” refers to traditional humanities fields with small research communities that attract limited scholarly attention and produce results slowly. Juexue, or “endangered disciplines,” refers to fields of exceptional cultural significance that require highly specialized expertise and risk disappearing as senior scholars retire. In other words, lengmen describes their circumstances, while juexue reflects their value. A true niche and endangered discipline must satisfy both conditions: it has only a small community of researchers while preserving an irreplaceable body of cultural knowledge at risk of being lost.

Many of these disciplines have a long history. Fields such as philology, Confucian classics, epigraphy, bibliography, ancient musicology, and calendrical studies were once central to Chinese scholarship but gradually became marginalized following the introduction of Western academic disciplines in the modern era. The term juexue itself dates back more than a thousand years. During the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), the philosopher Zhang Zai (1020–1077) wrote in his “Hengqu Yulu” of the need “to ordain conscience for Heaven and Earth, to secure life for the people, to continue the lost teachings of past sages, and to establish peace for all future generations.”

Today, however, “niche and endangered disciplines” is more than a descriptive label. It has become an institutional framework within Chinese academia. In 2016, President Xi Jinping called for greater attention to marginal disciplines with high cultural value and significance for Chinese heritage during a speech at the Seminar on Philosophy and Social Sciences in Beijing. Quoting an old Chinese saying, he argued that resources maintained over the long term prove their worth when they are eventually needed.

That vision took institutional form in 2018, when the National Social Science Fund of China established a dedicated funding program for niche and endangered disciplines. Since then, the Ministry of Education, the Chinese Academy of History, and other institutions have launched related initiatives. One flagship funding program provides around 350,000 yuan ($52,000) for individual research projects and about 800,000 yuan for collaborative projects, placing these disciplines on a similar footing to other major National Social Science Fund initiatives.

These disciplines contribute little to GDP growth and seem far removed from everyday life. So why do the state and the academic community devote such significant resources to supporting them?

The answer lies in their role in helping Chinese civilization understand itself and sustain its continuity. Civilizations do not endure by chance. Their longevity depends not only on creating new knowledge but also on preserving and interpreting their past.

These disciplines address fundamental questions about China’s history. Why were oracle bone inscriptions written the way they were? How was the millennia-old “Book of Documents” passed down through the centuries? How did ancient Chinese societies observe the skies and develop calendars? What does the Library Cave at the Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang reveal about cultural exchange? Such questions may seem remote, but they form the foundation of a civilization’s understanding of its own history.

These disciplines also safeguard cultural continuity. The longevity of the Chinese civilization has depended on generations of scholars who continuously compiled classical texts, interpreted ancient scripts, and preserved knowledge. Without this work, vast collections of cultural heritage might survive physically while becoming increasingly difficult, or even impossible, to understand.

These disciplines also shape China’s cultural narrative. Research into frontier history, ethnic writing systems, and Chinese texts preserved overseas extends beyond academic inquiry. It informs historical interpretation, cultural identity, and international exchange.

In short, niche and endangered disciplines preserve the historical memory of Chinese civilization. Once sustained by only a handful of scholars, they have become an important part of China’s broader cultural strategy.

So what qualifies as a niche and endangered discipline? There is no definitive list. Instead, the category has steadily expanded. It initially included fields such as oracle bone studies, Dunhuang studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, and ancient script studies. More recently, it has broadened to encompass the history of ancient Chinese science and technology, ancient astronomy and calendrical studies, ethnic scripts, Chinese texts preserved overseas, frontier history and geography, and research on exchanges between China and other civilizations. Today, these disciplines are generally grouped into four broad categories: ancient scripts and extinct languages; traditional classics and endangered classical studies; ancient specialized histories and niche skills; and research on China’s frontiers and its exchanges with other ancient civilizations.

Why has the category expanded? Not because more disciplines have become obscure but because there is growing recognition that many specialized fields are indispensable to understanding Chinese civilization.

Take ancient astronomy and calendrical studies. Without them, it would be difficult to understand how ancient China developed its calendar, organized agricultural production, and structured political authority. Likewise, without research into historical ethnic writing systems, countless documents produced by frontier peoples would become unreadable. Moreover, dedicated funding programs provide specialized institutions and researchers with the long-term support needed to sustain this work.

State support has already produced significant results. The Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, for example, has published major works including “Heroic Epic and Oral Tradition” and “Translations of Sanskrit Literature.” These works preserve and interpret historical texts, making them accessible to modern scholars and readers. Meanwhile, digital technologies are increasingly being used to collate ancient texts, digitize documents, and recognize historical scripts, greatly improving research efficiency. Even so, significant challenges remain.

The greatest challenge is not funding but time. One scholar may spend three decades studying just a few dozen oracle bones. Another may devote an entire career to deciphering a script that disappeared more than a thousand years ago. A third may spend decades reconstructing an ancient calendar.

Mastering a niche and endangered discipline often requires decades of training, yet an entire field can disappear within a single generation. Early Chinese astronomy, for example, demands expertise in ancient astronomy and calendrical systems, the ability to decipher ancient scripts, and a deep understanding of history. The barriers to entry are therefore exceptionally high. Since the deaths of leading scholars such as Bo Shuren (1934–1997), Xi Zezong (1927–2008), and Chen Meidong (1942–2008), the field has weakened significantly, with few young researchers able to replace them. Sustained institutional support is therefore essential.

These disciplines also sit uneasily within a modern research system that rewards speed and measurable output. Their work progresses slowly, while public awareness remains limited and relatively few young people are willing to commit to careers that require decades of patient study.

Protecting niche and endangered disciplines therefore requires training and evaluation systems tailored to their unique characteristics. Only then can more students be encouraged to enter these fields, allowing scholars to devote themselves to the long-term work of preserving and expanding humanity’s understanding of China’s past.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from International Dunhuang Programme and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.title: China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.content:
China’s central Henan province issued a notice last week urging companies to ensure employees take their full paid annual leave and encouraging employer flexibility around workers leaving early on Fridays, domestic media reported Wednesday. The move was designed to encourage travel and spending on holidays and weekend getaways.

However, on Friday, local authorities said that the notice contained “inaccurate wording” and had “not undergone proper approval procedures,” and in response to public concerns, would be revised and reissued.

The original notice required employers to simplify leave approval procedures and called on company leaders to “lead by example” by taking time off themselves. It also clarified that all employees are entitled to the same paid annual leave regardless of whether they are permanent, temporary, dispatched, or contracted workers.

In addition, it encouraged employees to maximize their breaks by combining leave with weekends and public holidays, and said those with school-age children should receive priority when applying for leave during school breaks.

Henan is among several provincial-level regions that have introduced measures this year to better enforce paid annual leave, in line with China’s latest and first specific five-year plan on boosting consumption, approved by the State Council in July.

The Henan notice sparked heated discussion on social media, jumping to the trending topics list on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users voiced support and called for a nationwide rollout of the policy. Others took the opportunity to criticize a long-standing workplace culture in the country that promotes skipping leave to demonstrate dedication.

“I no longer have to lose pay to travel,” an employee who has worked at a state-owned enterprise in the Henan city of Luoyang for 10 years told Sixth Tone. “We were so excited when we saw the news that afternoon, and everyone cheered when our company issued (its own) notice the next day.”

She said taking time off previously meant losing a significant portion of her salary. “Now, (the notice) makes me feel more motivated to work,” she said. “People will complete their tasks more thoroughly before going on leave.” The employee added that she is already planning to combine her annual leave with the weeklong National Day holiday, at the beginning of October, for a longer break.

Two private-sector employees in Henan, however, told Sixth Tone that they had yet to receive any notice of a change in annual leave from their companies.

Similar notices have also been issued this year in the northern port city of Tianjin, the eastern provinces of Zhejiang and Anhui, the northwestern province of Shaanxi, and the southwestern province of Guizhou.

Many notices state they aim to change “unhealthy workplace norms,” while attempting to allay workers’ concerns that taking leave could affect their pay, performance evaluations, or chances for promotion.

In 2025, Lü Guoquan, a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and then an official with the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, said only around 57% of China’s workers entitled to paid annual leave actually take it.

Under national regulations implemented in 2008, employees with one to 10 years of cumulative work experience are entitled to five days of paid annual leave; those with 10 to 20 years receive 10 days; and those with more than 20 years receive 15 days.

“To fundamentally change the situation, China also needs routine labor inspections, accessible channels for workers to defend their rights, and better job rotation systems to reduce operational pressure on employers,” Song Xiangqing, vice president of the Commerce Economy Association of China, told domestic business outlet Caijing.

In January, China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security also announced that it would revise national regulations to promote better enforcement of the paid leave system.

“Paid leave is no longer simply about work-life balance or employee welfare,” state-run Guangming Daily wrote in a commentary published Thursday. “It has become part of the country’s strategy to boost consumption and expand domestic demand. Only with sufficient, uninterrupted, and predictable time off will people have both the time and willingness to spend.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Horstgerlach/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.title: Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.content:
China’s industry associations are revoking hundreds of honorary designations that have increasingly been used as marketing tools.

In late July, the China Cuisine Association announced that all previously awarded titles — including “Chinese Culinary Master” and “Chinese Catering Service Master” — along with related certificates and uniforms, were now invalid. The association also revoked all honorary designations awarded to cities — such as the “capital of” and “hometown of” certain dishes. Local governments are now officially barred from using them in any form of publicity.

The revocation of the titles triggered renewed interest among social media users. This week, they questioned the reliability of the “National Stir-Fried Meat King” title awarded to restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, after discovering it was conferred following an online public vote on photos and videos submitted by contestants.

The title has not yet been revoked, though, in response, the China Cuisine Association said they will “communicate after reviewing relevant materials,” domestic media reported.

Originally intended to recognize exceptional craftsmanship, “master” titles were once rare state honors. But in the early 2000s, industry associations across the tea, ceramics, and jewelry sectors, and many others, began creating their own titles, allowing businesses to charge a premium by creating the perception of higher-quality products and services. However, numerous shadowy practices also emerged around the honors, including honorary title certificates being openly sold on e-commerce platforms.

Since the beginning of this year, at least a dozen national and local industry associations covering sectors ranging from cosmetic surgery to jade carving and wedding services have revoked or abolished previously-conferred honorary titles containing words like “master.”

An increasing number of industry associations began nullifying their own honorary titles after the Social Work Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Ministry of Civil Affairs jointly released new guidelines on governing social organizations’ awards and commendations in mid-July.

The guidelines, which took effect on Aug. 1, imposed stricter eligibility requirements on organizations seeking to present awards. It also prohibits organizations from charging fees for recognition programs or partnering with, or outsourcing such activities to, for-profit entities.

China has gradually tightened oversight of awards and commendations organized by social organizations over the past decade, with its first regulations governing the practice taking effect in 2012.

Restrictions were tightened further in 2018, when award programs using national designations such as “China,” “Chinese,” and “national” became subject to stricter controls. In 2022, authorities required organizations seeking to launch honorary recognition programs to hold at least a 4A rating, the second highest on the country’s social organization rating scale.

Lu Zhen, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of Beijing-based Hylands Law Firm, told local media that rather than eliminating professional evaluations altogether, the regulations are intended to draw a clearer distinction between professional qualifications and commercialized honorary awards.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An  for restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, at a shopping mall in Beijing, May 23, 2024. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018862/Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.title: Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018862/Skin in the Game: What Makes a Chinese Game Character Feel Real?
World.content:
Ask anyone to name a Chinese video game character, and chances are they will say Chun-Li. That is both her achievement and the problem.

When Japanese gaming giant Capcom debuted her character in the 1991 arcade game Street Fighter II, Chun-Li was an Interpol officer. But it was her blue qipao, double buns, and devastating kicks that made her famous.

Those details made Chun-Li instantly recognizable, but they also turned her Chinese identity into spectacle — graceful, formidable, and framed for the male gaze. Her image was already so familiar by 1993 that Jackie Chan could parody her in his film “City Hunter” without explanation.

The arcade era rewarded that kind of instant legibility. Fighting-game characters were built from bold silhouettes, familiar archetypes, and minimal backstory. In Japanese developer SNK’s 1994 arcade fighting game The King of Fighters ’94, Chin Gentsai was the drunken, disheveled old man cast as the quintessential kung fu master. Chinese culture was visible, but largely reduced to type: exotic, recognizable, and stripped of psychological depth.

It would take another generation of games for Chinese characters to move beyond such tropes. By the mid-2010s, globally popular multiplayer titles were reaching vast Chinese audiences, whose size and commercial importance made their expectations harder to ignore. As Chinese characters became more common, players increasingly expected them to feel culturally grounded rather than assembled from stock signs.

When American video game developer Blizzard released the first-person shooter Overwatch in 2016, its Chinese hero, Mei-Ling Zhou, seemed to mark a step beyond the old archetypes. A climatologist from Xi’an in northwestern China, Mei wears polar expedition gear and is portrayed as affable, resilient, and determined to protect both people and the planet.

Yet while Mei is more fully drawn than the arcade characters before her, her Chinese identity remains largely incidental. Her nationality adds diversity to Overwatch’s global cast without meaningfully shaping her inner life.

Nearly a decade later, Overwatch introduced its second Chinese hero, Wuyang Ye. A 19-year-old from the southwestern Sichuan province, he attends the fictional Wuxing University, whose colleges draw on the five traditional Chinese elements. Yet the most revealing detail is also the most ordinary: Wuyang is a college student, a figure immediately familiar to much of the game’s Chinese audience.

Overwatch also gave its characters linguistic markers of where they came from. In the English-language version, an allied Mei shouts “Freeze, don’t move!” when using her ultimate ability; an enemy Mei delivers the warning in Mandarin. For Chinese players, the switch allowed her nationality to be heard rather than merely listed in her biography.

By the time Wuyang appeared, simply hearing a Chinese character speak Chinese was no longer enough. In a 2025 promotional trailer, he dismisses a challenge with “xiao case,” a Chinese-English expression roughly equivalent to “piece of cake.” Some Chinese viewers found the line playful; others argued that a student from Sichuan should instead use the local expression “le ge hao long” — “this one’s easy.”

The disagreement was minor, but it showed how expectations had changed. Players expected his language to reflect where he came from and who he was.

In 2026, Wuyang’s elder sister, Anran Ye, joined the Overwatch roster. Associated with the element of fire, she is forceful, impatient, and quick to challenge her younger brother. Their exchanges introduce sibling rivalry, parental pressure, and family expectations, giving both characters a social world beyond their individual backstories.

This marks the clearest break from Mei. Mei’s Chinese identity is conveyed largely through nationality and language; the Ye siblings’ emerges through family relationships and everyday behavior. Anran feels familiar not as a symbol of China but as the demanding older sister who refuses to let her younger brother coast.

The 2020 tactical shooter Valorant, developed by U.S. video game company Riot Games — owned by Chinese tech giant Tencent — offers a different kind of Chinese character. Sage is built around protection rather than aggression: she heals injured teammates, raises defensive barriers, and can revive fallen allies. Players often call her “mom,” a playful nickname rooted less in her nationality than in the trust inspired by her abilities and calm authority.

Three years later, Valorant introduced its second Chinese character, Iso, a hired gun from the southwestern megacity of Chongqing. His abilities are built around single combat, allowing him to isolate opponents and force them into one-on-one fights. The contrast with Sage is immediate: Sage protects and restores her team, while Iso is aggressive, self-contained, and designed to fight alone.

Iso’s reveal trailer featured “Renegade,” an original track by Chinese rappers 99 God and C103, grounding the character in contemporary Chinese music without relying on traditional costume or martial-arts imagery.

Neither character is expected to represent China as a whole or reduced to a single cultural type. Together with Mei, Wuyang, and Anran, they mark a broader shift in global competitive games, where Chinese characters increasingly appear as individuals rather than national symbols.

Chinese culture has also become more visible beyond character rosters. In League of Legends, developed by Riot Games, and Honor of Kings, developed in China by Tencent’s TiMi Studio Group, players can buy skins inspired by Chinese mythology, clothing, and decorative motifs.

But visibility alone was not enough. Anran’s trailer presented her as fierce and commanding, while her in-game model appeared cuter and more delicate.

Chinese players objected to the mismatch, and Blizzard later announced changes to the design. The response showed that players were judging not merely whether Chinese elements were present but whether the character remained consistent with the world and personality the game had established.

From Chun-Li to the Ye siblings, and from Sage to Iso, Chinese characters in global competitive games have begun to move from spectacle to self. They are no longer recognized only through costume, accent, or archetype. Players now debate how they speak, how they look, where they come from, and whether those details add up to a convincing person.

In the years ahead, perhaps the misty canal towns of Jiangnan, in eastern China’s lower Yangtze region, will appear on a new arena map, Miao embroidery on a tournament skin, or Tang dynasty poetry woven into a champion’s identity. But such details will matter only when they do more than decorate.

When culture is lived rather than labeled, a Chinese figure stops being a symbol. They become someone players can root for, and perhaps someone who brings them closer to their own roots.

(Header image: Visuals from Street Fighter, Blizzard, and Riot Game, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018857/Do the Math: Why China’s First Fields Medals Are Just the Beginning
World.title: Do the Math: Why China’s First Fields Medals Are Just the Beginning
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018857/Do the Math: Why China’s First Fields Medals Are Just the Beginning
World.content:
When Wang Hong and Deng Yu became the first Chinese nationals to receive the Fields Medal — the so-called “Nobel Prize for mathematics” — on July 23, few people were as pleased as Shing-Tung Yau.

“For China’s math community, this is something we’ve hoped to see for decades,” Yau, a Chinese American mathematician who was awarded the Fields Medal in 1982, tells The Paper.

“It gives us new hope. We can now envision the day when decisive breakthroughs are made by scholars trained entirely in China and are carried out on Chinese soil.”

Yau is the founding dean of Tsinghua University’s Qiuzhen College, which was established in early 2021 to strengthen the cultivation of mathematical talent. One of its flagship initiatives, the YAU Mathematical Sciences Leaders Program, recruits gifted high school-age students from around the world, placing them on an eight-year track running from bachelor’s degree to Ph.D.

In recent years, however, a training industry has emerged around admission to the college, with some parents viewing it as a shortcut to one of China’s top universities. Public scrutiny also intensified in July when several recruits reportedly faced expulsion during the initial preparatory semester after failing to meet Qiuzhen’s academic standards.

In interviews, Yau has openly criticized China’s long-standing reliance on math competitions and commercial test-prep programs, saying that they only make students proficient in taking exams and standardized problem-solving routines, which has had “an extremely negative impact on the development of mathematical talent.”

He reveals that the college is planning a comprehensive overhaul of its admissions and exam systems, with the aim of enrolling students who truly love mathematics, not those solely motivated by the desire to enter an elite university.

Following Wang and Deng’s accomplishment, Yau now hopes China can cultivate many homegrown scholars within the next decade who can forge their own intellectual paths and produce work that shapes the direction of mathematics worldwide.

Here, Yau talks with The Paper about his feelings on math education, basic research, and scientific innovation.

The Paper: How should we understand the importance of basic research?

Yau: People have various understandings of basic research. In my view, basic research should make meaningful contributions to the nation and society. China faces many technological bottlenecks, and we scientists have a responsibility to help overcome them.

At the same time, we cannot remain content with following in the footsteps of others. If we’re always solving problems that others have defined, merely improving on existing work, then even if we eventually surpass them, we are still allowing someone else to set the agenda. There is certainly a place for this kind of research, but it cannot be the whole story.

People often say that China is good at taking innovation from “2 to 100” — refining and scaling existing ideas — but lacks the capacity for “0-to-1” breakthroughs: original discoveries that set new directions.

Some lines of inquiry may appear to have little practical value today. Yet pursuing them can deepen our understanding of the laws of nature, and that deeper understanding can lay the groundwork for transformative discoveries. Above all, curiosity is the driving force behind 0-to-1 innovation.

When scientists began investigating quantum phenomena in the early 20th century, their goal was to unravel the mysteries of atomic structure and quantum effects. No one imagined that this research would revolutionize electronics, industrial technologies, and countless other fields, reshaping the modern world. Even today, many of the technological challenges that constrain China’s development are rooted in areas closely connected to quantum mechanics.

That is why basic research must serve two purposes simultaneously: address the pressing challenges facing the country while safeguarding the freedom to pursue curiosity-driven research.

The Paper: Why does China seem to lag behind in 0-to-1 innovation, and what is the solution?

Yau: In many areas, once someone else opens up an important new direction, Chinese scientists move in quickly and, in many cases, improve on it or even outperform the first pioneers. But genuinely new fields that we ourselves have initiated from the outset remain exceedingly rare. Taking that first original step is the most important challenge facing the development of basic research.

The history of mathematics offers many examples of theories that were initially misunderstood or dismissed, only to have their significance recognized years later. Yet many young researchers lack the courage to pursue this kind of work.

One reason is that such research requires extraordinary patience. An unconventional idea may take five or six years before its value becomes apparent. During that time, researchers might struggle to secure even basic funding, and their career advancement could suffer. Most people naturally shy away from such risks.

Also, basic research is inherently a long-term endeavor. It rarely produces immediate rewards, so many people lose interest over time. But genuine interest cannot be manufactured overnight — it must be cultivated from an early age. We need to inspire young people to develop a love of scholarship and a sense of wonder about nature. Without that inner drive, it is impossible to nurture first-rate researchers.

Many people’s aspiration for pursuing research has changed. Increasingly, scholarship is viewed as a means to acquire academic titles or prestigious appointments. When my generation entered academia, there was no option but to keep moving forward. By contrast, young people today generally enjoy far greater material security, yet they face intense external pressures that make them more vulnerable to anxiety. At the same time, parents and society have become overly protective of children. Only by changing the broader culture of scientific research can China achieve genuine success in basic research and produce truly original breakthroughs.

The Paper: Does this also point to shortcomings in China’s system for evaluating academic research?

Yau: In some respects, our system for encouraging academic research places too much emphasis on material incentives and too little on the intrinsic value of scholarship. At some universities, generous salaries and housing allowances are reserved primarily for scholars with fancy titles. As a result, many young researchers feel compelled to chase these credentials rather than focus on the pursuit of knowledge.

Another issue is that China’s academic evaluation system makes relatively little use of international peer review. At Harvard University, for example, tenure decisions are based on assessments from leading scholars around the world. In China, evaluations are often confined to domestic experts, and in some cases only to reviewers at the same institution.

China has relatively few researchers capable of achieving genuine 0-to-1 innovation — but the situation is changing. Many scholars returning from overseas have brought back new ideas, research cultures, and methodological approaches. That does not mean China must rely indefinitely on talent trained abroad. Outstanding scholars are also emerging from within the country. The key is to ensure that decisions are guided by experts who truly understand the field. Ultimately, we must chart our own course, but we should at least listen carefully to those with expertise.

Even where international evaluation has been introduced, many Chinese universities continue to judge research primarily by metrics such as publication counts and journal impact factors. Those measures are poorly suited to evaluating the most original and exploratory forms of research.

We need to encourage young scholars in Chinese universities to set their sights much higher. At the very least, a small but significant group should aspire to become world-leading researchers — people capable of producing groundbreaking work that shapes the direction of mathematics, and even basic research more broadly, for decades to come.

The Paper: China’s total research and development spending exceeded 3.92 trillion yuan ($581 billion) in 2025. Investment in basic research accounted for 7% of that, a record high but still far below the 15-20% seen in many developed countries. How do you view this gap?

Yau: Research cannot be driven solely by immediate applications or by what may prove useful over the next five years. Basic research must not be neglected simply because its practical impact is delayed. More often than not, its true significance becomes apparent only after 10, 20 years, or even longer.

In fact, basic research is not especially expensive. Most fundamental research relies on thinking, reasoning, and mathematical deduction; its principal resources are the minds of scholars. Although some experimental fields like high-energy physics require substantial investment, China’s major research institutions are fully capable of supporting such work.

Generally speaking, allocating around 10% of total national R&D spending to the most fundamental areas of basic science would be sufficient. What matters most is that we take a long-term view and invest not only for today’s needs but also for the future.

The Paper: You have long advocated identifying and nurturing talented young students. Why is this important for basic research?

Yau: I have been at Qiuzhen College for five years. Every Monday, I teach a course on the history of math, focusing on the most influential mathematicians of the past three centuries and the paths they took in their intellectual development. Almost all of them developed a passion for math at the age of 12 or 13.

The future of China’s basic sciences depends on such young people, too. At that age, their minds are not yet constrained by established thinking; they possess tremendous intellectual flexibility. But as people grow older, their habits of thought become more fixed, making it more difficult to produce the kind of 0-to-1 innovation that opens new frontiers. That is why identifying and cultivating exceptional talent must begin early.

Some people argue that this approach runs counter to the principles of compulsory education or educational fairness. But requiring every student to meet exactly the same standard can, in fact, bury the rare young talents we most need to nurture. That would be the greatest injustice of all.

We should establish a systematic mechanism for identifying and developing the small fraction of students with exceptional gifts, providing them with specialized education. That is consistent with the educational principle of teaching students according to their individual abilities, and that is what genuine fairness looks like.

The Paper: What qualities do you feel define a true scientist?

Yau: A scientist must possess an open mind and a broad intellectual outlook, and they must build a rigorous academic foundation. No matter how difficult it may be, the fundamentals must be mastered — and math is especially important. Interdisciplinary learning and cultivating the humanities are also important. We should strive for broadly educated scholars rather than narrow specialists.

Original thinking is key. American students often ask unusual, even eccentric, questions. That curiosity is fascinating, and it frequently leads them to creative research. Chinese students, by contrast, tend to be more inclined to follow established rules and are often reluctant to question accepted ideas. We should protect their curiosity, encourage them to think boldly, and give them the confidence to ask questions.

Ultimately, the spirit of science is about seeking to understand the mysteries of nature and uncovering the objective laws that govern the universe — not about pursuing fame or prestige.

We should create an environment in which researchers are free to explore nature and pursue scholarship out of genuine intellectual curiosity, allowing them to remain true to that original motivation. Young scientists should not spend their careers chasing academic titles or even a Nobel Prize. The purpose of scholarship is to discover the truth and beauty of the natural world.

Reported by Teng Han.

A version of this Q&A originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: As inflation bites, Filipinos have become ‘intentional’ shoppers
World.content:
To keep customers shopping despite the pressure on their wallets, SM is relying on what it calls its 'good, better, best' line-up of items in stores

MANILA, Philippines – Filipinos have not stopped shopping despite the creeping specter of inflation, though the country’s biggest retailer is seeing a consumer who’s increasingly deliberate about where each peso goes.

SM Investments Corporation (SMIC) said consumer spending across its stores and malls remained resilient in the first half of 2026, helping lift consolidated revenues by 6% to P339.2 billion and net income by 8% to P45.9 billion. SM Retail in particular had a net income of P8.9 billion, up 5%.

In this sense, SM is well-situated to be resilient in a Philippine economy largely powered by consumers. Household spending usually accounts for more than 70% of the economy. But even as GDP growth grew at an incredibly weak 2.3% in Q2 2026, household consumption still expanded 2.8%, while investments shrank by 9.2%.

“We continue to see stable and healthy consumer spending across our retail and also our malls, despite the fact that fuel prices took a big jump in Q2,” SMIC executive vice president for finance Franklin Gomez said during the conglemerates H1 briefing.

But underneath that resilience, SM’s own checkout data suggest consumers are shopping differently depending on what they are buying.

For food retail, the number of transactions is increasing, but the average amount spent each time has remained flat.

“People have to shop, people have to eat,” SM Retail president Jonathan Ng said. “We do see that the transaction count has been increasing. Basket size remains flat.”

In other words, supermarkets and other food formats are ringing up more purchases, but shoppers are not significantly expanding how much they spend on each transaction.

Non-food tells the opposite story. Transaction counts are flat, meaning SM is not necessarily seeing more purchases, but basket sizes are bigger. Ng said this suggests shoppers are becoming more “intentional” when they visit malls and stores.

“People have become more discerning, more intentional when they go visit the mall and shop inside our stores.”

‘Good, better, best’ strategy

A bigger peso basket also doesn’t necessarily mean consumers are buying substantially more goods either. SMIC president and CEO Frederic DyBuncio said the retailer has raised prices broadly in line with inflation, while Ng said higher fuel costs are pushing up logistics expenses and suppliers have begun increasing prices.

Inflation stood at 6.2% in July, bringing the seven-month average to 5%, with food, housing, and transport accounting for most of the increase.

To keep customers shopping despite the pressure on their wallets, SM is relying on what it called its “good, better, best” assortment, letting them pick cheaper alternatives if one option goes over budget.

“We always prepare ourselves in terms of assortment, so even if there’s an impact on the disposable income of our shoppers, we continue to offer them a portfolio – if you can’t afford this, then we have this,” Ng told reporters on Wednesday, August 12. “Always a good, better, best assortment of items that we have inside our stores.”

That said, Filipinos haven’t abandoned wants altogether. SMIC reported higher specialty retail sales in home, fashion and kids, while SM Prime said mall revenues climbed 8% to P41.8 billion on stronger tenant sales and higher occupancy.

SM Prime is also seeing consumers redirect leisure spending closer to home. Management said volatile fuel prices and a weaker peso discouraged some overseas travel, leading families toward domestic staycations, while air-conditioned malls and their dining and entertainment offerings encouraged customers to stay longer and spend.

SM Supermalls president Steven Tan said casual dining continues to post “very high double-digit” growth, with health and wellness another growing category. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: ICC did not junk Duterte’s case; post misrepresents old VP Sara statement
World.content:
The misleading post uses an old audio clip of Vice President Sara Duterte, in which she was referring to the defense’s challenge questioning the ICC’s jurisdiction over her father’s case

Claim: The International Criminal Court (ICC) junked the case against detained former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte, as confirmed by his daughter, Vice President Sara Duterte.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The Facebook reel, posted on August 2, has already received 1.6 million views, 65,300 reactions, 3,200 comments, and 6,700 shares as of writing.

It shows videos of the Vice President speaking before a crowd and her father shaking hands with US President Donald Trump. The text on the post reads, “Pagbabasura ng kaso ni DU30 (Dismissal of Duterte’s case).”

The post also includes audio of the Vice President in which she says, “Ngayon ay nakalagay na officially sa ICC website ‘yung pagbabasura ng kaso dahil sa kawalan ng jurisdiction ng ICC.”

(The dismissal of the case due to the ICC’s lack of jurisdiction has now been officially posted on the ICC website.)

The facts: The ICC did not dismiss the case against Duterte. He remains detained in The Hague, Netherlands, awaiting the start of his trial for crimes against humanity on November 30.

The misleading post uses old videos and misrepresented statements. The Vice President’s remark was about the defense challenge submitted by her father’s counsel in May 2025, questioning the ICC’s jurisdiction over the case, and how this was now officially published and accessible on the ICC website. The ICC pre-trial chamber judges upheld its jurisdiction over Duterte’s crimes against humanity case in a decision issued in October 2025.

VERA Files debunked a similar false claim taking out of context the same audio statement by the Vice President.

The video of the Vice President in front of Duterte supporters at a rally in The Hague, Netherlands on July 29 has nothing to do with the false claim. The misrepresented statement was not taken from that speech.

Meanwhile, the interaction between Duterte and Trump did not happen recently. It was in November 2017 during the opening ceremony of the 31st Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit.

Duterte ICC case: The case against Duterte is still ongoing; the ICC confirmed the charges against him in April and scheduled the start of his trial in November.

The former president was arrested in March 2025. He faces three counts of crimes against humanity due to his alleged involvement in the killings under his war on drugs and the Davao Death Squad.

ICC jurisdiction: Contrary to the claim, the ICC affirmed its jurisdiction over the Philippines as the alleged crimes were committed when it was still a state party of the ICC. The Philippines withdrew from the ICC in 2019.

In an April 2026 decision, the ICC Appeals Chamber rejected all four arguments raised by Duterte’s camp and also rendered moot the defense’s request for the immediate and unconditional release of the former Philippine leader.

Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar false claims about Duterte’s ICC detention:

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

Angelee Kaye Abelinde is a student journalist based in Naga City, and an alumna of Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: [Ask the Tax Whiz] PROGRESS or GINHAWA: Which reform can truly increase take-home pay?
World.content:
In this week’s Ask the Tax Whiz, we compare both proposals and examine how they can support a credible roadmap toward ₱1 million in tax-free income for every Filipino

The policy direction is clear: the Filipino middle class needs meaningful and lasting tax relief.

When the Tax Reform for Acceleration and Inclusion law (TRAIN) took effect in 2018, the first ₱250,000 of taxable income became tax-free. That threshold has remained unchanged despite years of higher food, housing, transportation, healthcare, and education costs. This creates bracket creep: salaries rise on paper, but workers may pay more tax without becoming better off in real terms.

The administration’s PROGRESS Bill—Promoting Growth, Revenue, and Equity Towards Socio-Economic Sustainability—and Senate President Win Gatchalian’s GINHAWA Bill—Granting Increase in Take-Home Pay for All Working Filipinos—address the same problem through different policy designs.

The real question is not which bill wins. It is whether Congress can combine tax relief, fiscal responsibility, and institutional reform.

In this week’s Ask the Tax Whiz, we compare both proposals and examine how they can support a credible roadmap toward ₱1 million in tax-free income for every Filipino.

1. What is the main difference between PROGRESS and GINHAWA?

Both bills seek to increase take-home pay, but they differ in scope and fiscal design.

The administration’s PROGRESS Bill would raise the annual tax-free threshold from ₱250,000 to ₱350,000, equivalent to about ₱29,167 in monthly taxable income. Government estimates that fully-exempt workers would increase from 5.1 million to 6.3 million, adding around 1.2 million beneficiaries. Those earning between ₱250,000 and ₱350,000 could save up to ₱15,000 annually. PROGRESS would also remove the minimum corporate income tax for qualified micro and small enterprises, benefiting more than 78,000 businesses.

The GINHAWA Bill offers broader worker-centered relief. It proposes a higher ₱400,000 tax-free threshold, or around ₱33,333 monthly, raises the tax-free ceiling for 13th-month pay and other benefits from ₱90,000 to ₱150,000, and exempts overtime, holiday, night-shift differential, hazard pay, service charges, and tips. It also proposes additional deductions and simpler compliance measures for micro and small taxpayers.

The key difference is fiscal strategy. PROGRESS projects ₱326.92 billion in tax relief from 2027 to 2030, offset by ₱518.71 billion in new revenues, for an estimated net gain of ₱191.77 billion. The Department of Finance proposes recovering the cost through expanded sin and wealth taxes, possible taxes on plastic products, and an updated motor vehicle road user tax.

In policy terms, PROGRESS emphasizes revenue balance, while GINHAWA provides deeper and more immediate relief based on how Filipinos actually earn their income.

The strongest reform would combine both approaches—PROGRESS’ fiscal discipline and support for small businesses with GINHAWA’s stronger worker protections—then automatically index tax thresholds to inflation so the value of relief does not erode over time.

2. How can government recover the revenue loss without passing it back to consumers?

PROGRESS proposes recovering much of the cost of tax relief through higher excise taxes on sweetened beverages, tobacco, vapor products, plastics, and other goods.

These taxes may serve valid health and environmental goals, but they should not become the main permanent funding source for lower income taxes. If health taxes work as intended, consumption—and eventually the taxable base—should decline. Higher rates may also push consumers toward cheaper illicit products when customs enforcement, licensing, product tracking, and border controls remain weak.

Tax relief should not simply be taken back through higher retail prices.

A more sustainable sequence is needed.

First, lift or substantially relax bank secrecy for legitimate tax investigations, with clear legal limits, due process, confidentiality safeguards, and independent oversight.

Second, launch a nationwide, risk-based audit and investigation of unexplained wealth. Tax returns should be lawfully matched with bank information, property records, beneficial ownership, procurement payments, campaign-finance disclosures, and other third-party data.

No one should be presumed guilty because of political affiliation, family name, campaign participation, or government contracts. But public officials, political families, major donors, and contractors should not be exempt from scrutiny when objective records reveal significant gaps between declared income and accumulated assets.

Government should also strengthen electronic invoicing, digital tax stamps, customs intelligence, inter-agency data sharing, and AI-assisted risk assessment to detect tax evasion, smuggling, and illicit trade.

The policy principle is simple: recover unpaid taxes and unexplained wealth before asking consumers to pay more.

3. Is ₱350,000 all government can give the overtaxed and underserved middle class?

It should be the beginning—not the ceiling—of reform.

Tax relief is not a government favor that workers must immediately repay through higher prices or new consumption taxes. Middle-class families already contribute heavily to public revenues while often paying privately for healthcare, education, transportation, housing, security, and other services that taxes are supposed to support.

This column proposes a legislated and fiscally responsible roadmap: raise the tax-free threshold to at least ₱400,000 in 2026, increase it to ₱800,000 in 2027, and move toward ₱1 million in 2028.

The threshold and tax brackets should then be automatically indexed to inflation. Without indexation, rising prices and nominal salary adjustments will continue to push workers into higher tax burdens even when their real purchasing power has barely improved.

Each increase should be tied to measurable institutional reforms: full modernization of the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) and Bureau of Customs, wider electronic invoicing, AI-assisted risk assessment, stronger inter-agency data sharing, reduced smuggling and customs leakages, and tougher enforcement against tax evasion and unexplained wealth.

The Philippines should also immediately adopt a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax under the OECD Global Minimum Tax. This would allow the country to collect the top-up tax on low-taxed profits generated by large multinational enterprises operating here, rather than allowing another jurisdiction to collect it.

Tax reform must also extend beyond salaried workers. Freelancers, professionals, online sellers, content creators, and small businesses need a simpler tax regime that lowers compliance costs, encourages voluntary registration, and expands the formal tax base.

The strongest outcome is therefore not simply PROGRESS versus GINHAWA.

It is PROGRESS plus GINHAWA—and accountability: the fiscal discipline of the administration’s proposal, the stronger worker protections of GINHAWA, automatic inflation indexation, simpler taxation for small businesses, modern revenue administration, and a credible roadmap toward ₱1 million in tax-free income.

The final policy question is not only whether government can afford to give taxpayers greater relief.

It is whether government is prepared to stop losing so much to inefficiency, smuggling, tax evasion, and corruption—and start collecting more fairly, efficiently, and honestly before asking compliant taxpayers to sacrifice again. – Rappler.com

Mon Abrea, CPA, MBA, MPA (Harvard) is a global tax policy expert and Chief Tax Advisor of Asian Consulting Group (ACGlobal). He advises governments, multinational enterprises, and international organizations on tax policy, investment competitiveness, and fiscal reform. He is the author of Reimagining the World Without Corruption and Why Invest in the Philippines? CREATE MORE Edition, and has represented the Philippines in policy dialogues at the OECD, World Bank, and other international forums.
