World.title: Gabby Lopez: Man on a mission
World.content:
After stepping down as chairman emeritus of ABS-CBN in September 2020, Gabby Lopez is stepping up to save the company he loves

Who would have thought he’d be back in the game — and in the limelight — again?

Two months after the House of Representatives during the Duterte administration rejected the franchise renewal of ABS-CBN on July 10, 2020, Eugenio “Gabby”Lopez III left his post as chairman emeritus and director of the Philippines’ biggest media network at the time.

Not only that. He also resigned as director of other Lopez firms: ABS-CBN Holdings Corp., Sky Vision Corp., Sky Cable Corp., First Philippine Holdings Corp., First Gen Corp., and Rockwell Land Corp.

His resignation was accepted.

Perhaps for some who were still working for ABS-CBN at the time (including this writer), there was only one way to look at it: Gabby had taken responsibility for what had happened. Recall that around 5,000 people lost their jobs after the franchise was rejected. One could compare Gabby’s move to the Japanese behavior for taking responsibility, a sort of hara-kiri by a CEO.

Many ABS-CBN employees had been frustrated (to say the least) over the company’s stance vis-a-vis Rodrigo Duterte and his administration: often silent, submissive, and accepting of whatever and whenever Duterte attacked the company, even if the then-president was wrong or inaccurate. (READ: TIMELINE: Duterte against ABS-CBN’s franchise renewal)

Looking back, it was a stark contrast to the combative position taken by Rappler during the Duterte years when at least 12 cases were filed against the company and its chief Maria Ressa. Rappler and Ressa have since won all but one of those cases. (READ: SolGen asks SC to acquit Maria Ressa, Reynaldo Santos Jr. in cyber libel case)

But perhaps, given the reality that by law, broadcast franchises in the Philippines are only granted by the House of Representatives, that was the only position a publicly listed company could take. (Disclosure: I had served as editor-in-chief of ABS-CBN’s news platform.)

Or so Gabby thought.

Gabby then hibernated for over five years in the US — until he quietly returned late last year as ABS-CBN’s financial crisis persisted following the loss of its lucrative franchise.

The Lopez cousins’ feud erupted in March, and it was, at the root, all about ABS-CBN and how to save it.

Part 1: Debt, discipline, and daring: Inside the Lopez Group’s high-risk bets

Part 2: The Lopezes, presidents, and the cost of dissent

Part 3: Lopez vs Lopez: The secrecy fight behind the Razon power deals

Gabby wanted more money to save the company; cousin Federico “Piki” Lopez thought otherwise.

As the dispute worsened, ABS-CBN issued a statement on April 15 on the “PR attacks” that 68 individuals had allegedly “received preferential treatment” in the “payout of their retirement benefits.” In a swipe at Piki Lopez’s argument that more money shouldn’t be poured into ABS-CBN, the statement cited a quote from ABS-CBN founder Eugenio “Kapitan Geny” Lopez: “Profit alone is not enough reason to go into business. But if we serve our people, then I think that our growth and success will follow. If we take care of our people, they will take care of us. That’s the kind of culture a company should have.”

Fast forward to this week, the next chapter in the ABS-CBN saga is being written.

After selling his family branch’s stake in the ultimate Lopez parent firm Lopez Inc. to San Miguel Corp. chairman Ramon Ang, Gabby has taken another step in his journey to make things right.

In a statement on Tuesday, August 12, ABS-CBN said that that three branches of the Lopez family – Crème Investment Corporation (Crème), Mantes Corporation, and Presta Holdings Company Inc. – would raise P6 billion in new equity for the troubled media and entertainment firm.

An investment holding company, I&C Holdings Corp., will subscribe to P3.5 billion worth of ABS-CBN shares, while Lopez Inc. will subscribe to an aditional P300 million.

“ABS-CBN has built valuable brands, intellectual property, content and deep relationships with Filipino audiences in the Philippines and overseas. As the media industry continues to evolve, we believe these assets provide a strong foundation for the company to adapt, build a sustainable content-led business, and create long-term value,” I&C Holdings Corp. said.

“This substantial investment is a vote of confidence in ABS-CBN,” said Mark Lopez, chairman of ABS-CBN Corporation. “It tells us there are people who continue to believe in the company and in our mission of being In the Service of the Filipino.”

The P6 billion will be used to “strengthen ABS-CBN’s balance sheet while giving the company additional resources to execute its transformation into a more sustainable, content-led media and entertainment business.”

Two days earlier or on Monday, August 11, after Crème Investment Corp., representing 25.7% or around one-fourth of Lopez Inc. was sold to Ramon Ang, Gabby said he sold for two reasons:

“This dispute has not been good for any of us, or for the people who work in our companies. This allows us to take a step towards the restoration of family peace. The second is that it allows me to channel our family’s resources into businesses aligned with our personal mission. We will announce more on this in due time. Our families have known Ramon a long time. I am confident he will be a good partner to Lopez Inc.”

Gabby’s move to make things right for ABS-CBN is back on track. As he emailed to Rappler on Sunday, April 9, “tomorrow (Monday) begins the end of the Lopez saga.”

Years from now, when Gabby’s own biography is written, this chapter is going to stand out. – Rappler.com

World.title: Total darkness, then sunset as full eclipse wows spectators in Spain
World.content:
LIGHT IN THE DARKNESS The moon partially covers the sun during a solar eclipse over mountains near the northern Spanish town of Reinosa, August 12, 2026.

The eclipse draws both casual viewers and dedicated 'eclipse chasers, with notable figures like Brian May attending and sharing their experiences on social media

MADRID, Spain – Spectators across Spain watched in wonder, some whipping off their protective glasses and rising to their feet in unison, as a rare total solar eclipse swept across the north of the country on Wednesday evening, plunging it into darkness.

Spain deployed a massive police contingent and set up special viewing spots across rural areas that offered the best views of the spectacle.

Viewers in Buitrago de Lozoya, a rural district north of Madrid, clapped and cheered as the sky dimmed and Baily’s beads – bright points of sunlight that shine around the edge of the moon during a total eclipse – glistened on the horizon just after 8:30 pm (1830 GMT), lasting barely a minute.

“It’s impressive how the colors return little by little after totality – first the reds, then the blues – just like at dawn and sunset, totally deceiving your brain,” said economist Diego Fernandez, 32.

Rafael Jiménez, 50, a resident of Madrid, said the event felt like science fiction. “It was an absurd scene; we even got soaked when the garden sprinklers kicked in,” he said. “And then, just like that, we were watching the sunset again.”

Spain’s turn with the eclipse followed shortly after a less remarkable spectacle over much of overcast Iceland, although a break in the clouds in the far west of the Nordic country allowed holidaymakers and locals a glimpse of the celestial phenomenon. The eclipse was hidden behind clouds in central Reykjavik although the darkness of the totality was still evident.

“It was like a whole day just came at once and I felt goosebumps because it just made us think about … the shortness of life, how time can be different and it depends on your perspective,” lawyer Eduarda Ortiz, 33, told Reuters in the Icelandic capital.

Millions of people gathered in Iceland and northern Spain to witness Western Europe’s first total solar eclipse in 27 years.

Brian May, former guitarist for the rock band Queen, was among them. He travelled to an observatory in Spain’s Teruel province and chronicled the experience on his Instagram page.

“Here we go, the sun is disappearing. It’s amazing,” he said as the eclipse reached its climax and bystanders burst into cheers and applause after a countdown.

In Spain, authorities were expecting up to 6 million visitors in mostly rural areas under the eclipse’s path across the north of Spain and the Balearic Islands.

Police, planes and helicopters on standby

The Iberian Peninsula last witnessed a total solar eclipse in 1912, but another is due on August 2, 2027, and an annular eclipse will follow in January 2028, completing the so-called “Iberian Eclipse Trio”.

The uncanny sensation when day briefly turns to twilight and some animals fall quiet, while the moon passes directly between Earth and the sun, has often been seen through history as an omen of cosmic struggle or a sign of divine power.

For Spain, the event has been a chance to showcase its less-traveled regions and draw tourists from its overcrowded beach resorts. Some seized the opportunity to get married, according to local press reports.

The eclipse took place in one of the country’s highest-risk periods for wildfires, with emergency crews fighting various fires on Wednesday, including a large one in the southern Andalucia region.

Authorities rolled out a large-scale police operation and public safety campaign to make sure the crowds did not set off wildfires.

A small fire erupted near an eclipse viewing point in the town of Peñíscola, in the Valencia region, local authorities said. The fire began in a vehicle and spread to 33 more before firefighters brought it under control, they said. Emergency crews, including aircraft, were dispatched to the area.

The authorities dispatched 25,000 police officers to guarantee security around the eclipse observation sites and deployed nearly 100 planes and helicopters.

As of late Wednesday, no wildfire incident tied to eclipse chasers was reported.

Eclipse fever in the land of sagas

In Reykjavik, glasses that allow spectators to view the phenomenon without damaging their eyes have been sold out for days, as the country of roughly 400,000 people welcomed up to 80,000 visitors.

Totality reached Iceland’s westernmost coast at about 5:44 pm (1744 GMT), casting the far west of the island nation into total darkness for up to 2 minutes and 13 seconds.

The event has drawn both casual observers and “eclipse chasers,” enthusiasts who crisscross the globe to be in the path of totality whenever and wherever an eclipse occurs.

In Spain, 43-year old Gema, who did not give her last name, said as she left the Buitrago de Lozoya viewing point: “Everybody tells you about it, but it is more beautiful than you imagine.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Powers Central Asia’s Economy, But Can Its Weight Drive Regional Growth?
World.content:
ALMATY – Central Asia’s combined economy has surpassed half a trillion US dollars, reaching an estimated $543 billion, with Kazakhstan accounting for more than half of the region’s gross domestic product, according to figures compiled by The Times of Central Asia.

Kazakhstan’s economy is estimated at $306 billion, representing nearly 56% of the combined GDP of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan. The figures highlight Kazakhstan’s continuing economic weight in a region where economic growth, trade links and international investment are increasingly reshaping Central Asia’s position.

Uzbekistan has the region’s second-largest economy at $147 billion, followed by Turkmenistan at $50 billion, the Kyrgyz Republic at $23 billion and Tajikistan at $18 billion. Kazakhstan’s position becomes even more pronounced when GDP is considered alongside trade and investment.

Kazakhstan accounts for two-thirds of regional exports

The five Central Asian countries generated a combined $139 billion in exports, of which Kazakhstan accounted for $92 billion, or 66%. Uzbekistan contributed $32 billion, representing 23% of regional exports. Turkmenistan accounted for $7 billion, the Kyrgyz Republic for $6 billion and Tajikistan for approximately $1.6 billion. The overview uses 2024 data for Kazakhstan and Tajikistan.

The figures point to a regional economic structure in which Kazakhstan remains the principal link between Central Asia and international commodity and trade markets. Its large energy and mineral sectors, as well as developed transport and industrial infrastructure, give it a substantially larger export capacity than its neighbors.

However, the concentration of exports also raises a broader question about the region’s future development. As Central Asian economies become more integrated through transport corridors and growing intra-regional trade, Kazakhstan’s economic scale gives it a major advantage, but also makes its diversification increasingly important for the region as a whole.

Nearly 70% of accumulated foreign investment is in Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan also dominates the region in terms of accumulated foreign direct investment. The combined stock of foreign direct investment across Central Asia is estimated at $220.5 billion, with $151.3 billion, or 68.6%, concentrated in Kazakhstan.

Turkmenistan follows with $44.6 billion, while Uzbekistan has accumulated $16.7 billion. The Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan each account for approximately $4 billion. This gap is significant because FDI is not simply a measure of capital inflows. Over time, accumulated investment can shape industrial capacity, infrastructure, technology transfer and a country’s ability to develop new sectors.

Kazakhstan’s share suggests that international investors continue to view the country as the region’s largest and most established investment market. At the same time, the figures illustrate how unevenly foreign capital remains distributed across Central Asia.

Economic weight exceeds Kazakhstan’s demographic share

Kazakhstan’s dominance is particularly notable given its population. Of Central Asia’s estimated 83.6 million people, Kazakhstan accounts for around 21 million, or nearly 25%. Uzbekistan, by comparison, has around 37 million people, representing 44% of the region’s population. This means Kazakhstan produces more than half of Central Asia’s GDP with roughly one-quarter of its population.

The comparison points to Kazakhstan’s considerably higher economic output per capita and reflects differences in economic structure, natural resources, industrial development and the scale of accumulated investment. Uzbekistan’s larger population and rapidly expanding economy, meanwhile, suggest that the balance of economic weight within Central Asia could gradually become more competitive in the coming years. For now, however, Kazakhstan’s economic lead remains substantial.

A stronger financial position

Kazakhstan also stands out through several financial indicators. Its reserves are estimated at $129.3 billion, while its state and state-guaranteed external debt stands at $34 billion. Reserves therefore exceed this debt by nearly 3.8 times, the highest ratio among regional countries for which comparable data were available.

Government debt amounts to 24.6% of GDP, while remittances from abroad represent just 0.1% of GDP and dependence on foreign aid is estimated at 0.03% of gross national income.

These indicators suggest that Kazakhstan’s regional influence is supported not only by the size of its economy, but also by relatively strong financial buffers and lower dependence on external income sources such as remittances or foreign assistance.

Central Asia’s economic center of gravity

Taken together, the figures reveal a clear pattern, as Kazakhstan accounts for nearly 56% of Central Asia’s GDP, 66% of its exports and nearly 69% of its accumulated foreign direct investment, despite representing only one-quarter of the region’s population.

That concentration makes Kazakhstan the region’s principal economic center of gravity. Its performance has implications beyond its own borders, particularly as Central Asian countries seek to develop new transport routes, energy links and industrial supply chains connecting the region with China, Europe and the Middle East.

But the data also point to a changing regional context. Uzbekistan’s $147 billion economy and large population make it an increasingly important second pole of growth, while other countries are seeking to attract investment and strengthen their roles in regional trade networks.

World.title: One Sea, Five Countries, Two Futures: Caspian Sea’s Next Test
World.content:
ALMATY – Caspian Sea Day is being marked on Aug. 12, the 20th anniversary of the entry into force of the Tehran Convention, the main regional agreement on protecting the Caspian Sea’s marine environment, as environmental concerns over declining water levels and the future of the world’s largest enclosed body of water continue to grow.

The anniversary coincided with the conclusion of the international Caspian Sea Action Week 2026, which brought together delegations from Azerbaijan, Iran, Russia and Turkmenistan, as well as representatives from Uzbekistan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan, alongside volunteers, environmental activists, scientists and young people in Aktau.

Held under Taza Kazakhstan environmental culture development concept, the week combined scientific discussions, environmental campaigns, volunteer initiatives and innovation projects aimed at drawing attention to the shared challenges facing the Caspian.

From regional agreement to environmental action

The Framework Convention for the Protection of the Marine Environment of the Caspian Sea, known as the Tehran Convention, entered into force in 2006. It created a regional framework for the five Caspian littoral states to cooperate on pollution prevention and the protection of the sea’s ecosystem. Two decades later, the nature of the challenge has become more complex.

Environmental cooperation initially focused heavily on managing pollution and protecting marine biodiversity. Today, the long-term decline in the Caspian’s water level has added another dimension to the region’s environmental agenda.

Laura Malikova, chair of the Association of Practicing Environmentalists, recently warned about rapid shallowing in the northern Caspian. She linked some of the concerns to dredging operations conducted by the North Caspian Operating Company and its contractors to support navigation and cargo deliveries.

“Photos and videos clearly show how far the water has retreated. The northern Caspian is becoming shallow at an extremely rapid pace,” Malikova said, as quoted by Kazinform.

According to Kazakhstan’s Ecology Ministry, climate change remains the principal driver of the long-term water-level decline. Precipitation in the Caspian region is decreasing while evaporation is increasing, making the region particularly vulnerable to rising temperatures.

The combination of climate pressures and human activity creates a more complicated policy challenge. As water levels decline, coastal infrastructure, shipping routes, ports and industrial projects may need to adapt, while efforts to maintain economic activity can themselves place additional pressure on an already changing ecosystem.

Science becomes central to the response

This growing complexity explains the emphasis on scientific cooperation during Caspian Sea Action Week. An international seminar and roundtable on Aug. 6-7 brought together scientists and experts from Caspian countries to discuss environmental monitoring technologies and ongoing research. The focus reflects an important question for regional environmental policy: whether countries have sufficiently coordinated data and scientific capacity to understand changes occurring across the entire Caspian basin.

The Caspian is one interconnected ecosystem, but environmental information, monitoring systems and policy responses are largely organized at the national level. More effective cooperation could therefore depend not only on exchanging research results but also on developing compatible monitoring systems and a clearer shared understanding of environmental risks.

The One Caspian – One Future session held during the week reflected this idea by bringing together volunteer communities from different countries to discuss common approaches to protecting the sea.

From environmental awareness to practical solutions

The week also demonstrated an effort to connect high-level environmental discussions with public participation. The Caspian Clean Challenge, held in Aktau on Aug. 8 with the participation of Kazakh Vice Minister of Ecology and Natural Resources Mansur Oshurbayev, brought volunteers together for a large-scale coastal cleanup and waste-sorting campaign. More than 80 trees were planted at the newly opened Friendship Alley of Caspian Region Volunteers, while participants also placed a time capsule with messages for future generations.

A cleanup campaign was also held on Aug. 9 in the Bozzhyra area of the Mangystau Region. The international hackathon also invited participants to develop projects aimed at protecting the Caspian ecosystem, while an open TED-style discussion brought environmental volunteers and experts together to exchange ideas. The event concluded on Aug. 12 with the Caspian Talks international volunteer summit, where participants discussed current environmental challenges and exchanged experiences.

A shared sea, facing two possible futures

The central difficulty of protecting the Caspian is that environmental consequences do not stop at national borders. Changes affecting one part of the sea can eventually influence fisheries, biodiversity, coastal communities, ports and economic infrastructure across the region.

Between 2006 and 2025, the shoreline in some areas retreated by 30 to 35 kilometers, according to officials. The average water level across Kazakhstan’s sector of the Caspian stood at –29.35 meters relative to the Baltic height system in 2025.

The longer-term outlook presents two possible scenarios. A forecast prepared by Kazhydromet outlines an optimistic scenario under which the sea level could fall to –32.4 meters by 2050. Under a more pessimistic climate scenario, it could decline as far as –34 meters.

Neither scenario points to a return to previous conditions. Instead, the difference between them represents two levels of adaptation that Caspian countries may have to prepare for. A decline toward –32.4 meters would require substantial adjustments to coastal infrastructure and economic activity. A fall toward –34 meters could bring far more profound changes, pushing the shoreline farther from existing ports and coastal settlements and transforming parts of the former seabed into land.

This changes the nature of the policy challenge. The Caspian countries are no longer dealing only with the task of protecting an existing ecosystem from pollution and overuse. They may increasingly have to manage the economic and environmental consequences of a sea whose physical geography is changing.

Twenty years after the Tehran Convention entered into force, this may be the next major test of Caspian cooperation. The region now faces two broad futures, neither of which assumes the sea will remain unchanged. The critical question is whether Azerbaijan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan can use scientific monitoring and shared data to anticipate the consequences of either scenario before environmental change turns into an economic and infrastructure crisis.

World.title: Can Science Replace Commodities? Kazakhstan Wants Universities to Drive Innovation
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan has more than doubled its research and development spending since 2023, expanded international university partnerships and increased support for young scientists as it seeks to build an economy driven increasingly by knowledge and technology.

Science and higher education have become strategic priorities under a broader modernization agenda. The government’s approach increasingly links three areas that have often developed separately: training skilled professionals, producing scientific research and commercializing new technologies.

Science as an economic resource

According to the Kazakh Prime Minister’s press service, the scale of investment in research has grown substantially. Domestic spending on research and development increased from 121.5 billion tenge (US$228 million) in 2023 to 260 billion tenge (US$489 million) by 2026, more than doubling over three years.

The number of specialists working in research and development reached 28,374 in 2025, nearly one-third higher than four years earlier. Young scientists account for approximately half of Kazakhstan’s research community.

The government has also introduced changes aimed at strengthening the profession’s institutional and social foundations. Legislation now formally defines the status of scientists and research workers, while an ombudsperson institution for scientists and research workers has been established. The age limit for researchers eligible for support as young scientists has been raised to 44.

Financing mechanisms are also shifting toward a greater emphasis on practical outcomes. Alongside conventional research grants, Kazakhstan is expanding support for experimental and engineering work designed to produce prototypes, pilot models and technologies ready for application. The approach reflects a recognition that increasing research spending alone does not automatically produce an innovation economy. The more difficult question is whether scientific results can cross the gap between laboratories and the marketplace.

Kazakhstan reported that more than 1,200 fundamental and applied research projects were completed in 2025. The country is also implementing 241 innovation projects, while more than 30 domestically developed solutions have entered international markets.

Several projects illustrate the potential of this approach. Researchers at Satbayev University developed and introduced a technology for producing high-purity technical selenium through vacuum distillation, reaching 99.5% purity and increasing the product’s value for export markets. Scientists at Nazarbayev University have also developed technology for producing precursor materials for lithium-ion battery cathodes from domestic raw materials.

Such projects could become increasingly important as Kazakhstan seeks to move beyond its traditional role as a supplier of raw materials and participate in higher-value segments of global industrial and technological supply chains.

Universities move closer to research and innovation

This transition is also reshaping the role Kazakhstan expects universities to play. In an article for The Astana Times published in January, Dr. Yerzhan Tokbolat, a lecturer in finance at Queen’s University Belfast, and Miras Dolayev, professor of practice at Almaty Management University and founder and CEO of Data Science Academy, argued that Kazakhstan’s higher education sector has reached an important turning point.

They wrote that 2025 saw record numbers of international students enroll in Kazakh universities and improved positions for local institutions in international rankings,

“The foundations are now in place: flagship universities, international partnerships, and a generation of globally trained professionals. The next stage is to link education more directly with science, research, and innovation, ensuring that universities function not only as centers of learning but as engines of discovery and growth,” Tokbolat and Dolayev wrote.

That challenge closely reflects the direction of current government reforms. Kazakhstan is developing scientific and innovation-focused territories in Almaty, Kurchatov and Astana, intended to bring together universities, research organizations, high-tech companies and innovation infrastructure. Local authorities have also received greater powers to finance research based on regional scientific and technological priorities.

The government is simultaneously working to digitalize science management through the unified Kazakhstan Science information system, which is expected to consolidate data on research projects, organizations, funding and results. Artificial intelligence tools are also expected to support planning and decision-making.

Investing in the next generation of researchers

Whether Kazakhstan can build such an ecosystem will depend heavily on its ability to retain and develop researchers. The country continues to fund young scientists through the Zhas Galym grant program, doctoral education and industrial PhD programs designed to address practical challenges faced by the economy.

Nearly 3,000 doctoral places were allocated for the 2025-26 academic year, including places in industrial doctoral programs. International experience remains another part of the strategy. Since 2021, more than 1,500 Kazakh scientists have completed internships at leading foreign universities, laboratories and research centers. The government has also expanded social support. Between 2023 and 2026, 760 young scientists received housing under state support programs.

Internationalization changes Kazakhstan’s university landscape

Kazakhstan’s higher education system is also becoming increasingly international. Thirty-two branches of foreign universities from countries including the United States, the United Kingdom, China, Germany, France, South Korea and Russia now operate in Kazakhstan.

The expansion is intended to make international education more accessible within the country while attracting international students and academic institutions to Kazakhstan. At the same time, Kazakh universities are expanding abroad, with branches operating in the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Russia.

More than half of Kazakh universities offer dual-degree programs in cooperation with 131 universities across 24 countries. The Kozybayev University and the University of Arizona partnership marked another milestone in 2026 with its first graduating class.

From expanding access to creating economic value

The reforms are changing the scale and structure of Kazakhstan’s science and higher education system. The government increased research spending and more young people are entering scientific careers, while universities are becoming more internationally connected and greater attention is being given to commercialization.

Kazakhstan’s success in becoming a regional higher education hub could therefore depend on what happens after students enter university and researchers complete their projects. The decisive question is whether universities can become the engines of discovery and growth, producing not only graduates and academic publications, but technologies, businesses and ideas capable of competing beyond Kazakhstan’s borders.

World.title: Kazakhstan Updates Astana Master Plan to Meet Demands of Fast-Growing Capital
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s government has approved an updated master plan for Astana through 2035, effective Aug. 8, setting out how the capital will accommodate a population projected to reach nearly 2.3 million while expanding housing, schools, transport and utilities.

The plan comes as Astana continues to expand rapidly, driven by sustained population growth. The city had approximately 300,000 residents when it became the capital in 1997. According to the Bureau of National Statistics, by June 1, its population had reached nearly 1.67 million.

Government projections now put the population at 1.97 million by 2030 and 2.28 million by 2035, meaning the capital could add nearly 600,000 residents within the next decade.

Planning for a city of more than 2 million

The updated master plan uses Jan. 1, 2025, as its baseline, with 2030 designated as the first construction phase and 2035 as the final planning horizon. The document’s baseline population is 1.528 million, a level Astana has already exceeded.

The plan sets out where residential, social, recreational and industrial areas will develop and how they will be supported by transport and engineering infrastructure. It also covers land-use restrictions, reserve territories, environmental protection, emergency resilience and functional zoning.

By 2035, working-age residents are projected to account for 59.5% of the population.

Planning also extends beyond the city’s administrative boundaries. The document takes into account Astana’s growing links with the surrounding agglomeration, where transport networks, utilities, housing and social infrastructure are increasingly interconnected with the capital.

Fivefold population growth since capital relocation

Astana’s development has accelerated sharply since Kazakhstan moved its capital from Almaty to Akmola on Dec. 10, 1997. The city was renamed Astana the following year and officially presented as the new capital on July 6, 1998.

Its population passed one million in 2018 and reached about 1.35 million by the beginning of 2023. Today, Astana has more than five times as many residents as it did when it became the capital. By 2035, Astana’s population is projected to be more than seven times its 1997 level.

Internal migration has contributed significantly to that expansion, with Astana remaining one of Kazakhstan’s main destinations for people relocating from other regions.

Housing, utilities and redevelopment

Housing construction will remain central to accommodating the city’s growth. The master plan sets a target of 30 square meters of housing per resident by 2035, requiring the total housing stock to reach approximately 68.3 million square meters.

Expansion will include both new construction and redevelopment of existing areas. The plan provides for the removal of dilapidated and unsafe housing where necessary, along with garages and some low-rise buildings in districts designated for renovation.

The master plan will also underpin more detailed development programs for electricity, heating, gas, water supply, sewage and stormwater systems, as well as Astana’s comprehensive transport scheme.

The master plan will also serve as the basis for more detailed programs covering electricity, heating, gas, water supply, sewage and stormwater systems, as well as the city’s comprehensive transport scheme. These plans will guide future construction, neighborhood renovation and the redevelopment of residential, industrial and utility areas.

Schools, public spaces and the next stage of growth

Population growth will place particularly strong pressure on schools and kindergartens.

By 2035, Astana is expected to require preschool capacity for 159,194 children. The plan provides for the construction of 206 kindergartens.

School demand is projected to reach 182,423 additional places by 2030 and 256,170 by 2035. To address that need, the plan envisages 123 schools during the first construction phase and another 55 by the end of the planning period.

Beyond new housing and infrastructure, the plan sets a framework for green and recreational areas, public spaces, renovation of established districts and the preservation of historic buildings and cultural heritage sites.

It also includes measures to protect water bodies, improve environmental conditions and guide future rules on compact development and neighborhood renewal.

World.title: Kazakhstan Economy Grows 4.1% as Non-Oil Sectors Expand
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s economy grew 4.1% in the first seven months of 2026, maintaining the pace recorded in the first half of the year despite an 8.9% decline in oil production, reported the Ministry of National Economy on Aug.11.

According to preliminary data from the Bureau of National Statistics (BNS), oil production totaled 53.2 million tons from January through July. Against that decline, the non-oil sector expanded by an estimated 5.4%.

Manufacturing remained among the strongest-performing sectors, growing 9% over the seven months. The fastest increases were recorded in pharmaceuticals at 38.5%, fabricated metal products at 35%, chemicals at 26.9% and mechanical engineering at 22%. Food production rose 13.9%, while building materials increased 9.4%. Growth was also recorded in construction at 15.3%, transport and warehousing at 7.4%, trade at 5.9%, agriculture at 5% and communications at 4.3%.

The figures point to a broader distribution of economic growth at a time when weaker oil output would normally weigh more heavily on overall performance. Economist Ruslan Sultanov said the latest data suggest growth is being generated across several parts of the economy rather than moving entirely in line with oil production.

“Growth is becoming more distributed. The BNS data show an interesting configuration: declining oil production is so far coinciding with the overall GDP growth rate being maintained. This has been possible because several sectors are growing simultaneously,” Sultanov wrote on his Tengenomika Telegram channel.

He also noted that high growth rates in individual industries do not necessarily mean they make an equally large contribution to GDP.

“What matters is their weight in the economy, the absolute volume of output and their ability to maintain this momentum over a longer horizon. The next point of assessment for the economy will be the quality of this growth: whether manufacturing, construction, transport, agriculture and trade can maintain their momentum and generate a sustainable contribution to GDP as conditions in the commodity sector change,” he said.

According to the ministry, the changing composition of growth reflects the gradual diversification of Kazakhstan’s economy, including stronger industrial capacity, development of transport infrastructure, support for domestic producers and small and medium-sized businesses, and increased investment in non-oil sectors. Oil extraction accounted for 7.8% of GDP in 2025.

Independent business indicators also point to activity across a broader range of sectors. In its second-quarter Business Activity Index report published July 28, Halyk Finance said the index stood at 55.2, above the neutral level of 50 that separates expansion from contraction, with growth recorded across manufacturing, construction, trade, transport, agriculture and most other major sectors. The index for small and medium-sized businesses reached 55.3.

The seven-month figures also show an improvement from earlier in the year. According to an April report by the Halyk Finance analytical center, Kazakhstan’s economy grew 3% year on year in the first quarter of 2026, when oil production fell nearly 20%, while manufacturing expanded 8.5%. By January-May, growth had reached 3.7%, according to a June 15 report by the International Monetary Fund.

The IMF projected Kazakhstan’s economy to grow approximately 4.6% in 2026, while identifying potential oil export disruptions, global uncertainty and inflationary pressures as key risks to the outlook.

World.title: Kazakhstan Considers Baku-Supsa Oil Route Amid CPC Disruptions
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is considering additional oil export routes through Azerbaijan and Georgia, including Baku-Supsa, after temporary restrictions on crude intake by the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) in July prompted the diversion of some volumes to alternative routes.

During the restrictions, some Kazakh oil was redirected through the Aktau port, the Atasu-Alashankou pipeline toward China and the Atyrau-Samara route, reported Kazinform, citing Kazakhstan’s Energy Ministry spokesperson and adviser to the minister, Assel Serikpayeva.

“Additional export options under consideration include transportation through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan system, trans-Caspian shipments through Azerbaijan and the Baku-Supsa route,” she said.

Kazakhstan currently transports approximately 1.5 million tons of oil per year through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline. According to Serikpayeva, Azerbaijan has expressed readiness to increase its intake of Kazakh oil to 2.2 million tons annually.

Under the BTC route, Kazakh oil is shipped across the Caspian Sea from Aktau to Azerbaijan before entering the pipeline, which crosses Georgia and reaches the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan in Türkiye.

Baku-Supsa provides another route through Azerbaijan and Georgia, reaching the Supsa terminal on Georgia’s Black Sea coast. Kazakhstan considered using the corridor in 2025, when the ministry said its potential use would depend on commercial terms, operational efficiency and agreements between the companies involved.

The search for additional capacity comes as Kazakhstan continues to rely heavily on CPC for crude exports. The pipeline carries oil from western Kazakhstan to a marine terminal near Russia’s Black Sea port of Novorossiysk. According to the ministry, 64.8 million tons of oil were exported through the route in 2025, out of Kazakhstan’s total oil exports of 78.7 million tons.

The route faced several disruptions in July. The Tengiz-Novorossiysk system resumed operations on July 8 following scheduled maintenance, while loading at the CPC marine terminal was later suspended after drone attacks on tankers on July 19 and 20.

Kazakhstan has previously redirected oil when CPC capacity was constrained. In December 2025, KazMunayGas rerouted approximately 300,000 tons through alternative channels, including shipments toward China and through the BTC system. Kazakhstan also exports oil through the Atyrau-Samara and Atasu-Alashankou pipelines and across the Caspian through the Aktau port.

World.title: Fewer Births, Better Chances: Kazakhstan Advances in Newborn Care
World.content:
ASTANA —Kazakhstan recorded nearly 150,000 births in the first half of 2026, down approximately 7% year on year, while neonatal mortality fell to 3.9 per 1,000 live births in 2025, the lowest rate in Central Asia, according to the Bureau of National Statistics and the Ministry of Healthcare.

The decline in births follows a broader downward trend in Kazakhstan’s total fertility rate, which measures the average number of children a woman would have over her reproductive years. A demographic review by the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund (UAPF) shows the rate fell from 3.32 children per woman in 2021 to 3.06 in 2022 and 2.57 in 2025. The review described declining fertility as part of a broader global trend.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, 335,000 children were born in Kazakhstan in 2025, with boys accounting for 51.5% of births and girls for 48.5%. The country recorded 64,700 deaths from January through June, resulting in a natural population increase of 85,100 people.

While the birth rate has been declining, the ministry data show improving outcomes for newborns requiring specialized medical care, particularly premature babies and children born with severe congenital conditions.

Survival improves in complex neonatal cases

Over the past five years, mortality among newborns with severe congenital conditions has fallen more than threefold, from 22% to 6.9%, while postoperative survival has risen to 93%. Approximately 1,400 operations are performed on newborns each year, with specialized care available at perinatal centers across Kazakhstan.

The ministry attributes the improvement to the development of obstetric and neonatal services, the introduction of modern medical technologies and the work of specialized medical teams. Such treatment can be particularly demanding for premature babies, who require specialized preparation before surgery and intensive care afterward.

Neonatal and pediatric surgeon Zhenis Sakuov told The Astana Times that successful treatment depends on coordination across the entire medical team.

“Operating on newborns is difficult, and operating on premature babies is even more difficult because they require specialized preparation for surgery. (…) The operation itself is complex, the postoperative period is complex, and they need specialized care afterward. This is teamwork,” he said.

About 17,000 premature babies were born in Kazakhstan last year, with each receiving a range of specialized medical care, according to the ministry.

Earlier diagnosis expands treatment options

Advances in neonatal care increasingly begin before birth. Modern prenatal diagnostics can detect many congenital conditions between 18 and 20 weeks of pregnancy, allowing doctors to determine how the pregnancy and delivery should be managed and prepare a medical team to assist the child immediately after birth. When fetal abnormalities are identified, expectant mothers are referred to specialized perinatal centers, where doctors determine the timing and method of delivery and prepare a treatment plan in advance.

This approach has also expanded through one-day clinics at fetal health centers. According to the ministry, since their introduction in 2024, prenatal screening coverage has increased by 10%, detection of fetal abnormalities by 12%, and childhood disability has declined by 8%.

Treatment in some cases can now begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, or the intrauterine correction of certain fetal conditions, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

For some conditions, treatment can begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, which involves correcting certain fetal conditions in the womb, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

After birth, about one-third of newborn surgeries are now performed using minimally invasive techniques. Kazakhstan has also used extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) since 2022 to support patients in critical condition with severe respiratory failure.

“Intensive care is developing, as well as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, anesthesiology, and diagnostics. All of this significantly increases children’s chances of recovery and a good quality of life. And most importantly, many families today can receive high-tech medical care without leaving Kazakhstan,” Pediatric Cardiac Surgeon Tlektes Nashkenov told The Astana Times.

The ministry’s data show survival rates of 80% to 90% for children born with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, 85% to 95% for esophageal atresia and more than 90% for gastroschisis. Mortality among premature babies with necrotizing enterocolitis has fallen more than 2.5 times as diagnostic and surgical treatment has improved.

World.title: eGov GPT Expansion Advances Kazakhstan’s Digital Government Push
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to expand its AI-powered eGov GPT assistant so that services available through it account for approximately 70% of citizen requests by the end of 2026, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said at an Aug. 11 government meeting.

The assistant currently provides access to 50 of the most frequently requested government services, which together account for approximately 30% of citizen requests. Since its launch in April, eGov GPT has been used more than 150,000 times. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the ministry and government agencies to increase the number of services available through the assistant to 150 by year-end.

The system allows users to describe their situation in ordinary text rather than search for the appropriate form, certificate or government agency. The assistant identifies the relevant service, prepares the required application and provides the result.

“eGov GPT should become a universal AI assistant for all matters involving interaction between the state and citizens,” said Madiyev.

The expansion is part of Kazakhstan’s broader effort to integrate artificial intelligence into public services under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, approved in June.

“The year of digitalization and artificial intelligence marks the starting point for achieving this goal. In June, the nationwide Digital Qazaqstan strategy was approved, with the digitalization of public services identified as one of its key priorities,” said Bektenov.

The Aug. 11 meeting, chaired by Bektenov, focused on developing an AI-based public service ecosystem and implementing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to accelerate digital transformation across the economy and public administration. The government is also seeking to make interactions with citizens and businesses increasingly digital and proactive.

Government agencies shift to QazTech

All government agencies are now working with QazTech, Kazakhstan’s unified platform for developing digital public services, while the migration of existing information systems continues under a two-year government plan. The platform has been operating since April 1 and is designed to shorten the development and launch of new digital services from several years to several weeks.

“This year, 39 systems are scheduled for migration, with work on 36 nearing completion. Another 25 systems are being migrated or developed outside the plan, while 10 systems are already fully operational on the platform. This means the work is progressing ahead of schedule, and today all government agencies are already working with QazTech,” said Madiyev.

A moratorium on creating new government information systems outside QazTech has also been in effect since the beginning of 2026. The move is intended to consolidate digital development within a common technological environment, reduce duplicative systems and establish shared standards across government agencies.

Kazakhstan launches eGov 3.0

The government has also launched eGov 3.0, an upgraded version of Kazakhstan’s electronic government portal built on the QazTech platform.

According to Madiyev, the previous eGov portal had reached the limits of its technological capacity, prompting the launch of eGov 3.0 on the QazTech platform. The upgraded portal simplifies services by removing unnecessary requirements and steps, with several of the most frequently requested services already available in the new format.

The modernization is aimed at simplifying access to public services while reducing pressure on government digital infrastructure as demand for online services continues to grow.

According to the latest United Nations e-government survey published in 2024, Kazakhstan ranks 24th among 193 countries in the E-Government Development Index, with a score of 0.9009, placing it in the UN’s “very high” e-government development group.

World.title: Georgian PM confirms “fuel was supplied to occupied Abkhazia from Tbilisi-controlled territory”
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that petrol had been supplied from Tbilisi-controlled territory amid a severe fuel shortage in occupied Abkhazia. A journalist asked Kobakhidze about the issue.

Occupied Abkhazia has recently faced a severe fuel shortage, leading to significant restrictions on supplies of petrol and other petroleum products.

“We did not introduce this; it was introduced by private businesses,” Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He added that such measures were being taken in line with Georgia’s existing legislation, including the Law on Occupied Territories.

He said the Georgian government was ready to help ease the situation for people living in occupied Abkhazia where possible.

“If we can ease the situation, including for the population living in Abkhazia, we will do so, but we will act within the framework of the Law on Occupied Territories,” Kobakhidze said.

Kobakhidze also referred to the government’s “A Step to a Better Future” programme. According to him, it provides support for people living in the occupied territories, including the Abkhaz population.

Comment

Opposition Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia reacted to Kobakhidze’s statement and called on the government to provide further clarification.

Gvaramia noted that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories generally prohibits direct unauthorised economic activity in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, although it provides certain exceptions, including for activities carried out for humanitarian purposes.

Gvaramia suggested that the fuel supplies in this case could have been intended for Russia’s “war machine”.

Nika Gvaramia: “We are dealing with an action that was presumably authorised by the government in advance. However, the public has not been told the grounds for such authorisation, or when and why it was issued.

“Given that:

— the Russian military machine is facing a severe fuel shortage, while Russian military bases are located in occupied Abkhazia;

— the Ivanishvili regime has repeatedly and deliberately stressed the need for cooperation with Russia;

— taking into account Georgia’s security and territorial integrity interests, as well as Western sanctions imposed on Russia, fuel supplies to territory controlled by Russia cannot be justified on legitimate humanitarian or socio-economic grounds,

“it becomes clear that the Ivanishvili regime has effectively acknowledged that, with its authorisation — and, in essence, by the regime itself — an action is being carried out that runs counter to Georgia’s sovereign interests. It:

violates Georgia’s Constitution;

violates Western sanctions imposed on Russia;

is aimed at assisting the Russian military machine by supplying strategically important products.”

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: EU report: Human rights and democracy in Georgia deteriorated significantly in 2025
World.content:
EU report on Georgia — 2026

According to the European Union’s annual report for 2025, the human rights and democracy situation in Georgia deteriorated significantly. Laws adopted by the government and its repressive measures further restricted fundamental freedoms.

Overall, the report portrays Georgia as a country where the weakening of democratic institutions, restrictions on fundamental rights and shrinking space for civil society are closely interconnected.

The report says the country’s EU integration process has effectively stalled, while much of Brussels’ financial and political support now goes to civil society and independent media rather than the government.

What does the report say?

Freedom of expression, assembly and association

The report says Georgia has restricted freedom of expression, assembly and association, as well as the rights to equality and protection from discrimination, respect for private and family life, liberty and personal security.

The document highlights widespread reports in 2025 of law enforcement officers mistreating protesters. According to the EU, some cases amounted to torture or inhuman or degrading treatment. The report says no one has been held accountable for such incidents, contributing to a climate of impunity.

The EU says arbitrary arrests, excessive use of pre-trial detention and disproportionately harsh sentences handed down to protesters and journalists raise serious concerns about the right to a fair trial.

The report also examines cases of physical violence, sexual harassment, rape and death threats against women taking part in demonstrations.

Media restrictions

According to the EU, new legislation adopted by the Georgian government has made it even harder for independent media and civil society organisations to operate. The report highlights amendments to the laws on broadcasting and “transparency of foreign influence”, as well as a legislative package concerning family values and the protection of minors.

The report also notes numerous reports of intimidation, threats, verbal abuse, physical violence and arbitrary detention targeting journalists and other media workers.

The European Union says the government’s repressive measures against civil society, the media and the opposition have significantly undermined democratic processes. They have effectively reduced public participation in political life and weakened the effectiveness of checks and balances.

The EU also highlighted the freezing of bank accounts belonging to several civil society organisations as part of the use of judicial mechanisms to suppress dissent.

Political pluralism has also deteriorated. The report notes an attempt by the ruling party to have several opposition parties banned through the Constitutional Court.

According to the EU, Georgia’s declining democracy indicators are also reflected in international rankings. The country ranked 114th in Reporters Without Borders’ 2025 World Press Freedom Index, 52nd in the World Justice Project’s Rule of Law Index and 56th in the Corruption Perceptions Index. It also scored 34 points on the CIVICUS Monitor, indicating a shrinking space for civil society.

Financial support for civil society

The statement notes that, amid democratic backsliding, the European Union extended its suspension of direct financial assistance to the Georgian authorities for 2025. At the same time, EU funding went towards supporting civil society and independent media.

Under the NDICI programme, €24 million was allocated to directly support civil society and independent media, with a further €10 million allocated for 2025–2027 under the Eastern Partnership Civil Society Facility.

Existing EU programmes cover areas including improving access to justice, protecting the rights of people with disabilities and children, and safeguarding the rights of ethnic and religious minorities and the LGBT community. They also support gender equality, efforts to combat disinformation and strengthening the institution of the Public Defender.

ECHR and international obligations

The EU report also takes a critical view of Georgia’s cooperation with the European Court of Human Rights and its implementation of the court’s judgments.

According to the document, the level of cooperation and compliance with court rulings was deemed insufficient. A total of 45 cases remain under enhanced supervision by the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe.

The EU also identified problems in Georgia’s cooperation with international organisations. The Georgian authorities did not issue an invitation to the OSCE observation mission in time to allow full monitoring of the municipal elections scheduled for October 2025. They also failed to take adequate steps to implement the organisation’s previous recommendations.

The report also notes that, despite retaining its seat on the UN Human Rights Council, Georgia has not joined several important international and EU initiatives.

World.title: Irakli Kobakhidze: “‘Deep state’ is trying to artificially fuel Russophobia in Georgia”
World.content:
“Radical anti-Russian sentiment in the country is being artificially fuelled and is part of a new campaign against Georgia,” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He said attempts to intensify Russophobia in Georgia were part of a plan carried out by agents of the “deep state”.

Kobakhidze recalled that the Georgian government had repeatedly said that, after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, the so-called “global war party” had tried to draw Georgia into the conflict and open a “second front” in the country.

The prime minister said this “window of opportunity” created an “existential threat” to Georgia and its population. He said calls for Georgia to join international sanctions against Russia soon followed. According to the government, complying with those demands would have had serious consequences for the country’s economy.

“Because the Georgian government refused to comply with these demands, pursued a sovereign policy and acted in the interests of the state, our country became a target for the European bureaucracy and Western leaders working in tandem with informal oligarchic forces,” Kobakhidze said.

He also addressed the sanctions imposed by Western countries on the Georgian government. According to Kobakhidze, pressure mechanisms, including sanctions, were already being used when the previous US administration under Joe Biden was in power.

Kobakhidze said the sanctions had targeted senior Georgian government officials, ruling party honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, judges, senior police officers and others.

He said the West had also used Georgia’s EU membership prospects as a tool to pressure the government.

“They failed to break the ruling party, which enjoys the support of the Georgian people, so now they are trying to use their agents to drag Georgia into a new provocation,” he added.

Kobakhidze said a “new stage of the attack” on Georgia, its people and its sovereignty had begun:

“This is a qualitatively new stage of the attack on Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s sovereignty, unfolding simultaneously on several fronts.”

Background

Several days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy letter addressing the issue of “Russophobia”.

In the letter, Kobakhidze discussed the links between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic political situation and the opposition’s position. He said the “global war party” benefited from the ongoing conflict in Ukraine because it wanted to “fuel Russophobia at the highest level among its agents around the world, including in Georgia”.

Kobakhidze accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current tough stance towards Moscow as “Russophobia”.

The letter reignited political disputes over the events of the 2008 war. This time, however, the debate focused not only on the circumstances that led to the war and Russia’s responsibility. The prime minister shifted the focus from Russia’s actions to the position of his Georgian opponents.

Georgian PM on “Russophobia”

World.title: Ilham Aliyev’s AzTV interview during Nakhchivan visit: industrial park, energy projects and Zangezur Corridor
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

On 11 August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. It was Aliyev’s 17th visit to Nakhchivan since he became president.

During the visit, officials held foundation-laying ceremonies and opened several facilities. Aliyev also visited historical sites and presented battle flags to military units.

The visit ended with an interview with Azerbaijan Television (AzTV), in which Aliyev outlined his plans for Nakhchivan’s development.

The interview focused on the autonomous republic’s economic and social development, energy security and transport infrastructure. Aliyev also discussed Nakhchivan’s place in Azerbaijan’s broader strategy, particularly its future development in conjunction with Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, territories that came under Baku’s control after the Second Karabakh War.

Key events during the visit

During the visit to Nakhchivan, President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva inspected work at the Shams-1 and Garbi Ufug solar power plants, which have a combined capacity of 50 MW.

One of the key events was the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park. It will be Azerbaijan’s second-largest industrial park by area, after the Sumgayit Industrial Park. A 300 MW thermal power plant is also planned for the site.

Nakhchivan’s total generating capacity currently stands at around 200 MW. Once the new plant comes online, this will increase by roughly half.

The visit programme also included:

the opening of the Nakhchivan Regional DOST Centre;

the presentation of new electric buses and an inspection of railway infrastructure reconstruction works;

the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan hotel complex, which is expected to be completed by around 2028;

the laying of the foundation stone for a social housing complex;

an inspection of restoration work at the Momine Khatun Mausoleum and the unveiling of a monument to architect Ajami Nakhchivani;

the presentation of Nakhchivan’s General Development Plan through 2044, which envisages expanding the city and increasing its population;

the presentation of battle flags to new commando units of the Separate Combined Arms Army.

Key points from the AzTV interview

Aliyev described his visit to Nakhchivan as a “sign of the autonomous republic’s comprehensive development”. He said every visit should produce concrete results. He highlighted strengthening defence capabilities, energy security, job creation, preserving historical and cultural heritage, and developing transport links as key priorities.

Defence and governance

Aliyev said Nakhchivan’s geographical position – particularly its lack of a direct land connection with mainland Azerbaijan – requires special attention to the region’s defence. He highlighted the creation of the Separate Combined Arms Army and new commando units as key steps.

According to the president, “Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces carry weight in the region”. He also said Nakhchivan had introduced a system of special presidential representatives, similar to the model used in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur. Aliyev said the benefits of this system of governance were already becoming apparent.

Energy

Nakhchivan has been fully supplied with gas for around 15 years, Aliyev said, thanks to a gas swap agreement with Iran.

The president also placed particular emphasis on the region’s solar energy potential. He said Nakhchivan was Azerbaijan’s most favourable region for solar power generation. More than 600 hectares of land have already been allocated for the development of this sector. The potential is estimated at at least 500 MW and could reach 1 GW in the future.

Aliyev also highlighted the growing role of the private sector. Projects to build solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 MW are already under way.

The president described electricity exports as a strategic priority. Iran and Turkey are currently the main destinations, but Azerbaijan ultimately hopes to export electricity from Nakhchivan to the European market as well.

Zangezur Corridor – TRIPP

Aliyev said that “the creation of the Zangezur Corridor was our initiative”, recalling that connecting mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, an integral part of the country, had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

He said he had insisted that a provision on the corridor be included in the trilateral statement signed by Azerbaijan, Russia and Armenia on 10 November 2020. Aliyev claims the Armenian side did not want to agree to this, but had no other alternative because continuing the war was not in its interests.

Noting that there had been no practical progress on the issue for five years, Aliyev said a solution emerged after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025, when the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) was launched.

Speaking about the current state of the work, the president said the Horadiz-Aghband highway was almost complete, with only minor technical issues remaining. He said construction of the railway was also progressing rapidly.

Aliyev added that a project for power transmission lines linking mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenia had already been prepared, and locations for the pylons had been identified.

Aliyev predicted that these projects would eventually turn Nakhchivan into one of the region’s key transport and energy hubs.

A unified development concept

The president stressed that Nakhchivan, Eastern Zangezur and Karabakh should develop under a unified concept. He said the geographical proximity of the three regions requires a common approach to their development.

Aliyev noted that master plans for cities in the territories that came under Azerbaijan’s control after the Second Karabakh War had already been approved. He also said he had ordered the preparation of a similar document for Nakhchivan. The “Nakhchivan City Development Master Plan through 2044” was presented to the president during the current visit.

Speaking about the region’s tourism potential, Aliyev said Nakhchivan had significant opportunities thanks to its rich historical heritage, scenic landscapes and clean air. At the same time, he acknowledged that the hotel infrastructure remained underdeveloped and that the existing hotels were generally of a low standard, hindering the growth of tourism.

He said that to address the problem, construction had begun on a new five-star hotel complex in the city centre. The project is expected to be completed around 2028.

Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

World.title: Child seats, rear-seat seat belts and alcohol interlocks: changes to Georgia’s traffic rules
World.content:
New road safety rules in Georgia

Georgia plans to tighten road safety rules under the National Road Safety Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the government on 5 August 2026. The strategy includes changes in several areas.

At this stage, the measures remain proposals, and some will require further legislative amendments before they can take effect.

What is changing:

Child seats will become mandatory for pre-school children. This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt.

This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt. Rear-seat seat belts could become mandatory. The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism.

The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism. Drunk drivers could be prevented from driving. The strategy provides for the introduction of so-called “alcohol interlocks”. These devices check a driver’s blood alcohol level and prevent the car from starting if it exceeds the permitted limit.

Georgia plans to establish a standard for alcohol-based ignition interlock systems. Under the strategy, authorities intend to take alcohol interlock technology into account when setting requirements for vehicles entering the Georgian market. No specific new rules have been announced at this stage, although additional regulation remains under consideration. More attention will be paid to pedestrian safety, including children’s safety. Authorities also plan to run awareness campaigns for pedestrians on the importance of following traffic rules. Infrastructure will be adapted for vulnerable groups. Future infrastructure projects are expected to give greater consideration to the safety of people with disabilities.

The government strategy says seat-belt use is one of the key ways to reduce deaths and serious injuries in road accidents. It pays particular attention to rear-seat seat belts because unrestrained passengers in the back can endanger not only themselves but also people sitting in the front of the vehicle.

The strategy is not limited to introducing new requirements. The government also plans to raise awareness of road safety, run public campaigns and educational programmes, and improve technical tools for detecting violations.

It is important to note that the government strategy sets out some of these measures only in broad terms. Where necessary, authorities will have to introduce additional legislative and regulatory amendments to implement specific commitments.
