World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Kobakhidze: Georgia does not publicly declare Russia an enemy because this would require follow-up steps
World.content:
Georgian prime minister on Russia

Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that the Georgian government does not publicly call Russia an “enemy” because such a political statement would require corresponding action.

A journalist asked Kobakhidze whether the Georgian government considers Russia an enemy. The prime minister replied:

“Your questions are shameful, you look ridiculous. Let me explain in simple terms why this question is shameful: you want to get a sensational headline, even in the Russian media, saying that I have declared the Russian Federation an enemy. This is a specific political statement that would have to be followed by specific steps – roughly the same, or exactly the same, as those your party” (referring to the United National Movement – JAMnews) “took in 2008 and before.”

The journalist asked whether this was precisely why the government was reluctant to openly call Russia an enemy.

“Of course. What, should I repeat it again?!” Kobakhidze replied.

Kobakhidze also addressed Russia’s occupation of Georgian territories and reiterated that the Russian Federation occupies 20% of Georgia’s territory.

“Of course, the Russian Federation is the only state and party that has occupied Georgian territories. This is an absolutely clear fact. Numerous statements have been made about this, and there is no doubt about it,” Kobakhidze stressed.

He said Russia’s occupation of Georgian territory was a “crime against the Georgian state and the Georgian people”:

“This is an egregious crime: first the occupation, and then the so-called recognition.”

Georgian prime minister on Russia

World.title: Deadly fungal disease threatens native snakes
World.content:
Sunshine Coast wildlife experts warn an "influx" of a deadly fungal disease is putting native reptile populations at risk.

Snake catcher Stuart McKenzie said snake fungal disease orophidiomycosis was killing snakes and lizards across south-east Queensland.

He said a large number of snakes with fungal disease symptoms were found over winter on the Sunshine Coast and sent to a lab for testing.

"There's been an influx of snakes with the infection recently," Mr McKenzie said.

Stuart McKenzie is worried about how the disease will affect snake numbers. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Snake Catchers)

A red-bellied black snake was found on a job site at Woodford this month which was "absolutely riddled with this fatal disease".

Mr McKenzie said it could be a "death sentence" for native reptile populations that experienced yellow-brown lesions, crusty scabs, rotting scales, bleeding, unusual skin shedding, and may seem lethargic or skinny when infected.

"It can be quite nasty," he said.

Disease first found on coast

University of Queensland wildlife veterinarian and researcher Shelly Butcher is worried about threatened reptile species as the infection spreads.

Dr Butcher was part of the team that diagnosed the nation's first reported case of snake fungal disease in an eastern bandy-bandy snake found on the Sunshine Coast two years ago.

Wild snakes with suspected or confirmed snake fungal disease are admitted to a wildlife hospital where they enter quarantine while awaiting test results.

Experts fear the infection is spreading. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Snake Catcher)

"For severe cases, euthanasia is often the most humane option, but treatment can be attempted in less severe cases," Dr Butcher said.

"I haven't successfully treated a snake and released. The disease has been too severe."

In 2024 her team recorded 10 cases of the disease but she said they had no way of knowing how many there had been since then.

One died in care and the other nine were euthanased.

Shelly Butcher hopes to spread awareness of fungal snake disease. (Supplied: Shelly Butcher)

Origin of fungal disease

Researchers are not sure where it came from but suspect an illegal pet trade or domestic pets from overseas.

Dr Butcher's PhD research is investigating broadscale surveillance of the fungal disease.

An infected snake was found at Woodford last week. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Snake Catchers)

"We're trying to spread the news to wildlife hospitals around the country to be testing for it because there is a possibility that it could pop up anywhere," she said.

She said a couple of closely related fungal diseases were found in bearded dragons and water dragons too.

Snakes can be tested for the disease either alive or dead. A tissue sample is collected to look under the microscope, and at the same time, a skin swab or tissue sample is collected and tested using PCR and DNA sequencing.

Experts say to call a snake catcher if a snake is found unwell. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Snake Catchers)

There is only one commercial laboratory that offers the test in Australia, the Hyndman Reptile Pathogen Laboratory at Murdoch University, Perth. Preliminary results may return in a week or two, but final results can take up to two months.

Why a fungal disease on water dragons has reptile experts concerned A fungal disease affecting Brisbane's water dragons could be a big deal for Australian reptiles, researchers say.

Dr Butcher said the disease also posed "major biosecurity concerns" because her team had no way to trace it outside of care.

"We don't know how widespread this disease is or the impacts it is having on wild snakes, so it's highly risky to release an infected snake that could spread the disease further," she said.

Queensland's departments of primary industries and the environment have been contacted for comment.

'Quite concerning'

Dr Butcher's team sampled eight snakes found on the Sunshine Coast with skin lesions in winter this year, including eastern brown snakes, red-bellied black snakes and carpet pythons.

"Considering this is the quieter time of year for snake activity, these numbers have been quite concerning," she said.

The results for these cases were still pending.

Experts say reptiles are an important part of the ecosystem. (Supplied: Sunsine Coast Snake Catchers)

Dr Butcher said Australia had the highest diversity of reptile species of any country, the majority of which were endemic.

"Reptiles are important ecosystem regulators; they keep pest populations in check and help to maintain healthy landscapes," she said.

"We are particularly concerned about this disease entering threatened reptile populations who are already under a lot of stress from other threats like climate change, habitat loss or invasive species."

The first recorded case in Queensland was in 2024. (Supplied: Sunshine Coast Snake Catcher)

Researchers believe the fungal disease could decrease reptile numbers or, if left unchecked, even lead to extinctions.

Both experts have asked Queenslanders to call a wildlife authorities as soon as possible if a snake is unwell.

Dr Butcher said every case reported would help improve their chances of treating the disease to save native reptile species.

World.title: 'Enough is enough': Bill Shorten revives UC-CIT merger after CEO exit
World.content:
The University of Canberra (UC) is proposing to merge with the national capital's other public tertiary education institution, the Canberra Institute of Technology (CIT).

The revived proposal from 2011, this time spearheaded by UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten, comes two days after embattled former CIT chief executive Margot McNeill resigned.

"With the latest CEO resigning on Tuesday night, I thought, well, enough is enough," Mr Shorten said

"I think that's the trigger for this public discussion," he told ABC Canberra 666 Breakfast presenter Ross Solly.

The prospect of a UC-CIT marriage has previously enjoyed ACT government support, with the then-education minister Andrew Barr supporting an unrealised merger 15 years ago.

Mr Shorten said the timing was better now.

"Maybe at that stage CIT didn't see the urgency ... or UC had a superior attitude about unis versus TAFEs."

He said it now came down to a couple of questions:

"In a jurisdiction the size of Canberra, is it really sensible to have two separate post-school organisations?

"And education is evolving. Is it sensible now to ask 15 and 16 year olds, to say for the whole of your life you're going to do a trade or you're going to go to uni?" he asked.

In his pitch, Mr Shorten denied the move was motivated by cost-cutting and said he believed consolidating the two institutes would create job security and opportunities for staff rather than redundancies.

Minister to query CEO's $445k

ACT Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson has reacted warmly to UC's pitch.

"I'm very grateful that the University of Canberra are stepping forward in a moment of crisis, as some would describe it, and trying to be helpful," Mr Pettersson said.

"We understand that current arrangements [at CIT] are not instilling confidence. We know that we need to do something different," he said.

He stopped short of supporting a merger and pointed to an already underway ACT government-commissioned independent governance review of the CIT.

Mr Pettersson said that review could help inform the CIT's future.

ACT Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson has welcomed UC's pitch. (ABC Canberra: Donal Sheil)

Meanwhile, Mr Pettersson has promised he will have a conversation with CIT board chair Tom Rogers about Dr McNeill receiving $445,000 upon her resignation.

"I will definitely have a conversation with the chair. I look forward to that conversation," he said.

But he qualified his response by highlighting the board's independence and the legal processes that have surrounded the saga.

Dr McNeill's appointment as chief executive in June 2025 was questioned earlier this year after revelations she had failed to disclose an investigation into misconduct in her previous role at TAFE NSW.

In May, Dr McNeill came under further pressure to resign after an ACT Legislative Assembly inquiry found she "should have disclosed the information about the misconduct investigation or findings to the CIT board in a timely manner and that she did not".

Mr Rogers previously said Dr McNeill had been awarded the settlement, but would not be drawn on whether the board had asked her to step down.

World.title: Alan Jones complainant's ex quizzed over 'look after you' text
World.content:
A woman who said her ex-boyfriend told her Alan Jones "inappropriately" touched him as a teenager has accepted a message he sent 20 years later could look like a financial promise for coming forward, but denied interpreting it that way.

The 85-year-old broadcaster is facing a local court trial in Sydney after pleading not guilty to 20 counts of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching relating to six male complainants between 2003 and 2020.

Complainant J, a former young athlete, has accused Mr Jones of kissing him and touching him indecently on multiple occasions when he was 17 or 18 years old.

The complainant, now in his 40s, alleged that during one overnight trip to Mr Jones's Fitzroy Falls property, the radio host touched him on the penis multiple times, kissed him on the mouth, and rubbed his genitals against his without his consent.

Complainant J's girlfriend at the time told the trial on Thursday her boyfriend came over to her house after leaving Mr Jones's property and told her, "Alan Jones has touched me inappropriately" before also saying, "You cannot tell anyone about this."

Complainant J's ex questioned over 'I'll look after you'

The trial heard the woman reconnected with the complainant almost two decades later and the pair caught up on several occasions to have coffee and breakfast between 2023 and 2024.

The woman said she provided a statement to police about Complainant J confiding in her years earlier after he officially reported his allegations, around two days following Mr Jones's arrest in 2024.

Under cross-examination, the woman was questioned about messages Complainant J sent her after she gave her statement in 2024, which said, "that was something that could change my life for the better and you should feel very happy" and "once it's all over, I promise to look after you".

Ms Bashir has spent the better part of this week cross-examining Complainant J and those close to him. (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

"Did you understand him saying 'could change my life for the better' was him telling you there was a prospect of financial reward for him?" defence barrister Gabrielle Bashir SC asked "No," the ex-girlfriend answered "You understood that promise was a promise to look after you financially?" Ms Bashir suggested. "No," the woman replied.

The woman did accept that she had "love hearted" the message and that it could be interpreted as a promise of financial support for backing up the complainant's case.

"It does look like that, but it never crossed my mind," she said. "I know he didn't mean that ever, we had never spoken about it."

As Ms Bashir began to question the woman about her ongoing sobriety and a $1,200 fine she received in 2024, Crown prosecutor Georgina Wright SC interjected and accused the defence of trying to "besmirch" the witness.

"This financial motive is based on nothing, this is a backdoor to get before your honour, matters which are an attempt to intimidate the witness," Ms Wright said.

During the fiery exchange, Ms Bashir asked the prosecution to withdraw the intimidation claim describing it as a "grave allegation", but Ms Wright refused.

Judge Glenn Walsh allowed the line of questioning to continue and called for the "air to be cleared" between the two parties.

The woman denied needing financial help from the complainant and strongly rejected suggestions from the defence that the conversation about inappropriate touching took place.

The woman finished giving evidence to the judge-alone trial on Thursday morning.

World.title: Cartoonists fear for industry with rise of AI-generated illustrations
World.content:
Cartoonists say they are worried about the future of their craft, as media companies continue to grapple with integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into their industry.

On Wednesday, the Herald Sun newspaper published an AI-generated illustration alongside an article about Victorian Premier Ben Carroll.

The illustration, which was clearly marked by the publisher as being AI generated, depicted Mr Carroll with a pirate's leg scraping barnacles off a ship decorated with former Labor premiers Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews.

The ABC understands News Corp has been using AI-generated illustrations for about two years.

The move has left some cartoonists concerned for what they say is a shrinking industry.

Cartoonist Fiona Katauskas said seeing the spread of AI illustrations on social media and in newspapers felt like a "punch in the gut".

"There's sadness because just as a cartoonist and an illustrator, it is AI taking someone's job," she said.

"But also, they're just ugly … it's very easy to spot an AI illustrational cartoon because they've all got the same style."

Fiona Katauskas has used her art to make statements about AI. (Supplied: Fiona Katauskas)

The Herald Sun and News Corp have been contact for comment.

The company's code of conduct requires any image altered by digital tools, including AI, to be labelled as being digitally altered or similar.

It also states that the "same editorial rigour and standards" be applied to content that is sourced from AI technology, including images and graphics.

"Content from AI technology cannot be published on any platform including social media without being first reviewed and approved by an editor or relevant editorial manager," the policy reads.

'Damaging' for industry, cartoonist association says

Katauskas said she had seen more Australian newspapers using AI to create illustrations over the past year, which she believed most people had not noticed.

"This is happening at a time when the media is collapsing and has less money," she said.

"So the fear is that it'll just be easier for editors to fill a space and hope that the vast majority of people don't notice."

Katauskas, who has worked in the industry for more than 30 years, said it had changed a lot during that time.

"Cartooning as an industry has been shrinking dramatically for years now," she said.

She said she was recently told her contract with the Guardian Australia would not be renewed, meaning she would be working as a freelance cartoonist from next week.

"Cartooning is a wonderful, centuries-old art … and I would just love it to be kept alive," Katauskas said.

The Guardian has been contacted for comment.

Media companies are adopting AI technologies and developing policies. (Four Corners: Mark Hiney)

Deputy president of the Australian Cartoonists Association, David Blumenstein, recently published a book about the infiltration of AI in the world of illustrations.

He said while it was disappointing to see newspapers use AI-generated illustrations, it wasn't surprising.

"I think it's damaging for the cartooning and illustration industry, obviously," he said.

"It's been growing pretty steadily since these [AI] platforms that were free to the public sort of popped up back in 2022 or thereabouts.

"The thing that frightened me the most ultimately, was that perhaps the people who hire us … maybe they don't care about the ethics."

Media implementing AI tools, developing policies

University of Melbourne academic Jeff Sparrow said the use of AI was a complex issue.

"I think that we are likely to see AI used as the pretext for a lot of job shedding," Dr Sparrow, a senior lecturer at university's Centre for Advancing Journalism, said.

"It's really important that the unions in the media industry take this on as a serious issue and make a concerted effort to protect people's jobs and to promote their interests."

Many media companies in Australia have started implementing AI tools, including the ABC, which has recently launched an AI writing trial to create digital news articles based on radio bulletins.

The ABC also updated its AI guidelines earlier this year. The organisation's previous principles on AI said it would inform audiences about how it was using AI technologies.

AI companies 'stole' Australian culture, news bosses say Media leaders say AI developers should pay to license Australian journalism and culture used to train their models.

The current version says the ABC will be open with audiences when AI use "could materially affect their understanding" of content.

An ABC spokesperson declined to comment for this story but pointed to an internal email sent by acting news director Donna Field last month.

"AI only assists us with journalism and creating content," she said in the email dated July 9.

"It supports but does not replace editorial thinking and decision-making.

"People will always be involved in production, with human oversight at every crucial step when AI is employed."

The ABC also contacted Nine Publishing, which publishes mastheads including The Age and the Sydney Morning Herald, as part of this story.

Nine's AI guidelines state that "AI will not be used to generate photo-realistic images or illustrations for publication, except in cases where the AI-generated nature of the image is the point of the story".

The policy adds that AI can be used to create graphics with editor approval.

Transparency needed as industry moves forward: academic

Mr Blumenstein said the technology was not the issue.

"Technology is always interesting and technology can be used to help artists and used to help people in a way that is ethical," he said.

"But so much of this stuff is totally unethical."

Dr Sparrow said it was why journalists and the community needed "to start demanding for transparency in the use of AI".

"We need to know what the policies of the various outlets are, the kinds of platforms they're using and the circumstances in which they're using [them]," he said.

The Media Entertainment & Arts Alliance (MEAA) said editorial cartoons were an important part of Australia's media landscape and contribute to political commentary, satire and public debate.

"Editorial cartooning is a skilled and specialised profession that requires artistic ability, political understanding and journalistic judgement," a spokesperson said.

The peak union body for creative professionals said just like any form of journalism, professional cartooning needed to be accountable to the Journalist Code of Ethics.

"This code calls on journalists to inform citizens and animate democracy; to scrutinise power but also exercise it; to be responsible and accountable," the spokesperson said.

" It requires complex and critical thinking and accountability, which cannot be automated. "

It was also concerned skills required for cartooning would be devalued as AI becomes more widely used.

"The long-term success of Australia's media industry depends on supporting sustainable, skilled jobs that foster creativity, uphold quality journalism and contribute to the nation's cultural and economic future."

Katauskas said there were important elements in the creative industry that AI could not replace.

"Whether it's reading books or writing or whatever, the journey and the process is what makes it … it's not just about the result," she said.

"This is the thing that really bothers me about AI, that jumping straight to the finish line rather than appreciating the process, which I think is what art in general is all about."

World.title: Hulking prop set to be 1,000th Wallaby as Kiss reshuffles deck
World.content:
The 1,000th Wallaby is poised to be capped in Townsville after hulking prop Massimo De Lutiis was named on the bench to face Japan.

Les Kiss, in his second game in charge, has also recalled fly half Carter Gordon at Declan Meredith's expense.

With Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii injured, he has given Isaac Henry a starting debut at outside centre a week after he earned his first minutes in a tight Osaka defeat of Eddie Jones's side.

Lukhan Salakaia-Loto's Test return has also been secured, the Queensland Reds firebrand set to partner Lachlan Shaw — in his starting debut — in the second row, with Jeremy Williams on the bench and Josh Canham rested.

The Kiss era has begun, and new coach Les is seeking the 'Wallaby way' The new Wallabies era under Les Kiss began with a win in tough conditions against an improving nation, but coach Les Kiss wants more than just wins to be the legacy of his tenure.

Kiss has also shaken up the back row, with Charlie Cale and Carlo Tizzano to partner skipper Harry Wilson, leaving Fraser McReight on the bench and Rob Valetini out of the 23.

Brandon Paenga-Amosa will get his chance under Kiss as replacement hooker while Filipo Daugunu has also been included on the bench as backline cover.

Angus Bell and Taniela Tupou also return to the starting side after stirring second-half cameos in Osaka, while the back three are unchanged and Tate McDermott and Ben Donaldson again provide play-making options on the bench.

It continues the theme of Kiss's tenure, with the new coach keen to assess his options before a long run of Tests ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

"The coaches have looked to find some balance in the selection after what was a physically taxing Test week in the heat in Japan," Kiss said.

"The whole group has worked hard this week and we know where we need to improve.

"This Saturday in Townsville gives us an opportunity to grow and strengthen our game on home soil in front of our supporters."

Gordon impressed at fly half against Ireland, before missing the next two Tests with a calf injury.

Meredith started in the past three Tests alongside Brumbies clubmate Ryan Lonergan, who has been retained the starting scrum half role.

WALLABIES (1-15): Angus Bell, Josh Nasser, Taniela Tupou, Lachlan Shaw, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Charlie Cale, Carlo Tizzano, Harry Wilson, Ryan Lonergan, Carter Gordon, Harry Potter, Hunter Paisami, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright.

BENCH (16-23): Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Jeremy Williams, Fraser McReight, Tate McDermott, Ben Donaldson, Filipo Daugunu

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the second Test between the Wallabies and Japan on Saturday afternoon from 2pm (AEST).

AAP

World.title: Why Ukraine's strikes on Russia could come with dire consequences
World.content:
Ukraine has been firing drones hundreds of kilometres into Russian territory almost every day since June.

The attacks have hit oil refineries, other critical infrastructure and more recently, warehouses belonging to Russia's version of Amazon.

Even Siberia is no longer out of reach; the long-range, sophisticated drones have travelled more than 2,000 kilometres to target energy facilities.

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his aim was to make ordinary Russians feel the pain of the war by crippling the country's economy and disrupting everyday life.

But some analysts argue there is a risk the strategy could backfire and give Russian President Vladimir Putin an excuse to escalate fighting and galvanise public support for the war.

Loading...

Ukraine has become increasingly aggressive in attacking its neighbour in recent weeks.

Kyiv carried out one of its deadliest strikes on Sunday night, killing at least 13 people, including a child. Russian authorities said they shot down 456 Ukrainian drones during the attack, but some got through and hit an oil refinery and a hostel in the city of Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,000km east of Moscow.

Last week, seven people were killed on a busy beach in southern Russia when a Ukrainian drone was intercepted and crashed.

"It seems like Ukraine is in quite a precarious situation … this sort of a strategy is one of last resort, because Ukraine has its back against the wall," Marina Miron, from the Department of Defence Studies at King's College London, said.

Ukraine has attempted to justify the strikes by arguing they are a response to Russia's bombardments of civilian targets in its cities, which have also increased recently.

If the goal is to put pressure on Russia's economy, the campaign has been working, London's Royal United Services Institute associate fellow Charles Hecker said.

"It's been effective on a number of fronts. It continues to take the Russians by surprise and to remind them that their air defences are surprisingly weak," he said.

"The damage that Ukraine has done to Russian energy capacity is really quite significant. Oil refining capacity in Russia is now down by about 20 per cent."

Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks On the outskirts of Russian cities, warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer are being struck by Kyiv's drones, with some analysts saying it could lead to a financial crisis.

Repeated strikes on oil facilities mean long queues at petrol stations have been a common sight around Russia this summer.

Hecker said while there was no question Russia was under crushing economic pressure from the attacks on its energy infrastructure, predictions of the impending collapse in the Russian economy were "probably exaggerated".

But Ukraine's assault on Russia's largest online marketplace, Wildberries, a company often compared to Amazon, is making the cost of the war harder for ordinary Russians to ignore.

'People could be saying, Putin was right all along'

More than 20 Wildberries warehouses have been hit by Ukraine, which said the company was a legitimate wartime target because it sold military equipment.

The retail giant's reach in Russia is huge. It is used by 79 million people each month and accounts for about 2 per cent of the country's GDP.

New Eurasian Strategies Centre head of foreign policy John Lough said there was a chance the strategy could backfire.

"It is a real possibility that a section of the Wildberries consumer base will say, yeah, we should be fighting this war more aggressively," he said.

"They could also say we shouldn't have allowed this to happen because the Ukrainians did this to us with the support of their Western partners and we understand what Putin's saying, that we are at war with the so-called collective West."

Loading

Even inside Ukraine, the long-range drone strategy has its critics. Some of the country's opposition MPs are questioning whether it is worth the risk.

They argue Ukraine's drone strikes in Russia are provoking Moscow to retaliate with a more destructive response.

Miron warned the campaign could backfire on Zelenskyy and potentially rally more Russians behind Putin.

"One portion of the [Russian] population might be dissatisfied and afraid [because of the attacks], the other portion of the population, which was neutral or perhaps against the war, might now be supporting the war," she said.

"People could be saying, Putin was right all along, they're attacking Wildberries. It's a civilian target, so this can be perfectly used by the Russian government to convince the population of the righteous cause of the war."

As Ukraine has taken the war deeper into Russia, Moscow's response has been swift. It has targeted critical infrastructure such as the Odesa Port, which has been struck repeatedly, suspending vital shipping and threatening one of Ukraine's economic lifelines.

Associate professor and senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Perth's Edith Cowan University, Alexey Muraviev, told ABC News Radio that Russia's strikes were causing massive problems in Ukraine.

"Russia are systematically destroying petrol stations, certainly in Ukraine's east, which also causes enormous problems with people refuelling, and they are targeting bridges and railway systems," he said.

"So Ukraine is actually [receiving] more damage in addition to now-growing international criticism while Russian civilian casualties are actually increasing."

While Russia was attacking Ukraine's cities and hitting civilian infrastructure such as apartment buildings long before Kyiv's latest campaign, things have escalated lately.

Earlier this month, the United Nations said there had been a "disturbing escalation" in civilians deaths, with hundreds killed and thousands injured in Ukraine this summer.

Kyiv is also grappling with a critical shortage of interceptor missies.

"A few days ago, Putin hurled buckets of ballistic missiles at Kyiv and Ukraine wasn't able to shoot them down," Hecker said.

" That's when Ukraine suffered a very large spike in civilian casualties. "

Ukraine said it had received only a third of the air defences from its allies this year, compared to the same period last year.

"That situation is really quite desperate," Hecker said.

Analysts said Ukraine's increasing drone strikes could be an attempt to pressure Putin back to the negotiating table in a bid to end the war. So far, there is little indication of that happening.

Zelenskyy's strategy of making Russians feel the war more is working. What is less clear is whether the pain his own people are feeling will pay off in any way.

World.title: Qld child safety minister axes key survey of children in care
World.content:
Queensland's child safety minister said she "had no hesitation" in axing a key survey, that she previously lauded as integral.

The My Life in Care Survey has been conducted every year since 2022, but minister Amanda Camm today confirmed it had been quashed.

This despite her once labelling the survey as a "cornerstone" of the Government's approach to tackling the broken child safety system, and proof that it was "on the right track".

The outcomes of the 2024 survey were tabled as part of a submission to the now-finalised Child Safety Inquiry.

Ms Camm's comments were in a draft foreword as part of that submission.

The outcomes of the 2024 survey were tabled as part of a submission to the now-finalised Child Safety Inquiry. (ABC News: Daryna Zadvirna)

"We will use what we learn from the My Life in Care survey each year to check on our progress, assess the impact of our reforms and continually refine our approach," Ms Camm said.

The survey asks teens and children a number of questions, including their background, how they felt coming into care versus how they felt now, whether they felt that had sufficient privacy, safety and security and felt cared for.

In 2024, nearly 1,000 youths between the ages of 10 and 18 responded to the survey, and 88 children aged between five and nine responded.

It stated in that year, 40 per cent of children aged between 10 and 18 had made a complaint about their time in care, of those, 39 per cent were unhappy with how their report was handled.

But Ms Camm said the survey wasn't an accurate representation of the experiences of children in care, pointing out the survey stated 67 per cent felt happy in care.

"The Children in Care census outlined the real facts of children in care and the fact that over 69% of children coming into care had suffered more than three types of abuse," she said.

"This survey painted a picture of a child safety system, one that was full of happy emojis," she said.

She then showed the front of the 2024 survey which contained emojis.

Amanda Camm showed the 2024 report. (ABC News)

Ms Camm also said that children, under the former Labor government had been "bribed" to complete the survey.

Previously, children were given vouchers to grocery stores if they completed the survey.

The Opposition said it was in line with advice from the Queensland Family and Child Commission, stating the views of young people "should be compensated accordingly" through "gift cards, travel subsidies, formal recognition of participation and in-kind renumeration, such as skills building".

Child safety worker union alarmed by possible removal of key reporting tool The union representing child safety workers in Queensland has highlighted concerns about the possible removal of a key reporting tool.

But Ms Camm said it was "unacceptable".

"I will not be guided by a survey that was conducted where children were bribed to answer the survey and given money to answer the survey," Ms Camm said.

"So, I make no apology for axing that."

The removal of the My Life in Care survey removes a complaint mechanism for children in care, despite the state's peak child safety oversight body calling for more to be put in place.

The Queensland Family and Child Commission's Too Little, Too Late report outlines the state's "narrow focus" on the complaints process; reporting that children "fear speaking up about their workers and providers, and [hold] cynicism that their worries would be acted on".

World.title: Recently arrived teenager wins Scrabble world title for Australia
World.content:
Dineth Fernando has only been in Australia for less than a year and has already brought home a world youth title for his country.

The 14-year-old took out the World Youth Scrabble Championship in Nairobi this week, beating out 140 competitors from across the world.

Dineth, who originally hails from Sri Lanka, credits the win to a steady diet of practising 200 words a day from the board game's official dictionary.

"All the hard work paid off," Dineth said.

Prior to the youth championship, Dineth Fernando played against Adam Logan, who won the World Scrabble Championship in 2025. (Supplied: Prasanna Fernando)

The Melbourne-based teenager, for whom English is his second language, said the game has helped him find his feet in Australia and make friends.

He said he got into the game when he was eight years of age through school. He took a liking to the game, competing in national championships in 2022 and 2024.

In July this year he won the Australian Youth Scrabble Championship, inspiring him to compete at the world youth event.

He says Scrabble is very popular in Sri Lanka because of competitions held between schools.

Around 140 competitors featured at the event in the Kenyan capital Nairobi. (Supplied: Prasanna Fernando)

"There are school Scrabble clubs and it's extremely competitive," Dineth said.

" There are a tonne of youth players who study really hard daily for tournaments and they aim to go to the national team. "

While he has achieved a great feat in a language game, Dineth hopes to be a doctor one day and said he had an interest in mathematics and science.

His father, Prasanna Fernado, who was a medical doctor in Sri Lanka, said the family moved to Australia in February this year owing to his study and work.

Mr Fernando said he was very proud of his son winning the championship, especially given the 25 hours of flying time to the Kenyan capital which was at times threatened by the war between the US and Iran.

"It feels as if its a dream," Mr Fernando said.

"I knew that he would one day win it, but its still surreal.

"At the last moment I thought we would take the risk and the two of us would go. So luckily it paid off and I'm delighted about it."

He also credits his coach Rashid Sudin, who worked with Dineth for several years.

Australian competitive Scrabble relatively underdeveloped

Mr Fernando said countries like Sri Lanka, India, Pakistan, Malaysia and Thailand encourage the game because of its benefits in academics and sportsmanship.

He said in contrast Australia did not have much school-level Scrabble.

Youth Australia Scrabbler Players Association president Tony Hunt said just one school in Australia had Scrabble as a part of the curriculum, Cabramatta Public School in Sydney's south-west.

He said some gifted and talented programs in Victoria offered Scrabble as an extension activity.

Mr Hunt said he would like to see the board game rolled out into more schools.

"We want other people to think of it as a sport, but a sport that addresses literacy and numeracy," Mr Hunt said.

"We would like educators to consider Scrabble as an extension activity for [gifted and talented] kids. Number one, they're going to be good at it, and number two, they're going to like it."

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day seven of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Court reporter Clare Sibthorpe and I will be bringing you the latest from the hearing today.

If day seven looks familiar, you’re right. Yesterday was to be the seventh day of the trial, but the Crown foreshadowed that it wanted to amend seven of the charges in the case. This triggered an adjournment for the parties to make legal arguments.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Thursday. Oscar Colman

After hearing those arguments, Judge Glenn Walsh said the Crown did not require the court’s permission to make the changes, which do not relate to the alleged physical acts in the case. He concluded that it did not result in prejudice to Jones and his right to a fair trial.

Jones’ lawyers did not object to an amendment to one of the charges but had opposed the amendments to the remaining six.

The trial is expected to resume in earnest today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre building with more evidence relating to complainant “J”, the first witness to give evidence in the trial.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12. Jones denies the claims.

On Tuesday, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they say he told them about the alleged assaults.

His brother said he had not witnessed Jones acting inappropriately towards “J”, but that the complainant told him in 2024, after Jones’ arrest, that he was one the men who had come forward.

The ex-girlfriend of “J” said he confided in her 20 years ago that Jones had touched him inappropriately. She said he looked like he had “seen a ghost” before he made the disclosure and swore her to secrecy.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Queensland’s under-fire minister for domestic violence has refused to provide an update on key reforms to protect at-risk women and children, days after another woman was allegedly murdered by a former partner in Brisbane. Minister Amanda Camm, whose portfolios cover domestic and family violence and child safety, on Thursday announced $3.3 million for DV services to support referrals and assessments. The boost comes a month after Camm was forced to defend the government’s decision to cut nearly $40 million in funding from the sector in its latest budget, which was exposed following the alleged murder of another woman west of Brisbane. Under-fire Minister for Domestic and Family Violence Amanda Camm refused to provide an update on key reforms for victim-survivors and at-risk women on Thursday. Courtney Kruk Camm deflected questions about government spending and said the LNP had made a record investment into domestic and family violence.



“We’re also getting our fair share of Commonwealth investment, which we haven’t seen in other parts and other portfolios. Related Article Exclusive

Queensland government Taskforce chair worries LNP has ‘abandoned’ key DV recommendations “So that’s my job as minister – being able to ensure that Queenslanders have confidence that we are investing in the things that matter.” The minister was also asked for an update on the Women’s Safety and Justice Taskforce recommendations, and a figure showing how many had been implemented to date. World.title: Private equity company set to buy controlling stake in Melbourne Storm
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Private equity company set to buy controlling stake in Melbourne Storm Adrian Proszenko August 13, 2026 — 1:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A private equity firm that became the first private investor in tennis’ ATP tour is poised to become a part-owner of the Melbourne Storm. EQT, a Swedish firm with more than $333 billion in assets under management, is close to completing a deal that will result in it buying a controlling share of the Storm, according to the Australian Financial Review. The Melbourne Storm, and their star man Cameron Munster, remain valuable propositions. Getty Images This masthead contacted Storm chairman and co-owner Matt Tripp, who said he couldn’t comment because he was bound by a non-disclosure agreement. Storm CEO Justin Rodski was also contacted for comment. The Storm are one of the most successful clubs in the NRL and one of only a handful that are privately owned. Tripp has previously made no secret of his desire to raise additional capital at a time when the value of NRL clubs, courtesy of a $5.3 billion broadcast deal, is at an all-time high.



Current owners Tripp, Bart Campbell, Gerry Ryan, Tom Carroll and Brett Ralph engaged investment bank Jeffries last year to run the sale process. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to confidentiality clauses said that a firm linked to an Australian sporting icon was among the interested parties. However, EQT – which claims to be the second-biggest private equity firm in the world based on capital raised – is likely to be the latest co-owner of the franchise. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images Some estimates have valued the Storm at between $150-$200 million, a figure that places the club at the top end of Australian sporting franchises along with Collingwood in the AFL and the Brisbane Broncos in the NRL. The AFR reported that the Storm had delivered $40 million in revenue up to October 31, according to its statutory accounts. Tripp – who owns a 33 per cent stake in the club – has previously stated that the current Storm owners had no interest in selling out, and that he was committed to remaining its chairman.

World.title: NeuroScientific locks in key US FDA meeting
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears NeuroScientific locks in key US FDA meeting Murray Ward August 13, 2026 — 1:12pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Perth-based biotech NeuroScientific Biopharmaceuticals has bagged a crucial meeting with the United States Food & Drug Administration (FDA) as it looks to push its patented “StemSmart” technology into a Phase 2 clinical trial in the lucrative US market. The company says the Pre-Investigational New Drug, or Pre-IND, meeting has been scheduled for August 31 and represents a critical regulatory step towards testing its treatment for refractory Crohn’s disease on American patients. The meeting will see the powerful US federal agency review the clinical, scientific and product development plan for StemSmart to ensure it is up to scratch for a formal IND submission. Getting early feedback from the FDA is a well-trodden path for biotech hopefuls as it can de-risk the expensive and lengthy approvals process and ensure the planned trial design meets the regulator’s exacting standards. NeuroScientific Biopharmaceuticals has locked in a Pre-Investigational New Drug meeting with the US Federal Drug Administration ahead of its Phase 2 trial for its StemSmart product in treating Crohn’s disease. NeuroScientific says it plans to submit its full IND application for approval by the end of this calendar year. The company’s StemSmart product is a stem cell technology platform derived from adult human donor bone marrow-sourced mesenchymal stem cells. It is manufactured using a patented process designed to improve the cells’ therapeutic activity and control the inflammatory immune responses often associated with severe and chronic inflammatory conditions such as Crohn’s disease.



‘Outcomes from the Pre-IND meeting will strengthen our ongoing Phase 2 clinical trial preparatory activities.’ NeuroScientific Biopharmaceuticals chief executive officer Nathan Smith The initial target is refractory Crohn’s disease, a severe and treatment-resistant form of inflammatory bowel disease. For patients who have exhausted other options, the condition can be seriously debilitating creating a significant unmet clinical need. The global market for Crohn’s disease treatments is estimated to be worth well in excess of US$10 billion (A$14.2 billion) annually underscoring the commercial opportunity for new and effective therapies. NeuroScientific chief executive officer Nathan Smith said: “Our upcoming Pre-IND meeting with the US FDA marks an important milestone in NSB’s clinical development for our patented StemSmart™ technology platform. Interfacing with the FDA on the development of StemSmart at this time is critical to ensuring that the planned clinical trial design is of a standard to support clinical translation of the product.” The company is not going into its discussions with the FDA cold. It says early indications from a previous Special Access Program (SAP) trial in fistulising Crohn’s disease suggested its StemSmart product was potent, effective and safe. All five patients in the trial showed improvement following treatment, with no serious adverse events recorded marking a strong outcome in a group typically resistant to conventional therapies.



The upcoming Phase 2 trial is planned to evaluate the safety and preliminary efficacy of the treatment in patients in both Australia and the US suffering from refractory and/or fistulising Crohn’s disease. For any biotech company, getting a product in front of the US FDA is a significant moment. The American market is by far the largest and most valuable pharmaceutical market in the world, and a green light from its regulator is a globally recognised seal of approval. With an August date now locked in, NeuroScientific is one step closer to potentially tapping that market. The outcome of the August meeting with the FDA will help set the agenda and requirements for the company’s up coming Phase 2 trial and importantly, its commercial pathway in the months ahead. “We are calmly and methodically working through those recommendations,” she told reporters on Thursday. “The way we are prioritising those recommendations is in line with our government’s delivery plan … We will provide that update to Queenslanders in a timely manner.” Asked why the Crisafulli government was working through domestic and family violence reforms slowly when it was able to rush “adult crime, adult time” legislation through within months of taking office, Camm said Queenslanders had endorsed harsher penalties to criminalise children. “Domestic and family violence is complex … and we have seen the complexity of it grow in our communities,” she said.



“Ensuring that our responses and our delivery is keeping pace with the changing complexity of domestic and family violence is critical, and that is why I will not be rushed in providing that update.” Related Article Updated

Domestic violence Swift backlash after Hanson says domestic violence a ‘two-way street’ On Wednesday, a 27-year-old woman from Woody Point was allegedly killed by her former partner, Logan man Ronald Cora, at a home in Slacks Creek, Logan. Four women have died in alleged domestic-violence-related incidents in Queensland in the past two months. Sherele Moody, the founder of Australian Femicide Watch, which tracks women and children killed by violence, said the incident brought the national toll of Australian women killed this year to 45.



Last year, 79 women were lost to violence. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Private equity company set to buy controlling stake in Melbourne Storm
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Private equity company set to buy controlling stake in Melbourne Storm Adrian Proszenko August 13, 2026 — 1:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A private equity firm that became the first private investor in tennis’ ATP tour is poised to become a part-owner of the Melbourne Storm. EQT, a Swedish firm with more than $333 billion in assets under management, is close to completing a deal that will result in it buying a controlling share of the Storm, according to the Australian Financial Review. The Melbourne Storm, and their star man Cameron Munster, remain valuable propositions. Getty Images This masthead contacted Storm chairman and co-owner Matt Tripp, who said he couldn’t comment because he was bound by a non-disclosure agreement. Storm CEO Justin Rodski was also contacted for comment. The Storm are one of the most successful clubs in the NRL and one of only a handful that are privately owned. Tripp has previously made no secret of his desire to raise additional capital at a time when the value of NRL clubs, courtesy of a $5.3 billion broadcast deal, is at an all-time high.



Current owners Tripp, Bart Campbell, Gerry Ryan, Tom Carroll and Brett Ralph engaged investment bank Jeffries last year to run the sale process. Sources speaking on the condition of anonymity due to confidentiality clauses said that a firm linked to an Australian sporting icon was among the interested parties. However, EQT – which claims to be the second-biggest private equity firm in the world based on capital raised – is likely to be the latest co-owner of the franchise. Sualauvi Fa’alogo celebrates a try for Melbourne. Getty Images Some estimates have valued the Storm at between $150-$200 million, a figure that places the club at the top end of Australian sporting franchises along with Collingwood in the AFL and the Brisbane Broncos in the NRL. The AFR reported that the Storm had delivered $40 million in revenue up to October 31, according to its statutory accounts. Tripp – who owns a 33 per cent stake in the club – has previously stated that the current Storm owners had no interest in selling out, and that he was committed to remaining its chairman.

World.title: Ngāi Tahu unveils South Island council boundary plan
World.content:
Ngāi Tahu has unveiled a plan to reorganise the South Island's council boundaries, replacing the 24 councils within its rohe with five bigger ones aligned to major river catchments.

The iwi has lodged a Head Start proposal after the government asked councils to submit amalgamation plans by 9 August or have one imposed on them.

Ngāi Tahu was not invited to submit a proposal, but kaiwhakahaere Justin Tipa said the conversation was too important to sit on the sidelines.

"As an iwi whose takiwā spans most of Te Waipounamu, we have a unique perspective on the opportunities and challenges facing our communities. We've stepped back and looked at the South Island as a whole and asked what kind of local government would best serve future generations.

"A lot of the discussion to date has focused on where the lines should be drawn between urban and rural communities but council boundaries need to be at the right scale to deal with the challenges in front of us… planning around natural water catchments is simply a better way of managing systems and communities that are already connected."

The five councils would be supported by locally elected boards and a South Island-wide shared services entity, Ngāi Tahu said.

Ngāi Tahu has unveiled a plan to reorganise the South Island's council boundaries. Supplied

The iwi said the proposal would help counter the pressures of rising infrastructure costs, climate change, unequal population growth and high rates bills, while keeping a strong voice for local communities.

Tipa said smaller councils were being asked to tackle complex and expensive infrastructure challenges that were difficult to manage alone.

"Rather than every council trying to build that capability on its own, our proposal would create a takiwā wide shared services entity, giving councils access to specialist skills and expertise that would otherwise be difficult or expensive to maintain."

One of the most significant changes would be the creation of a large council encompassing Christchurch, Selwyn, Waimakariri, Hurunui and Kaikōura - areas which were experiencing similar growth and infrastructure pressures, Ngāi Tahu said.

Tipa said people would continue to elect representatives and make decisions about the future of their districts and cities, with democratic local government at the plan's core.

"We don't pretend to have all the answers. These ideas will need to be tested, refined, and strengthened as the conversation develops.

"But if local government reform is going to succeed, we need to be ambitious and prepared to seize the opportunities in front of us. Our focus is on what will best serve the people of Te Waipounamu, now and for generations to come."

Ten other Head Start proposals have been submitted by the South Island's 27 councils, including a vast new unitary authority spanning the central and eastern parts of the Mainland and two conflicting models for Southland.

Approved plans will be signed off in 2027, with changes expected to take effect from the 2028 local elections.
